Prologue: One loan, two answers.

On the eleventh of April, twenty twenty four, at ten o'clock in the morning, the Court of Appeal handed down a judgment remotely. Its front page records the time. The case was BlackRock HoldCo Five versus H M R C, decided by the Court of Appeal in twenty twenty four. H M R C means His Majesty's Revenue and Customs.

The case was about one set of loans, worth about four billion dollars, made inside one group of companies. Two rules of United Kingdom corporation tax looked at those loans. The first rule asked what strangers would have done, and it found nothing wrong. The second rule asked why the borrower had borrowed, and it took away every pound of the interest deductions. The taxpayer won the first argument and lost the case.

This prologue tells that story and then stops. It opens a book written for the Chartered Tax Adviser Advanced Technical paper, Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups. The law throughout is the law for the financial year twenty twenty six. You met the basic loan relationship rules, and group relief, in The Living Law, chapters twenty one and twenty four. Here the same rules meet a group on a far larger scale.

A British link in an American chain.

In two thousand and nine, the BlackRock group bought the business of Barclays Global Investors. Part of the money for that acquisition travelled down a chain of companies formed in Delaware. Each was a limited liability company, and the judgments number them like stepping stones. The one that matters is L L C Five.

L L C Five was a Delaware company. But it was managed and controlled in the United Kingdom, so for corporation tax it was a company resident here. Its American parent, L L C Four, put cash and shares into it. In return, L L C Four took ordinary shares and loan notes worth about four billion dollars. L L C Five then put the money and shares into the next company down the chain, L L C Six, and took preference shares. L L C Six used the funds towards the purchase.

Picture the chain as a sandwich. American bread on top, American bread underneath, and one British filling in the middle. The filling had a very particular taste.

Look at L L C Five's tax position. Its income was the dividends on its preference shares, and those dividends were exempt from United Kingdom tax. Its expense was the interest on the loan notes. Under the loan relationship rules, that interest was a deductible debit. So each year L L C Five had no taxable income and a large deficit. It surrendered that deficit, as group relief, to other BlackRock companies in the United Kingdom, without asking for payment. They set it against their own profits.

Commentators put the deductions claimed at about six hundred and fifty four million pounds. H M R C refused them. It gave two reasons. The first was transfer pricing. The second was the unallowable purpose rule. The case climbed through three courts. On each rule the answer changed at least once.

What strangers would have done.

Start with transfer pricing. The rules now live in Part four of the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act. They apply when two connected parties make a deal on terms that differ from the terms independent parties would have agreed. If the actual terms give one side a United Kingdom tax advantage, that side is taxed as if the arm's length terms had applied. The arm's length deal can even be no deal at all, where strangers would never have done business.

H M R C argued exactly that. No independent lender, it said, would have lent four billion dollars to L L C Five on those terms.

The First-tier Tribunal disagreed. Judge John Brooks gave its decision on the third of November, twenty twenty. He found that an independent lender would have made loans of the same amount, on the same interest terms. There was one condition. A stranger would have demanded covenants, the promises a borrower gives to protect its lender. The tribunal found those covenants would have been given.

The Upper Tribunal reversed him. Mr Justice Michael Green and Judge Rupert Jones decided the appeal on the nineteenth of July, twenty twenty two. They held that you cannot import covenants that never existed in the real deal. Without them, the comparison failed, and H M R C won.

Then the Court of Appeal reversed the Upper Tribunal. The court was Lord Justice Peter Jackson, Lord Justice Nugee and Lady Justice Falk, and Lady Justice Falk gave the main judgment. Her reasoning ran like this. In the real deal, the lender belonged to the same group as everyone else in the chain. A stranger lending to L L C Five would face risks the group lender did not face. Other companies in the group might act in ways that damaged the loan. An independent lender would protect itself against that, so the hypothetical deal must include the protection. The covenants were part of a fair comparison, not an invention. The tribunal's finding was restored.

So on transfer pricing, BlackRock won. The interest was priced at a level strangers would have accepted.

Commentators read one passage of Lady Justice Falk's judgment as a hint. H M R C might have done better by looking at the borrower's side. Would L L C Five, if it were independent, have wanted to borrow at all? That argument was not run, and the case did not decide it. Chapter twenty seven returns to it.

Why this company borrowed.

The unallowable purpose rule is in section four four one of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act. It works like this. If a loan relationship has an unallowable purpose in a period, the debits are disallowed. Only the share attributable to that purpose goes, on a just and reasonable apportionment.

A purpose is unallowable if it is not among the company's business or other commercial purposes. A tax avoidance purpose can count as commercial, but only if it is not the main purpose, or one of the main purposes. And the tax advantage need not be the company's own. A tax advantage for any other person counts too.

The First-tier Tribunal found that L L C Five had two main purposes. One was commercial. The other was to obtain a tax advantage. But it apportioned all the debits to the commercial purpose, so everything stayed deductible. The Upper Tribunal disagreed. It treated the commercial benefit as a by-product of a decision driven by tax, and it apportioned all the debits to the tax purpose.

The Court of Appeal agreed with the Upper Tribunal's result, though not with all of its reasoning. Purpose, it was common ground, is a question of the company's own subjective intention. The court began with a plain question. Why did L L C Five enter into the loans? The answer was to obtain a tax advantage.

The court did not say that every deductible interest payment is suspect. Lady Justice Falk was careful on this. A company's awareness that interest is deductible does not make tax a main purpose. Nor does the size of the deduction, on its own. Something more is needed. Here there was more. L L C Five's board did see a commercial margin, because dividends in would exceed interest out. But the tax advantage belonged to the group, and the group's plan was why L L C Five was there. In the words Lord Justice Nugee repeated from Lady Justice Falk's judgment, taking the loans to secure that advantage was the company's sole raison d'être.

Then came the apportionment. The court asked what the debits would have been but for the tax purpose. The answer was nothing, because without the tax advantage the loans would not have been made. So all the debits were attributable to the unallowable purpose, and none was deductible. The approach echoes an earlier Court of Appeal case, Fidex, from twenty sixteen.

BlackRock asked the Supreme Court for permission to appeal. Lord Hodge, Lord Hamblen and Lady Simler refused it, because the appeal did not raise an arguable point of law. The refusal appeared on a list in the autumn of twenty twenty four. The Court of Appeal's judgment stands.

Why one loan can get two answers.

Here is the heart of it. The two rules ask different questions, so they can give different answers about the same loan.

Transfer pricing is a valuer's question. It looks at the terms and compares them with a market of strangers. It does not ask why the group did the deal. A loan can pass that test even if tax was the whole reason for it.

The unallowable purpose rule is a detective's question. It looks at motive. It does not care whether the interest rate was fair. A loan can pass the market test perfectly and still fail on purpose.

That leads to a common misconception. Many people believe that if an intra-group loan is priced at arm's length, the interest is safe. It is not. Arm's length pricing gets you through the first gate. It says nothing about the second.

BlackRock was not alone. Within weeks the Court of Appeal decided two more cases on the same rule. Kwik-Fit came on the third of May, twenty twenty four, and was about an internal reorganisation of loans so that trapped losses could be used. J T I Acquisition Company came on the thirteenth of June, twenty twenty four, and concerned borrowing to fund a real acquisition. In J T I the court treated the tax advantage as bolted on to a commercial deal, and still disallowed everything. H M R C won all three. The Supreme Court refused permission in all three on the same list. Chapter twelve tells the other two stories and the case still working its way up.

There is also a gate that BlackRock's loans never had to pass. They were made in two thousand and nine. The corporate interest restriction arrived later, for periods of account starting on or after the first of April, twenty seventeen. It caps a group's net interest deductions in the United Kingdom, usually at thirty per cent of tax E B I T D A. E B I T D A stands for earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Below a de minimis of two million pounds a year, there is no restriction. A group borrowing like this today, in the financial year twenty twenty six, would meet all three gates. Chapter twenty eight teaches the third.

The questions this book asks.

This one loan leads straight into the four questions that run through the book.

First, is a group one taxpayer or many? L L C Five was a separate company with its own return. Yet its purpose was read through the group's plan, and its deficit was used by other companies through group relief. The law treated it as one company when that suited the rule, and as part of a group when that told the truth.

Second, where are profits made, and what stops them drifting? A British link in an American chain created a United Kingdom deduction with no matching United Kingdom income. Much of this book is about the rules that watch borders.

Third, what does the law follow? The accounts, the deal, or its own purpose? The loan relationship rules start from the accounts. Transfer pricing tests the deal against the market. The unallowable purpose rule overrides both when the purpose is wrong.

Fourth, what must a group's tax function spot? An adviser who checked only the interest rate would have missed the point that decided the case. The examiner wants you to identify the issues, all of them, and know which specialist rule answers each one.

So when you meet an intra-group loan, in practice or in the exam, ask three things. Are the terms what strangers would agree? Why did this company borrow? And how much of the group's interest can the United Kingdom take, in total? Chapter twenty seven answers the first, chapter twelve the second, and chapter twenty eight the third.

Most of this book follows an invented group of companies, Tarnmoor, whose story begins in chapter one. Everything about Tarnmoor is made up. BlackRock is real, and so is every rule in this prologue.

Next comes the introduction, and a map of the ground ahead.


Introduction.

The prologue followed one loan through three courts and found two answers. Keep that picture in mind, because it is a fair picture of the ground ahead. A larger company is not a small company with more noughts on the end. It borrows from its own relatives. It owns companies that own companies. It trades across borders, reports to investors, and answers to a board that must publish its approach to tax. Almost every rule you met in The Living Law still applies to it. But around those rules sits a second layer of law, written for scale.

This introduction is a map. It sets out the four questions the book keeps asking, the paper the book serves, the way the chapters are arranged, the invented group whose story carries the law, and how the two editions of each chapter work. It ends with some advice on using the book alongside the question practice you already have. The law throughout is the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, under the Finance Act twenty twenty six.

Five ways the larger company is different.

The first difference is scale. Size switches rules on. A company with profits above one and a half million pounds pays its tax in instalments, and above twenty million pounds it pays even earlier, both thresholds shared out among the companies it is associated with. A group with net interest above two million pounds a year meets the corporate interest restriction. Above two hundred million pounds of United Kingdom turnover, or two billion pounds of balance sheet, a group needs a senior accounting officer, a published tax strategy and a habit of telling H M R C, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, about uncertain positions. Above seven hundred and fifty million euros of consolidated revenue come country-by-country reports, transfer pricing records and the global minimum tax. Chapter one sets out that ladder, rung by rung.

The second difference is the group. United Kingdom law taxes each company separately. There is no group return for corporation tax. Yet a group plans, borrows and invests as one business, and the law builds bridges between its companies, with group relief for losses, tax-free transfers of assets, a shared allowance here and a shared threshold there. Each bridge has its own entry test, and the tests do not match.

The third difference is the border. A large group earns profits in many countries and moves money, goods, people and ideas between them. Most of the second half of this book is about the rules that decide where those profits are taxed, and the rules that stop them drifting to wherever tax is lowest.

The fourth difference is governance. A large company's tax is not only computed. It is managed, certified and reported. H M R C's large business directorate says it works with around two thousand of the largest businesses, and its customer compliance managers assess each group's tax risk and how well the group manages it. The law adds personal duties for a named officer and a criminal offence for failing to prevent the facilitation of tax evasion.

The fifth difference is the accounts. For a larger company the accounts are not a starting point that tax quickly leaves behind. They decide the timing of loan relationship profits, intangible asset profits and much else. And the accounts must also show a tax charge that investors read, current and deferred, which is a different number from the tax bill.

Four questions.

Those five differences produce four questions, and the book asks them in every chapter.

The first is this. Is a group one taxpayer or many? The law taxes each company on its own profits, yet it lets losses travel, assets move and gains be rolled over across the group. Where does it build those bridges, and where does it refuse? Chapters one, fifteen and seventeen carry this question furthest, and the interest restriction and the global minimum tax push it in a new direction.

The second is this. Where are profits made, and what stops them drifting? Residence, permanent establishments, treaties and the foreign branch exemption decide where profits are taxed. Transfer pricing, controlled foreign companies, hybrid mismatches, the interest restriction and the global minimum tax stop them moving to where they are not. Part Four of the book is built around this question.

The third is this. What does the law follow? The accounts, the deal, or its own purpose? Tax starts from the accounts. It respects many commercial transactions, such as share exchanges and demergers, on their own terms. And then, again and again, it asks why a company did something, and overrides both the accounts and the deal when the answer is tax. The prologue's loan was the first example. It will not be the last.

The fourth is this. How does a large group govern its tax, and what must an adviser spot? The Chartered Institute of Taxation says that candidates for this paper are not expected to have deep knowledge of all tax areas but should be able to identify what the potential tax issues are. So every chapter asks what the tax function must do, by when, and what a good adviser would flag.

The paper this book serves.

This book is written for the Chartered Tax Adviser Advanced Technical paper, Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups. Until twenty twenty three it was called Taxation of Major Corporates. The paper lasts three and a half hours. It normally has six questions, each worth ten, fifteen or twenty marks, and one hundred marks in total. The pass mark is fifty per cent.

The Institute describes its scenarios plainly. They will typically be based around multinational groups and larger companies that may be listed, with no individual controlling shareholders. So owner-managed companies, close company loans and profit extraction are not this paper's business, and they are not this book's either.

The syllabus has three elements. Corporation tax, including corporation tax on chargeable gains. Capital allowances. And stamp duty and stamp duty land tax, at awareness level. Within the corporation tax element, at least seventy per cent of the marks come from core material.

Core is a grade. The Institute's syllabus grid gives every topic a grade. Grade one is core, examined at depth, with computations. Grade two is non-core, where you need working knowledge and the main computation. Grade three is awareness, where you need to recognise the rule and state it. This book gives core topics full depth, non-core topics a working treatment, and awareness topics their principles. Each chapter's reading edition says which grade applies to what.

The grid this book follows is the twenty twenty six grid. As this book was finished, in October twenty twenty six, the Institute had not yet published a grid, a prospectus or tax tables for twenty twenty seven. The settled pattern is that the exams in one year test the Finance Act of the year before, so a sitting in twenty twenty seven should test the Finance Act twenty twenty six. The likely sitting is the fourth of May, twenty twenty seven, with the twenty sixth of October, twenty twenty seven, as the fallback. When the twenty twenty seven grid and tables appear, check them against what this book says.

The book also follows the paper's habits. Between May twenty twenty three and May twenty twenty six, every sitting had a corporation tax computation worth fifteen or twenty marks. Capital allowances appeared in nearly every paper. Groups and consortia came six times. Property gains and leases, and the shareholding exemption with reorganisations, came five times each. International questions, on residence, permanent establishments, the branch exemption or migration, have come at every sitting since November twenty twenty four. Controlled foreign companies came four times, transfer pricing five times, the interest restriction four times, and compliance and governance eight times. The longest chapters in this book sit where the marks have been.

How the book is built.

After this introduction come thirty two chapters in five Parts, then a conclusion and a note on sources.

Part One, The Larger Company, has four chapters. They ask what makes a company large and who counts as its group, where corporate tax law lives, how returns, payments and enquiries work for a large group, and how the law governs a group's tax through officers, strategies, disclosures and the anti-avoidance rules.

Part Two, Measuring Profit, has ten chapters. It starts with the accounts and deferred tax, builds the large company computation line by line, and then opens each line in turn. Plant and machinery. Buildings, fixtures, leasing and successions. Research and development. Intangible assets and intellectual property. Loan relationships and derivatives. Companies with investment business. And losses.

Part Three, The Group, has seven chapters. Group relief, consortia and joint ventures. Company gains on property and leases. Gains inside the group. Shares, the shareholding exemption, reorganisations and earn-outs. Reconstructions, demergers and distributions. Buying and selling companies. And stamp taxes for groups.

Part Four, Across Borders, has nine chapters. Where a company lives and how it leaves. Non-resident companies, permanent establishments and withholding. Treaties and double tax relief. The choice between a foreign branch and a subsidiary. Controlled foreign companies. Transfer pricing and advance pricing agreements. The corporate interest restriction. Hybrid mismatches. And the global minimum tax, with the end of diverted profits tax.

Part Five, Putting It Together, has two chapters. Chapter thirty one follows one acquisition through every relevant rule, the way a long examination question does. Chapter thirty two is about the craft of the paper itself, from the exam software to the layouts the examiners expect.

Where The Living Law ends.

This book assumes that you know The Living Law, the earlier book written for the Tax Knowledge and Skills paper. It does not teach those foundations twice. Where a chapter builds on one, it recaps it in one to three sentences and names the chapter, for example The Living Law, chapter twenty four, on groups. Then it goes further.

Going further means two things. Some topics The Living Law touched, such as group relief, loan relationships, research and development, company gains and the foreign branch exemption, are taught again here in full, because the Advanced Technical examiner expects mastery, not recall. And some topics The Living Law only signposted are taught here from first principles. Transfer pricing, controlled foreign companies, the interest restriction, hybrid mismatches, the global minimum tax, company migration, deferred tax and demergers all belong in that second group.

Tarnmoor, an invented group.

Most chapters follow one group of companies, Tarnmoor. Everything about Tarnmoor is invented for teaching. Its companies, its people, its numbers and its two overseas countries, Vallaria and Marrovia, are all made up. Ireland is real, and so are its twelve and a half per cent trading rate and its treaty with the United Kingdom, but Tarnmoor's Irish company is not.

Tarnmoor P L C, a public limited company, is a listed engineering group with its head office in Leeds and no controlling shareholder. It was built to match the examiner's description of a typical scenario, and to be large enough to switch on every regime the paper tests. Its main trading company makes industrial valves, actuators and pumps. Around it sit a property company, a treasury company, a joint venture, overseas subsidiaries, and the companies it buys and sells as the story runs.

The story begins in chapter one, when Tarnmoor buys Calder Valve Engineering for thirty two million pounds. If you have read The Living Law, you know Calder. It is the invented valve maker where Dan Hartley worked as an engineer, and his story continues here. So does his sister Jess's. Some years after the group's story begins, Tarnmoor buys her business, and chapter thirty one tells that deal.

Tarnmoor lives in Group Years, not calendar years. Group Years are Tarnmoor's accounting years to the thirty first of December. Group Year One is the year in which Calder joins, Group Year Two the next, and so on. No calendar year is ever attached to a Tarnmoor event, and every Tarnmoor computation applies the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, whichever Group Year the story has reached. There is a reason for that. Real rules start on real dates, such as accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. Where a chapter needs to teach a real commencement date, it uses a labelled example with real dates, outside the story. That keeps the story simple and the dates honest.

The story is the spine of the book, not its cage. When the examiner tests a variation the story never reaches, a chapter will say suppose, and work a labelled example. Those examples never become part of the story.

Two editions.

Every chapter comes in two editions.

The audio script is written to be heard once. Numbers are spoken as words, and worked examples are told as stories with a few memorable figures. Statutes are named in full the first time in each chapter and then given a short name. The Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine becomes the two thousand and nine Act, and the Corporation Tax Act twenty ten becomes the twenty ten Act. The Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten becomes the International Act. The Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act nineteen ninety two becomes the Gains Act. Long section numbers are said the way practitioners say them, so section eleven forty one, or section one seven one for no gain, no loss transfers, or section four four one for unallowable purpose. Abbreviations are spelled out first, and then spoken as separate letters where practitioners use letters, such as H M R C, or C F C for a controlled foreign company. Each script ends with a section called What to take away, a spoken recap of the rules and numbers to keep.

The reading edition is the same chapter for the page. It has digits, statutory references and case citations in their standard form, and it lays out every computation the way the examiner expects, with one unit in each table. It adds three kinds of box. A worked example box gives the full numbers behind each story. A going further box covers planning, the tax function's tasks and deadlines, and the interaction between regimes. And an exam lens box gives each topic's syllabus grade, its past appearances on the paper, what the examiners said, and the traps. Each reading edition ends with a table of key rules and figures and a list of statutory and case references.

Both editions use the same words for the status of a claim. The law says means the statute. The courts have held means case law. H M R C's view is means guidance, which is not law. Disputed, or being litigated, means what it says. Announced means a government statement. Proposed, not law, means a consultation or draft legislation that Parliament has not passed. And in our invented case means Tarnmoor.

How to use this book.

The book teaches. It does not test. There are no practice questions here, because you have the Institute's past papers and your own question bank, and those are the right tools for practice.

A good rhythm is this. Listen to a chapter for the story and the reasons. Then read its reading edition with a pen, working through each computation yourself. Then sit a past question on the same topic, under time, and mark it against the Institute's suggested answer and marking guide. Read the examiners' report for that sitting. From May twenty twenty four the Institute has also published example scripts, banded by mark. Comparing a scraped pass with a strong answer to the same question is one of the best lessons available, and chapter thirty two shows what to look for.

Practise on the student legislation product you will use on the day, Croner-i or Tolley, because in the exam the legislation is your only reference. And practise with the right numbers. The twenty twenty six tax tables, the only ones published as this book was finished, reflect the Finance Act twenty twenty five, with a main pool writing down allowance of eighteen per cent. The law this book teaches, and the law for a twenty twenty seven sitting, has fourteen per cent and a new forty per cent first-year allowance. When the twenty twenty seven tables appear, check every rate against them.

Finally, keep the status words in your ear. Several things described in this book are proposals, not law. A draft Finance Bill was published in July twenty twenty six, and a Budget is due on the twenty eighth of October, twenty twenty six. None of that changes the law for your sitting. The conclusion says what may be coming, and the note on sources says how to keep up.

So the book starts where Tarnmoor's story starts, on the first of April in Group Year One, with a family firm that becomes one company among many.


Part One: The Larger Company.

Chapter one: One company or many?

On the first of April, at the start of what our story will call Group Year One, a regional engineering business owned by one family stopped being a family firm. Calder Valve Engineering Limited woke up that morning as it had gone to bed. Same works, same three hundred staff, same order book. By lunchtime its shares belonged to Tarnmoor, an invented listed engineering group, which had paid thirty two million pounds for them.

Listeners to The Living Law have met Calder before. It is invented too, like every company and person in Tarnmoor's story. In The Living Law, chapter five, Calder was a company on its own, with no associated companies. It had taxable total profits of two million pounds and a corporation tax bill of five hundred thousand pounds, paid in four quarterly instalments of one hundred and twenty five thousand pounds. One company, one return, one bill.

Nothing in the purchase changed Calder's legal identity. It still computes its own profits, files its own return and owes its own tax. And yet, from that first of April, almost every number around it moves. The point at which it must pay tax early moves. The rules on how it prices its dealings with sister companies switch on. A board in Leeds now answers for its tax governance. Its interest costs are tested against a group it has never met.

So here is the question this chapter answers. When a company joins a large group, is it still one taxpayer among many, or has it become a small part of one large taxpayer? The short answer is both, and the skill of this paper lies in knowing which rule takes which view.

This is the first chapter of Part One, on the larger company. It sets up the whole book. It builds on The Living Law, chapter twenty, on the foundations of corporation tax, and chapter twenty four, on groups. No single syllabus row belongs to it. Instead it gives you two tools you will use in every later chapter, a ladder of size thresholds and a family of group definitions, and it introduces the invented group whose story runs through the book.

Meet Tarnmoor.

Tarnmoor P L C, a public limited company, is our invented parent company. It is incorporated in England, its head office is in Leeds, and its shares are listed on the main market of the London Stock Exchange. Nobody controls it. Its shareholders are pension funds, insurers and thousands of private investors. That shape is deliberate. The Chartered Institute of Taxation describes this paper in these words. Scenarios will typically be based around multinational groups and larger companies that may be listed, with no individual controlling shareholders. Tarnmoor is exactly that kind of group.

Under the parent sit the companies you will come to know. Tarnmoor Engineering Limited is the main trading company, making industrial valves, actuators and pumps. In Group Year One it sells six hundred and thirty million pounds of them. Tarnmoor Estates holds the group's property. Tarnmoor Finance is the treasury company, with five hundred and fifty million pounds of listed notes paying five and a half per cent. Tarnmoor Water Systems runs a water infrastructure business. There is a dormant company, Tarnmoor Pumps, that does nothing at all, and it will matter precisely because it does nothing.

Abroad, three companies carry the group across borders. Tarnmoor Vallaria makes and distributes valves in Vallaria. Tarnmoor Capital is a finance company in Marrovia. Both countries are invented, carried over from The Living Law. Tarnmoor Ireland is incorporated in Ireland, a real country, but its directors meet in Leeds, so for now it is resident in the United Kingdom. Finally there is Helmside Energy, a hydrogen joint venture formed on the first of January of Group Year One. Tarnmoor holds forty five per cent, an invented utility called Greyfell holds forty, and an invented infrastructure fund called Northlight holds fifteen.

Every company in the group draws up accounts to the thirty first of December, except Calder, which keeps its thirty first of March year end for now. Group Years are Tarnmoor's accounting years. We never attach a calendar year to them, and we run every computation on the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, whatever Group Year the story has reached.

In Group Year One, consolidated revenue is one thousand one hundred and eighty million pounds, and the group employs about six thousand people. Three invented people will guide us. Nadia Kerr is Tarnmoor's chief financial officer. Tom Hesketh is the group head of tax, and his team is where the book's questions land. Graham Pike is Calder's finance director, before and after the deal.

And one more person. Dan Hartley, a chartered engineer from The Living Law, works in Calder's process valves division. Listeners to chapters eight to ten of that book followed his commute, his benefits and his pay, and by now his long secondment to a client's plant on Teesside is over. They also know how his time at Calder ends. This book will show the company's side of that story. For now, Dan is about to be asked to give most of his time to a new research project.

Why one company stays one taxpayer.

The Living Law, chapter twenty, told how a company became a person in law, separate from those who own it. The leading case is Salomon versus A Salomon and Company Limited, decided by the House of Lords and reported in eighteen ninety seven. The Lords held that a properly formed company is a legal person distinct from its members, however its shares are held. Corporation tax, created by the Finance Act nineteen sixty five, was built on that foundation. The taxpayer is the company.

This is the separate entity principle. Each company in a group computes its own taxable total profits, for its own accounting periods, on its own return. Each pays its own tax. Each has its own losses, its own capital allowance pools, its own base costs in its own assets. If Tarnmoor Estates sells a building to Tarnmoor Engineering, two taxpayers have dealt with each other.

Why does the law insist on this, when a group plainly runs as one business? There are good reasons. Company law gives each company its own assets and debts, and its creditors look only to it. Groups change shape constantly, buying and selling companies, and a tax system based on the separate company follows those changes without reopening a consolidated position. Minority shareholders, like Greyfell and Northlight in Helmside, need each company's profit to be its own. And when a company is sold, the buyer inherits its tax history, which only makes sense if that history belongs to the company.

But the principle has costs. A loss in one company and a profit in another would both be taxed as if strangers held them. An asset moved between sisters would trigger a gain on paper, though nothing has left the group. So Parliament has built a toolkit of exceptions. Group relief lets current losses move between companies. Assets move between members of a gains group at no gain, no loss. Roll-over relief looks across the group. Stamp duty and stamp duty land tax spare transfers between companies under common ownership.

Notice the pattern. The United Kingdom never abandons the separate entity. It bridges it, rule by rule, and each bridge has its own conditions. Only in its newest rules, the corporate interest restriction and the global minimum tax, does the law begin to look at the group as a single economic unit. That tension, between many companies and one business, is the first of this book's great debates, and it returns in chapters fifteen, twenty eight and thirty.

The group's tax charge is not its tax bill.

Here is a misconception worth killing early. In The Living Law, chapter twenty four, the myth was that a group pays tax as one. A trainee at a large firm rarely believes that in its simple form. The grown-up version is subtler. It says that the tax charge in the consolidated accounts is the group's tax bill.

People believe it because it is the number they see. Tarnmoor's annual report shows one income tax expense in one income statement, and analysts quote the effective tax rate that comes from it. Boards are measured on it.

But that consolidated charge is an accounting figure. It adds up current tax across every company in the group, United Kingdom and overseas, so it includes Vallarian and Marrovian tax that H M R C never sees. It includes deferred tax, which is not a payment at all but a recognition of tax that will fall due, or be saved, in later years. Chapter six explains it. It reflects consolidation adjustments that no tax return contains.

The United Kingdom tax bill is something else entirely. It is a set of separate liabilities, company by company. Each is computed on that company's own taxable total profits and paid on that company's own timetable. In Group Year One, Tarnmoor Engineering's liability, after group and consortium relief, comes to about two point six three million pounds. Calder, in its first accounting period in the group, computes its own liability of seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds before setting off its research credit. Nobody adds these together to file one return, because there is no group return for corporation tax.

There is a second reason the two numbers differ. The accounts measure profit under accounting standards, and tax law then adjusts that profit, adding back some costs, deducting others, and replacing depreciation with capital allowances. Some of those differences reverse in later years and some never do. The consolidated charge captures the reversing ones as deferred tax. The return simply taxes this year's adjusted profit, and has no place for tax that belongs to other years.

The practical lesson is that a tax function reconciles. It explains the consolidated charge to the board, the auditors and the market, and it builds up the company returns underneath it, and it must make the two stories agree. When an examiner asks for the tax charge in the accounts, that is a different question from what tax is payable, and a different answer. The examiners have been asking it more often, as a tail to a computation question, and candidates who confuse the two lose easy marks.

House rules with their own guest lists.

The Living Law, chapter twenty four, pictured a group as a family of separate wallets living under one roof, with house rules about when money can pass between them. Here is the extension this book needs. Each house rule has its own guest list. Who counts as family depends on which rule you are applying. A cousin may be welcome at one table and turned away from the next.

Take the lists one at a time. Start with associated companies. Under the Corporation Tax Act twenty ten, which I will call the twenty ten Act, two companies are associated if one controls the other or both are under common control. Control here is a broad test of power over the company's affairs. Overseas companies count. A company that carries on no trade or business, such as a dormant one, is ignored, and so is a passive holding company that does nothing but hold shares and pass dividends up. The number of associated companies divides the marginal relief limits and, under H M R C's guidance and the instalment regulations, the thresholds for paying tax by instalments.

Next, the fifty one per cent group, built on owning more than half of a company's ordinary share capital, directly or indirectly. It defines who may join a group payment arrangement, the group for the substantial shareholding exemption, the group from which H M R C can recover unpaid tax on a gain, and the groups whose size is measured for uncertain tax treatment and for publishing a tax strategy.

Then the seventy five per cent group for group relief. The parent must own at least three quarters of the ordinary share capital, and also be entitled to at least three quarters of the profits available for distribution and of the assets on a winding up. Losses can pass only between companies within the charge to United Kingdom tax. Alongside it sits the consortium, where companies each holding at least five per cent together own at least three quarters of a trading or holding company.

The gains group, under the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act nineteen ninety two, which I will call the Gains Act, uses seventy five per cent subsidiaries again, but adds a twist. Every member must also be an effective fifty one per cent subsidiary of the principal company, judged on profits and assets all the way down the chain. Overseas companies can be members, though the reliefs mostly bite only on assets within the United Kingdom charge.

Stamp duty and stamp duty land tax use their own seventy five per cent tests of shares, profits and assets, with extra conditions aimed at arrangements for the buyer to leave the group.

Now the wide lists. The corporate interest restriction, in the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act, works on the worldwide group. That is the ultimate parent and every subsidiary it consolidates in its accounts under international accounting standards. Pillar Two, the global minimum tax, uses a similar consolidated group. The country-by-country reporting regulations count the whole consolidated group too.

Finally, the control tests for cross-border rules. Transfer pricing applies where one party participates in the management, control or capital of the other. The controlled foreign company rules ask whether a United Kingdom company controls an overseas one. Chapters twenty six and twenty seven take these apart.

The reading edition sets all of this out in one matrix. Learn it as a matrix, because the exam rarely names the test. It describes a shareholding and expects you to see which lists it puts a company on.

Applying the guest lists to Tarnmoor.

Run Tarnmoor through the lists in Group Year One and the family changes shape before your eyes.

Count the associated companies first. Tarnmoor P L C controls everything it owns outright, so it, Tarnmoor Engineering, Estates, Finance, Water Systems, Vallaria, Capital and Ireland are all associated, and Calder joins them on the first of April. That makes nine. The two overseas companies count, because association looks at control, not residence. Tarnmoor Pumps does not count, because it is dormant. Helmside does not count, because forty five per cent is not control, and no single shareholder controls it. For marginal relief, a company counts if it is associated at any time in the period, so each company's limits are divided by nine at once, the company itself plus its eight associates. The instalment thresholds count on a different day, as we will see.

Now group relief. Every company that Tarnmoor owns outright passes the seventy five per cent tests. But group relief moves losses only between companies within the charge to United Kingdom corporation tax. Tarnmoor Vallaria and Tarnmoor Capital are outside it, so their losses stay abroad. Tarnmoor Ireland, though incorporated in Ireland, is resident here while its board meets in Leeds, so it can surrender and claim like any other United Kingdom company. Helmside is not in the group relief group at all. It is a consortium company, and its losses flow in proportion to the members' holdings. Chapter fifteen works through the numbers.

The gains group is almost the same list, overseas companies included, with the principal company at the top. The worldwide group for the corporate interest restriction is larger still. It is Tarnmoor P L C and every subsidiary in its consolidated accounts, including Tarnmoor Vallaria, Tarnmoor Capital and the dormant Pumps company. Helmside sits outside it, as a joint venture that Tarnmoor does not consolidate.

So which is the real Tarnmoor group? The question has no single answer, and that is the lesson. There is a nine-company association, a United Kingdom group relief group, a gains group, a stamp duty group, a fifty one per cent group and a worldwide group. A good adviser carries all of them in mind, and asks of every transaction which list matters. Move a building from Estates to Engineering, and the gains group and the stamp duty land tax group matter. Lend money from Finance to Vallaria, and the control tests for transfer pricing matter. Borrow from a bank, and the worldwide group matters.

Calder's purchase shows why. On the first of April it joins every list at once. It becomes associated, a member of the group relief and gains groups, part of the worldwide group, and a company controlled by a listed parent. Each membership switches on a different consequence, and the rest of this chapter is about the ones that come from size.

What makes a company larger, the threshold ladder.

The paper's title speaks of larger companies, and this book uses larger company as a working term, not a legal one. No statute defines it. Instead, dozens of rules each draw their own line, and a company or group above the line meets extra obligations.

Why should size matter at all? Three reasons recur. The first is revenue. A small number of large businesses pay a large share of corporation tax, so the state wants their money sooner and their risks visible. The second is capability. A group with a tax function, auditors and systems can carry burdens that would crush a small company, so Parliament places reporting and governance duties where they can be borne. The third is international. Large groups can move profit across borders. Working through the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, governments have agreed common lines, most famously seven hundred and fifty million euros of revenue, above which shared reporting and the global minimum tax apply.

There is a cost to every line. A threshold is a cliff edge. One pound or one euro either side of it changes a company's obligations completely, and groups cross thresholds by accident, through acquisitions, mergers, currency movements or a single good year. That is why a tax function watches them, and why this chapter fixes them in one place.

Picture a ladder. A company starts at the bottom with the ordinary obligations every company has. Each rung it climbs switches on something more. The rungs come from different statutes and use different measures, profits on some, interest on others, turnover or revenue on the rest, so climb carefully. The reading edition sets them out in a single table.

The first rung is about paying early. A company is large for the instalment rules if its profits exceed one and a half million pounds, and very large if they exceed twenty million pounds. H M R C's guidance says both figures are divided by the number of associated companies, counting the company itself. Its manuals count them on the day before the accounting period begins, not at any time in the period as for marginal relief. That has been the rule since the associated company rules returned in twenty twenty three. Both figures are also reduced for short periods. A large company pays in months seven, ten, thirteen and sixteen, counted from the start of the period. A very large company pays in months three, six, nine and twelve, all inside the period. Chapter three owns the detail, including the first-year exception for large companies, which very large companies do not get.

The second rung is interest. The corporate interest restriction can bite only where a worldwide group's net interest expense exceeds two million pounds a year. Below that, there is no restriction.

The third rung is losses. Carried forward losses can be set without limit against the first five million pounds of profit each year, the deductions allowance, with only half of the profit above it available. A group shares one allowance.

The fourth rung is two hundred million pounds of turnover, or two billion pounds of balance sheet total. Above it, a United Kingdom incorporated company must have a senior accounting officer who certifies its tax accounting arrangements. The group must publish a tax strategy. And the group must tell H M R C about uncertain tax treatments worth more than five million pounds. Chapter four covers all three. H M R C's Large Business directorate works with most businesses whose turnover is above that same line.

The fifth rung is seven hundred and fifty million euros of consolidated revenue. Above it, the group files a country-by-country report. Its United Kingdom companies must keep a master file and a local file of transfer pricing records. It must publish a tax strategy even if the fourth rung did not catch it. And if revenue exceeds that figure in at least two of the previous four years, Pillar Two's minimum tax applies.

One more line runs the other way. Small and medium-sized enterprises are exempt from most transfer pricing, and the test looks at the whole group of linked enterprises. Fewer than two hundred and fifty staff, and turnover no more than fifty million euros or a balance sheet no more than forty three million euros, keeps a company medium-sized. Join a big group, and the exemption is gone.

Tarnmoor on the ladder.

Now put Tarnmoor on the ladder, using our invented figures for Group Year One.

Consolidated revenue is one thousand one hundred and eighty million pounds. Our story assumes an exchange rate of one point one five euros to the pound, invented for illustration, which gives about one thousand three hundred and fifty seven million euros. That is far above seven hundred and fifty million euros, and it would be even at parity. So Tarnmoor files a country-by-country report, keeps transfer pricing master and local files, and, assuming as our story does that it has been this size for years, falls within Pillar Two.

United Kingdom turnover is far above two hundred million pounds. Tarnmoor Engineering alone sells six hundred and thirty million pounds. So the senior accounting officer rules, the tax strategy rules and uncertain tax treatment reporting all apply. Nadia Kerr, the chief financial officer, is the senior accounting officer for every United Kingdom incorporated company in the group. There is a subtlety even here. Tarnmoor Ireland is resident in the United Kingdom but incorporated in Ireland, and the senior accounting officer rules apply only to companies incorporated in the United Kingdom.

Interest is far above the two million pound de minimis. Tarnmoor Finance alone pays thirty point two five million pounds a year on its notes. Chapter twenty eight shows that in Group Year One the group loses relief for about two point two one million pounds of interest.

Now the instalment rung, company by company. For marginal relief the divisor is nine at once, because Calder is associated for part of the year. Instalments count on the day before the period begins. For the companies with a thirty first of December year end, that day is the thirty first of December before Group Year One, when Calder had not yet joined. Eight companies make a divisor of eight. So each one's large threshold is one hundred and eighty seven thousand, five hundred pounds, and its very large threshold two and a half million pounds.

Watch what that does to Calder. On its own, with profits of two million pounds, Calder was large, because it was over one and a half million pounds, but nowhere near very large. It paid in months seven, ten, thirteen and sixteen. In its first group period, its taxable total profits are three million pounds. For instalments, its associates are counted on the thirty first of March, the day before that period began, when it still belonged to one family and had none. Its divisor is still one. So Calder stays large, not very large, and pays four instalments of one hundred and eighty seven thousand, five hundred pounds, in months seven, ten, thirteen and sixteen. Its research credit does not reduce them, as chapter three explains. The change comes one period later. On the day before its next period begins, Calder has eight associates, a divisor of nine, and a very large threshold of about two point two two million pounds. From then on it is very large, and pays in months three, six, nine and twelve. Its profits rose, but on its own three million pounds is nowhere near twenty million. Its cash timetable moves four months earlier because it acquired eight associates.

And transfer pricing arrives. Calder, with three hundred staff, was too large to be a small or medium-sized enterprise even on its own. Many targets are not. The moment they join a group like Tarnmoor the exemption vanishes, because the size test looks through to the whole group. In the story, Calder's dealings with Tarnmoor Vallaria will be priced at arm's length, and tested. Chapter twenty seven tells that story. The full working for all of this is in the reading edition.

Who does the work.

A larger company's tax is not done by one person with a spreadsheet. It is done by a system, and the paper expects you to know the parts.

At the centre is the group tax function. In our invented case it is Tom Hesketh's team. It prepares or reviews every company's return, manages instalments, runs the transfer pricing documentation, prepares the interest restriction return and the tax numbers in the accounts, and keeps a map of the thresholds and group lists we have just built.

Above it sits the board, which approves the published tax strategy and owns the group's appetite for tax risk. The chief financial officer, Nadia Kerr in our story, is the senior accounting officer and personally certifies, each year, whether the tax accounting arrangements are appropriate. The audit committee and the external auditors test the tax numbers in the accounts.

Across the table sits H M R C. Its Large Business directorate works with around two thousand of the country's largest businesses. Each has a Customer Compliance Manager, a senior H M R C official who learns the business and coordinates H M R C's own specialists. H M R C's guidance rates each business's tax risk on a scale running from low to high. A good relationship means issues raised early and resolved in real time.

The work runs to a calendar. Instalments fall due through the year. The tax numbers for the annual report are prepared at the year end and audited. Returns follow within twelve months, and the interest restriction return with them. The senior accounting officer's certificate is due when the accounts are due to be filed, six months after the year end for a public company. Each deadline belongs to a particular company, and missing one costs penalties.

Finally, the specialists. Transfer pricing economists, valuers, research and development claim teams, stamp taxes lawyers, accountants who know international standards. Nobody holds all of it.

That is why the Chartered Institute frames this paper the way it does. Candidates, it says, are not expected to have deep knowledge of all tax areas but should be able to identify what the potential tax issues are. They should know specialist areas well enough to coordinate the work of the firm's specialists. Read that as a job description. The examiner rewards the adviser who sees every issue a transaction raises, says what it means, and knows who to call.

Mapping the thresholds every year.

The planning lesson of this chapter is unglamorous and vital. A tax function maps every threshold and every group list, every year, and again whenever the group changes shape.

Acquisitions are the usual trigger. A group just under seven hundred and fifty million euros can cross it by buying one company, and Pillar Two, country-by-country reporting and transfer pricing records follow. Each new subsidiary also changes the associated company count, which lowers every company's instalment thresholds. When Tarnmoor buys an invented sensor developer called Brackenwell in Group Year Two, the marginal relief count rises to ten at once. The instalment count catches up from Group Year Three, when the very large threshold for a full year falls to two million pounds and the large threshold to one hundred and fifty thousand pounds. Disposals and demergers work the other way. Currency can do it too. The highest line is drawn in euros, so a weaker pound can carry a sterling group across it without a single extra sale.

A joiner brings its own checklist. Its year end may differ from the group's, as Calder's does. Its returns and instalments need taking over. Its losses may be restricted after the change of ownership. It may lose a relief it enjoyed as a small company. It may have been paying corporation tax on one timetable and then, as Calder does from its second group period, have to pay on another, earlier one. If it was a small or medium-sized enterprise claiming the enhanced relief for research intensive companies, it loses that relief and falls back on the expenditure credit. Its directors may have been the only people answerable for its tax, and now a senior accounting officer in Leeds must certify its arrangements too. Chapters three, four, ten, fourteen and twenty pick up each of these.

There is a professional point too. Thresholds are measured on different numbers, from different accounts, over different periods. One rule looks at the previous financial year, another at the current accounting period, another at two of the last four. A careless adviser applies one test to all of them. The examiners have noticed. In May twenty twenty five, candidates asked about the tax strategy thresholds apportioned subsidiaries' figures instead of using the right accounts. A good tax function writes the tests down, with the source of each figure, and the senior accounting officer can rely on them. It also reviews the map whenever the deal team is busy, because the tax function is often the last to hear about a purchase and the first to be blamed for a missed deadline.

How the paper is built.

A brief word on the exam this book serves, because it shapes every chapter. Chapter thirty two owns the craft.

The paper is three and a half hours long and normally has six questions, each worth ten, fifteen or twenty marks, for a hundred marks in total. The pass mark is fifty. It was renamed in twenty twenty three, from Taxation of Major Corporates, a change that signals its focus on groups. Its syllabus covers corporation tax, including tax on chargeable gains, then capital allowances, and stamp duty and stamp duty land tax at awareness level. At least seventy per cent of the corporation tax element comes from core material.

Each syllabus row carries a grade. Core items are examined in depth, non-core items at working level, and awareness items for recognition. In the grid the book is built on, most rows are core, including transfer pricing, controlled foreign companies, the interest restriction and hybrids. When the twenty twenty seven grid appears, check the grades against it.

The scenarios follow a pattern. A United Kingdom listed group with overseas subsidiaries. A foreign parent buying a United Kingdom company. A joint venture. Expansion abroad by branch or subsidiary. A property reorganisation, a disposal or a company leaving the country. Every one of them is a story about crossing a threshold or joining a list.

The questions want technical prose and computations, not letters. They ask you to calculate with explanations, to explain, to discuss and sometimes to recommend. Marking guides award half a mark or a mark for each relevant point, so breadth of spotting matters as much as depth.

This chapter's material has been examined head on. In November twenty twenty four, a twenty mark question had an American multinational buy a United Kingdom company that had been a small or medium-sized enterprise. The marking guide gave marks for instalments now that the company sat in a large group, for country-by-country reporting, for transfer pricing switching on, for the interest restriction, and for stamp duty on the share purchase. That is the threshold ladder and the guest lists, applied to one acquisition. The examiners reported that most candidates found transfer pricing, but some wrote at length about it and missed easier points. Spot everything first, then go deep.

The pass rates are reassuring. Between May twenty twenty three and May twenty twenty six they ran from fifty nine to seventy four per cent, and the chief examiner reported after the May twenty twenty four sitting that Joint Programme candidates had the highest pass rates. That is no reason for complacency. Particular questions, on controlled foreign companies and on group relief, have been answered badly. With three and a half hours for a hundred marks, you have a little over two minutes a mark, and spotting the issues quickly is what buys the time.

What to take away.

A company that joins a large group is still a separate taxpayer. Salomon's case, decided by the House of Lords and reported in eighteen ninety seven, confirmed that a company is a person distinct from its members, and corporation tax taxes that person. Each company computes, files and pays its own tax. There is no group return for corporation tax.

The law bridges the gap between the many companies and the one business with a toolkit of group regimes. Each regime has its own guest list. Associated companies turn on control and include overseas companies, but ignore dormant and passive holding companies. The fifty one per cent group governs group payment arrangements, the shareholding exemption, recovery of tax on gains, and the tax strategy and uncertain tax treatment groups. The seventy five per cent group, with its profits and assets tests, governs group relief, and a consortium needs members of at least five per cent owning at least three quarters. The gains group adds the effective fifty one per cent test. Stamp duty and stamp duty land tax use their own seventy five per cent tests. The worldwide group of consolidated companies governs the interest restriction, and Pillar Two and country-by-country reporting use consolidated groups too.

The consolidated tax charge is not the tax bill. It includes overseas and deferred tax. The United Kingdom bill is a set of company liabilities.

Then the ladder, for the financial year twenty twenty six. Profits over one and a half million pounds make a company large for instalments, and over twenty million pounds very large, both divided by the company plus its associated companies. Net interest over two million pounds brings the interest restriction into play. Five million pounds is the deductions allowance for losses. Two hundred million pounds of turnover or two billion pounds of balance sheet switches on the senior accounting officer, the tax strategy and uncertain tax treatment reporting. Seven hundred and fifty million euros switches on country-by-country reporting, transfer pricing records and Pillar Two. Leaving the small and medium-sized category switches on transfer pricing.

For Tarnmoor in Group Year One, that means revenue of one thousand one hundred and eighty million pounds, about one thousand three hundred and fifty seven million euros at our invented rate, and a marginal relief divisor of nine at once. For instalments, associates are counted on the day before each period begins. So the December companies divide by eight in Group Year One, and Calder stays large in its first group period and becomes very large one period later.

And the job is to identify the issues, explain them precisely, and coordinate the specialists.

To answer this chapter's question, then. Calder is one company among many for computing and paying its tax, and part of one large group for almost every threshold that decides how. Next, chapter two asks where all of these rules actually live, and how an adviser finds them.


Chapter two: Where corporate tax law lives.

On the eighteenth of March, twenty twenty six, the Finance Act twenty twenty six received Royal Assent. Sixteen years earlier to the day, on the eighteenth of March, twenty ten, the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten had received its own. That earlier Act was the last product of a fourteen year project to rewrite the United Kingdom's direct tax statutes in a clearer, better ordered form. Its aim was to restate the law, not to change it.

The twenty twenty six Act went a step further than any rewrite Act. In its transfer pricing and permanent establishment rules, it points to texts written by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the O E C D, and it tells us to read them as they stand from time to time, not as they stood on the day Parliament voted.

So where does corporate tax law actually live? In Acts and regulations, certainly. But also in treaties, in accounting standards that Parliament never wrote, in judgments, and now in international texts that change without a vote at Westminster. Around all of that sits a large body of H M R C guidance that is not law at all, yet shapes every enquiry.

This is the second chapter of Part One, and it is the book's how we know chapter. The Living Law, chapter two, explained statute, interpretation, the tribunals and the status of guidance. Here we go further, into the sources a larger company's tax function uses every week. No single row of the syllabus grid is owned by this chapter. But the grid treats the application of the O E C D Model and supplied treaty extracts as core, and the impact of accounting standards on taxable profits as core too. We finish in the exam room, with what the screen gives you and what it does not.

The statute book a group lives in.

Start with the Acts. As The Living Law, chapter two, explained, statute is the law, and everything else either interprets it or applies it. For a larger company, the statute book is a handful of big Acts, and most of them come from the Tax Law Rewrite Project. That project began with a blueprint paper in July nineteen ninety six. It produced seven Acts, from the Capital Allowances Act two thousand and one to the International Act in twenty ten. Its explanatory notes say the rewritten Acts do not generally change the meaning of the law. They restate it, in a new order.

Here is the map, and the names I will use for each statute.

The Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act, is the computing Act. It contains the charge to corporation tax and company residence, the profits of permanent establishments, the foreign branch exemption, trading income, loan relationships, derivative contracts, intangible fixed assets and research and development relief.

The Corporation Tax Act twenty ten, which I will call the twenty ten Act, is the reliefs and structure Act. Losses, group relief, the loss restriction, change of ownership, distributions and demergers live there, with the definitions the rest of the code borrows, including the meaning of a permanent establishment and of control.

The Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act, holds the cross-border and anti-avoidance machinery. Double tax relief, transfer pricing, advance pricing agreements, hybrid mismatches, controlled foreign companies and the corporate interest restriction all sit there. The twenty twenty six Act added a new Part for unassessed transfer pricing profits.

Then come the older Acts that were never rewritten. The Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act nineteen ninety two, the Gains Act, governs company gains. The Taxes Management Act nineteen seventy, the Management Act, still carries much of the administration, alongside the company return rules in Schedule eighteen to the Finance Act nineteen ninety eight. The Capital Allowances Act completes the set. And the global minimum tax lives in the Finance Number Two Act twenty twenty three, which I will call the Pillar Two legislation.

Each year's Finance Act mostly amends these Acts, so the amended Acts are what you read. But some rules never move into the main Acts. The senior accounting officer rules still live in Schedule forty six to the Finance Act two thousand and nine. The tax strategy rules live in Schedule nineteen to the Finance Act twenty sixteen. The uncertain tax treatment rules live in Schedule seventeen to the Finance Act twenty twenty two. A researcher who searches only the Corporation Tax Acts will never find them.

Beneath the Acts sit statutory instruments, made by ministers under powers the Acts give them. They carry the same force of law and often hold the detail that costs money. Five matter all through this book. The instalment payment regulations decide when large and very large companies pay. The Disregard Regulations keep certain exchange and hedging movements out of taxable profit for the time being. The change of accounting practice regulations govern what happens to loan relationships and derivatives when a company changes its accounting framework. The country-by-country reporting regulations set the seven hundred and fifty million euros revenue threshold. And the transfer pricing records regulations require the master file and local file, for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty three.

Treaties arrive by yet another route. Section two of the International Act lets the Crown give effect to a double taxation agreement by Order in Council, and section five requires a draft of that Order to be approved by the House of Commons first. So a treaty is negotiated by governments, but it reaches a company's tax return only because Parliament has said it may.

When Parliament points at Paris.

For most of the history of transfer pricing in this country, the O E C D's Transfer Pricing Guidelines entered the law of the United Kingdom, the U K, through a narrow, fixed door. Section one six four of the International Act told the reader to construe the transfer pricing rules consistently with the guidelines. But the guidelines meant one particular version, frozen in time, and a newer version counted only when the Treasury designated it by order. The twenty seventeen guidelines were designated in twenty eighteen, for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April that year. The twenty twenty two guidelines were designated later, with effect for corporation tax accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty three.

The Finance Act twenty twenty six opened the door wide. For chargeable periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, the law refers to the O E C D's materials in three places, and in the two most important it refers to them as amended or replaced from time to time.

The first is transfer pricing. Section one six four now refers to Article nine of the O E C D Model Tax Convention, in the version approved by the O E C D Council on the eighteenth of November, twenty twenty five, and to the Transfer Pricing Guidelines published on the twentieth of January, twenty twenty two.

The second is the attribution of profits to a permanent establishment. New subsections in section twenty of the two thousand and nine Act require attribution to be read consistently with Article seven of the twenty twenty five Model and its Commentary, the O E C D's twenty ten Report on the Attribution of Profits to Permanent Establishments, the twenty twenty two Guidelines and further guidance published in March twenty eighteen. Chapter twenty three calls the method the authorised O E C D approach and owns it.

The third is the definition of a permanent establishment itself. A new purpose clause, section eleven forty A of the twenty ten Act, ties the whole domestic definition to Article five of the twenty twenty five Model and its Commentary.

In the transfer pricing and attribution rules, the reference is to the documents as later amended, subject to the reservations the United Kingdom has entered, and the Treasury may make regulations so that a particular update does not apply. For transfer pricing, H M R C's International Manual says the Model and the Guidelines are now interpretative aids whether or not a treaty is in place, and the references are to their most recent versions.

Think of the statute as the rulebook and the O E C D materials as the official commentary that the rulebook now tells the referee to read. The referee still applies the rulebook. But when a rule could bear two meanings, the referee must prefer the one that fits the commentary, and the commentary is updated in Paris.

Why would Parliament do this? Because transfer pricing and permanent establishment disputes are fought between tax authorities, under treaties, through mutual agreement procedures. A U K rule that drifted from the international reading would invite double taxation. The cost is a loss of control. Parliament no longer votes on each change of reading, so the Treasury's power to switch off an update is the safeguard.

That brings us to this chapter's misconception. It runs like this. The O E C D cannot legislate for the United Kingdom, its documents call themselves guidelines and commentaries, so they are just guidance, like H M R C's manuals, to be quoted when helpful and ignored when not.

People believe it for good reasons. The O E C D is not a parliament. And for most of the corporation tax code it remains true that nothing outside the statute and the cases binds you.

For transfer pricing it has not been true for a long time, because section one six four has long required consistency with the designated Guidelines. What the twenty twenty six Act adds is reach and currency. The permanent establishment rules now carry the same kind of instruction, and the transfer pricing reference follows the texts as they change. Ignoring them is not choosing a different view of the guidance. It is misreading the statute. An argument about the arm's length price for a group's intra-group loan, or about how much capital a branch should be treated as having, must now be built from two things together, the words of the Act and the O E C D text the Act points to.

Two limits keep the picture honest. First, the O E C D texts guide interpretation. They do not override clear statutory words, and the United Kingdom's reservations and any Treasury opt-out still apply. Second, the texts are long and they change. This book could not open the O E C D's own website while it was being written, so where it describes the Guidelines it relies on the statute and on H M R C's descriptions, and says so.

There is also an exam wrinkle. The examination screen gives you the O E C D Model as a P D F of the twenty seventeen articles, while the twenty twenty six Act points to the version approved in twenty twenty five. In the exam, use what you are given, and use a supplied treaty extract in preference to either.

Treaties, and the judges who read them.

A double tax treaty is an agreement between two states. In the main it allocates taxing rights and limits what each state may take. It is not a free-standing source of tax charges. Its words were negotiated by officials, usually following the O E C D Model, and they are read differently from a U K statute. A treaty is meant to mean the same thing in both countries, so its words take an international meaning rather than a purely domestic one.

The leading modern authority is Fowler versus H M R C, decided by the Supreme Court on the twentieth of May, twenty twenty. Mr Fowler was a diver resident in South Africa who worked in the U K sector of the continental shelf. U K domestic law deems an employed diver to be carrying on a trade. Mr Fowler argued that the deeming carried through into the treaty, so that his income fell under the article for business profits, which South Africa alone could tax. The Supreme Court unanimously disagreed. Lord Briggs, giving the judgment, held that the domestic deeming rule did not change which treaty article applied. Treaty words take their ordinary international meaning, and the income fell under the employment article, so the United Kingdom could tax it.

On the O E C D Commentaries, Lord Briggs said they carry persuasive force, as the cogency of their reasoning deserves, even where a Commentary post-dates the treaty. That phrase is worth remembering. It describes the general position for treaties. The twenty twenty six Act goes further for transfer pricing and permanent establishments, because there the statute itself directs you to the O E C D texts.

Treaties also change in bulk now. The Multilateral Instrument, in force for the United Kingdom from the first of October, twenty eighteen, modifies many treaties at once, and H M R C publishes synthesised texts showing how each covered treaty reads after the modification. The U K and Ireland text is an example. One of the Instrument's most important additions is a principal purpose test. It denies a treaty benefit where obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement, unless granting it would accord with the object and purpose of the treaty. So a tax function reading a treaty asks three questions. Which text applies after the Instrument? What do its words ordinarily mean in context? And could a purpose test take the benefit away? Chapter twenty four owns treaties in depth.

The accounts as a source of tax numbers.

The largest source of numbers in a corporation tax computation was not written by Parliament at all. It was written by accounting standard setters.

Section forty six of the two thousand and nine Act says that the profits of a trade must be calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting practice, subject to any adjustment required or authorised by law. The loan relationship and derivative rules go further. The amounts brought into account are, in general, those recognised in profit or loss under that practice. The twenty ten Act defines generally accepted accounting practice to include both U K standards and international accounting standards. In practice that means the Financial Reporting Council's standards, chiefly Financial Reporting Standard one hundred and two and the reduced disclosure framework in Financial Reporting Standard one hundred and one, or full international standards for listed group accounts.

Why build tax on accounts? Because they exist already, they are audited, and they follow a consistent logic from year to year. A second, tax-only set of books for every company in a group would be costly and easy to manipulate. So the law starts from the accounts and then adjusts them where policy demands, replacing depreciation with capital allowances, for example, or refusing a deduction for entertaining.

The courts have generally held to this line.
