Work through the tests. Tarnmoor Engineering is a qualifying company, because its own United Kingdom turnover is six hundred and thirty million pounds. The provision is the first trigger. The tax advantage for the year is twenty four million pounds at twenty five per cent, which is six million pounds. That is above five million pounds. H M R C has not been told about it, so the exemption does not help. Notification is required.

The deadline follows the corporation tax return. Tarnmoor Engineering's year ends on the thirty first of December. Its accounts are due nine months later and its return twelve months later, so the notification is due by the thirty first of December in Group Year Three. Tom files it with the return.

The notification itself is made on H M R C's online form. H M R C's statutory notice says what it must contain, including the company's name, the tax concerned, the tax references and the periods affected, and it warns that an incomplete notification will not be accepted as valid. It describes the treatment and the amount in question. It is not a full technical paper. Notice too that most of the advantage here is about timing. If the costs are capital, Tarnmoor Engineering may get relief later, through capital allowances or the intangibles rules. But the statutory question is the tax advantage in the period of the return, and in Group Year Two that is six million pounds.

Two practical points follow. First, notification is not a concession. It records that the position is uncertain. It does not admit that it is wrong. Second, the provision that triggered the notification also feeds the accounts. Chapter six explains how the tax charge and the uncertain tax provision appear in the financial statements.

The corporate criminal offence.

Back to the offence that opened the chapter. Part three of the Criminal Finances Act twenty seventeen created two corporate offences. They came into force on the thirtieth of September, twenty seventeen. They are modelled on the failure to prevent bribery offence in the Bribery Act twenty ten, and they share its logic.

The law asks for three stages. First, a taxpayer, which might be a customer, a supplier or anyone else, commits a criminal tax evasion offence. Second, a person associated with the company criminally facilitates that evasion while acting in that capacity. Third, the company failed to prevent the associated person from doing it.

An associated person is an employee, an agent, or anyone else who performs services for or on behalf of the company, acting in that capacity. That reaches far beyond the payroll, to sales agents, distributors, consultants and contractors.

Section forty five covers the evasion of United Kingdom tax. Section forty six covers foreign tax, with two extra conditions. There must be dual criminality, meaning the conduct is criminal under the foreign law and would be criminal here. And there must be a United Kingdom connection. The company is incorporated under United Kingdom law, or carries on business here, or part of the facilitation happens here.

The defence is reasonable prevention procedures. A company is not guilty if, when the facilitation happened, it had in place such prevention procedures as it was reasonable in all the circumstances to expect, or if it was not reasonable to expect it to have any. The burden is on the company to prove it. The penalty on conviction is an unlimited fine. The offences apply to a relevant body, which means a body corporate or a partnership. The individuals involved, the evader and the facilitator, remain liable for their own offences, which are prosecuted separately.

Notice what the offence does not require. The company need not benefit. The board need not know. The company need not have been dishonest in any way. That is why the offence matters so much to a large group's governance. The only protection is to have the procedures in place before anything goes wrong.

This is a core topic for your paper, but the examiners have not set a question on it in the sittings from May twenty twenty three to May twenty twenty six. When it comes, expect the three stages, the meaning of associated person, the foreign tax conditions and the defence.

Reasonable prevention procedures.

What counts as reasonable? H M R C's official guidance is not law, but it is the yardstick a court is likely to use. It sets out six guiding principles. Risk assessment, which drives everything else. Proportionality of procedures to the risk. Top level commitment from senior management. Due diligence on associated persons, proportionate to risk. Communication, including training. And monitoring and review.

The guidance points to the risk factors a group should look at, among them the countries it operates in, its sector, and the kinds of transactions and business opportunities it pursues. A group that sells through agents in jurisdictions with weak tax administration has a different risk from one that sells only to United Kingdom utilities.

Now the invented incident. In Group Year Three, a customer of Tarnmoor Engineering in the invented country of Marrovia rings the group's whistleblowing line. Tarnmoor Engineering's local sales agent, a self-employed individual paid on commission, has offered to split an invoice so that part of the price can be paid offshore and kept out of the customer's Marrovian tax return.

Tom's team works through the stages. The agent performs services for Tarnmoor Engineering, so he is an associated person. The tax is foreign, so section forty six is the relevant offence. Tarnmoor Engineering is a United Kingdom company, so the connection condition is met. Whether a facilitation offence was committed would depend on whether the conduct is criminal under Marrovian law and would be criminal here, and whether the customer went on to evade. In our story the customer refused and reported it at once.

What protects Tarnmoor is what it had done earlier. Its risk assessment had flagged agents in Marrovia as high risk. Its agency contracts prohibited facilitation and allowed termination. Its agents had completed training. And its whistleblowing line worked. The agent is dismissed. The group reviews its other Marrovian agents and records what it found. Tom takes legal advice on whether to report the matter to the authorities. That is a judgement for lawyers, and the book does not pretend to answer it here.

The incident also shows how the rungs of the ladder connect. The same risk assessment that protects Tarnmoor under the Criminal Finances Act is evidence for Nadia that the group's systems are sound. The procedures are only as good as the evidence of them, so Tom keeps the records of training, contracts and the investigation. If a prosecutor ever asked what Tarnmoor had in place, the answer would be in the files, not in anyone's memory.

Avoidance, evasion and the disclosure rules.

The Living Law, chapter three, drew the line between evasion and avoidance. Evasion is illegal. It involves dishonesty, such as concealing income or inflating costs. Avoidance uses the law to reduce tax, sometimes in ways Parliament never intended. It is lawful, but it often fails. Since the Ramsay case in nineteen eighty one, the courts have read tax statutes purposively and looked at transactions realistically, and the Supreme Court confirmed that approach in the Rangers case in twenty seventeen. The profession's own standards, in Professional Conduct in Relation to Taxation, go further. They forbid advisers to create, encourage or promote planning that sets out to achieve results contrary to the clear intention of Parliament, or that is highly artificial or highly contrived and seeks to exploit shortcomings in the legislation.

Parliament added machinery on top of the courts. The first piece is the disclosure of tax avoidance schemes regime, called DOTAS, in Part seven of the Finance Act two thousand and four. Its logic is speed. If H M R C learns about a scheme when it is first marketed, it can close it by legislation or challenge it before it spreads.

Arrangements are notifiable if they fall within one of the prescribed descriptions, called hallmarks, and are expected to give a tax advantage as one of their main benefits. The hallmarks include confidentiality, where a promoter would want to keep the scheme secret from H M R C or from other promoters, and the premium fee, where the fee is attributable to a significant extent to the tax advantage or is contingent on it. Others cover standardised tax products and particular kinds of loss, leasing and employment schemes. Both of those hallmarks are tested hypothetically, by asking what a promoter might reasonably be expected to want or to obtain, not what was actually paid. In a twenty twenty two case brought by H M R C against a promoter, the First-tier Tribunal found the premium fee hallmark met and held the arrangements notifiable.

The promoter must normally notify H M R C within five days of making the scheme available or of its first implementation. H M R C issues a scheme reference number. The promoter passes it to clients, and each user reports it to H M R C on its return. Where there is no promoter, as with a scheme devised in-house, the user notifies.

Failure is expensive. The Finance Act twenty twenty six rebuilt the penalty regime in a new section three fifteen of the Finance Act two thousand and four. The core is a daily penalty of up to six hundred pounds, rising to five thousand pounds a day once H M R C has obtained an order that the arrangements are notifiable, and up to one million pounds where a lower penalty would be inappropriately low. And if a user's tax loss is connected with a failure to comply with DOTAS, H M R C can make a discovery assessment up to twenty years after the end of the accounting period.

Follower notices and accelerated payment notices.

Disclosure tells H M R C about a scheme. It does not collect the tax. For years, users of failed schemes kept the money while their appeals ran, sometimes for a decade. Part four of the Finance Act twenty fourteen changed the economics with two notices.

A follower notice can be given where a return or claim relies on particular arrangements, an enquiry or appeal is open, and H M R C is of the opinion that a final judicial ruling in another case, on arrangements like these, would deny the advantage. The taxpayer is told to take corrective action, which means giving up the advantage. If it refuses and later loses, it pays a penalty of thirty per cent of the denied advantage, reduced to twenty per cent in one statutory case.

The Supreme Court set a limit on this power in Haworth versus H M R C, decided on the second of July, twenty twenty one. H M R C had issued a follower notice relying on the Court of Appeal's earlier decision in Smallwood, about a scheme that moved a trust round the world. The court unanimously upheld the quashing of the notice. It held, as the commentators summarise it, that H M R C may give a follower notice only where it considers there is no scope for a reasonable person to disagree that the earlier ruling defeats the taxpayer's claim. A notice cannot be used where the earlier case is merely helpful to H M R C.

An accelerated payment notice goes further. It requires the disputed tax to be paid while the dispute continues. H M R C can issue one where an enquiry or appeal is open and a follower notice has been given, or the arrangements are notifiable under DOTAS, or a counteraction notice has been given under the general anti-abuse rule. The tax must be paid within ninety days, or thirty days after H M R C has considered any representations, if later. There is no appeal against the notice itself. The taxpayer may make representations to H M R C within ninety days, and beyond that only judicial review is available. If the taxpayer later wins, the money comes back with interest.

For a large group, the effect is direct. A marketed scheme now carries a cash cost from the start. The tax saving is no longer an interest-free loan from the Exchequer while the case runs. And a group that receives a follower notice must decide quickly. Taking corrective action means amending the return and accepting the tax. Refusing means betting the penalty on beating a ruling that H M R C, after Haworth, must believe is decisive.

The general anti-abuse rule.

The general anti-abuse rule, the GAAR, is in Part five of the Finance Act twenty thirteen, and it has applied since the seventeenth of July, twenty thirteen. The Living Law, chapter three, told how it grew out of Graham Aaronson's report for the government. Here we need its mechanics.

It works in two stages. First, there must be tax arrangements, meaning that it would be reasonable to conclude that obtaining a tax advantage was the main purpose, or one of the main purposes, of the arrangements. Second, those arrangements must be abusive. That is the double reasonableness test. Arrangements are abusive if entering into them or carrying them out cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action in relation to the relevant tax provisions, having regard to all the circumstances. The circumstances include whether the result is consistent with the principles and policy of the provisions, whether the arrangements involve contrived or abnormal steps, and whether they exploit shortcomings in the legislation. The statute lists indicators of abuse. Income or profits for tax purposes far lower than the economic reality. Deductions or losses far higher. A claim to repay tax that has not been paid and is unlikely to be. Each counts only if that result was probably not anticipated when the rules were made. And indicators point the other way, such as arrangements that accord with established practice H M R C has accepted.

If the GAAR applies, the advantage is counteracted on a just and reasonable basis. Before that, the case must go to the independent GAAR Advisory Panel, whose opinion the tribunal must take into account. And since the Finance Act twenty sixteen, a penalty of sixty per cent of the counteracted advantage applies.

Why does it exist alongside the hundreds of targeted anti-avoidance rules in the corporate code? Because targeted rules can only reach the schemes their drafters foresaw. The GAAR is designed for the egregious scheme nobody foresaw. It is deliberately narrow. Ordinary tax planning, such as choosing between debt and equity, claiming an allowance, or electing for a relief, is not abusive.

The GAAR is not limited to income tax. It applies to corporation tax, including amounts charged as if they were corporation tax, and to the other main direct taxes and stamp duty land tax. It also works alongside the courts' own approach. The Ramsay line of cases asks what the statute, read purposively, means for the facts viewed realistically. The GAAR asks a different question, whether the arrangement is abusive even if it works on a purposive reading. In a large group, the targeted rules usually decide the case first. The specific purpose tests you will meet in this book, such as the unallowable purpose rule for loans in chapter twelve and the main purpose tests on share exchanges in chapter eighteen, catch most corporate schemes long before the GAAR is needed.

The loss refresh pitch.

Now watch the whole architecture work at once, in our invented story. In Group Year Three, a promoter approaches Tom with a proposal for Brackenwell Sensors. Brackenwell's losses from before Tarnmoor bought it, eight point six million pounds of them, are fenced off by the rules on changes of ownership, which chapter fourteen explains. At twenty five per cent they would be worth about two point one five million pounds. The promoter offers a way, in his words, to refresh them. The structure would route income and deductions around the group in a pre-packaged series of steps. His fee would be a percentage of the tax saved. And he asks Tom to sign a confidentiality agreement before he will explain the steps.

Tom does not need to see the steps to know the answer. The fee contingent on the saving and the demand for secrecy are DOTAS hallmarks, so the scheme is very likely notifiable. That means a scheme reference number on Tarnmoor's return, a target for an accelerated payment notice, and a twenty year discovery window. Part fourteen B of the twenty ten Act, the targeted rule against using arrangements to unlock carried-forward losses, is aimed at exactly this kind of plan, and chapter fourteen teaches it. The GAAR stands behind it all. Then the governance ladder. Tarnmoor's published tax strategy says the group does not use marketed avoidance schemes. Nadia would have to consider whether the scheme fitted the group's tax accounting arrangements. And a position like this, if provided for in the accounts and worth more than five million pounds, would need an uncertain tax treatment notification.

The board declines the proposal in a single meeting. Tom's paper to the board is short. It sets out the hallmarks, the targeted rule, the GAAR, the cash cost of an accelerated payment notice, and the conflict with the published strategy. It recommends that the group decline, that the approach be recorded, and that the promoter receive a short written refusal. That is the purpose of the architecture. It is not only that the rules defeat the scheme. It is that they make the scheme unattractive before anyone has to defeat it.

The Finance Act twenty twenty six continues this pressure on the promoters themselves. Its Part six adds a prohibition on promoting certain marketed avoidance arrangements and new promoter action notices. This is non-core detail for your paper. Know that it exists.

Working with H M R C when things are disputed.

Large groups do not meet H M R C as strangers. H M R C's large business directorate gives many of the largest groups a named Customer Compliance Manager, and H M R C's uncertain tax treatment guidance refers to businesses raising uncertain issues through that contact. A good relationship means early conversations, agreed positions, and fewer surprises on enquiry.

When disputes do arise, H M R C resolves them within its Litigation and Settlement Strategy, set out in its internal guidance. As H M R C describes it, each dispute is resolved on its own merits, not as part of a package deal, and H M R C will not settle for less than the tax it believes the law requires simply to save costs. A strong case is settled for what a tribunal would be likely to award. A weak one is conceded.

Alternative dispute resolution is the awareness-level tool. It is non-statutory. An H M R C mediator, not involved in the case, helps the two sides narrow the issues or reach agreement. It can be used during a compliance check when talks have stalled, or after an appealable decision. It does not affect the taxpayer's rights of appeal or review. H M R C also has guidance on using it in large or complex cases.

Remember the formal route that sits behind all of this, which The Living Law, chapter two, set out. A company that receives an appealable decision, such as a closure notice or an assessment, can ask for a statutory review by an H M R C officer not involved in the decision, or appeal to the First-tier Tribunal. Alternative dispute resolution does not replace either. It can run alongside them, and if it fails the appeal continues. For a large group, the choice between negotiating, mediating and litigating is a commercial one as well as a technical one. Litigation is public, slow and expensive, and a precedent may affect other companies in the sector. Settlement is private but must follow H M R C's strategy, which means that a group cannot trade one issue against another. Each issue stands or falls on its own merits.

In our invented story, H M R C opens an enquiry into Calder's return for its nine month period in Group Year Three. That dispute, about the price Calder charged its Vallarian sister company, is told in chapter twenty seven.

How the examiner tests governance.

The examiners like a ten or fifteen mark administration question, and governance is a favourite subject for it. In November twenty twenty three, a ten mark question asked which companies in a group counted towards the senior accounting officer thresholds, and then about the main duty, the certificate, notification and penalties. The examiners reported that candidates knew the thresholds but misapplied them. They also reminded candidates to show their workings, because marks are available even when the conclusion is wrong. In May twenty twenty five, a fifteen mark question on the tax strategy rules turned on group companies with different year ends, and candidates apportioned figures they should have taken from the accounts.

So build every answer the same way. List each company. State whether it is incorporated in the United Kingdom, whether it is in the fifty one per cent group, and which year's figures you are using. Then aggregate and conclude. And do not confuse the regimes. The senior accounting officer rules aggregate United Kingdom incorporated companies. The uncertain tax treatment rules aggregate group members within the charge to corporation tax. The tax strategy rules add the country-by-country route.

The anti-avoidance material, DOTAS, the GAAR and the notices, has not been examined in the sittings from May twenty twenty three to May twenty twenty six. When it comes, it is more likely to be a few marks within a scenario, such as a promoter's proposal, than a whole question. The reading edition sets out the grades and the traps in its Exam lens boxes.

A word on style. These questions ask you to explain and apply, not to write a letter. A typical marking guide gives half a mark or a mark for each correct point. Half a mark for stating that the company must be incorporated in the United Kingdom. A mark for applying that to the foreign incorporated company. Half a mark for the deadline. A mark for each penalty correctly stated. So short, precise sentences, each carrying one rule applied to one fact, score better than long general paragraphs. And where the question gives you the group's companies, deal with every one of them, even if only to say why it does not count. Finally, read the requirement for its tax. If it asks about the senior accounting officer, the uncertain tax treatment rules earn nothing, however well you know them.

What to take away.

The law regulates how large groups govern tax through a ladder of accountability, with an anti-avoidance structure beside it.

First rung, the senior accounting officer, under Schedule forty six to the Finance Act two thousand and nine. A qualifying company is incorporated in the United Kingdom, whatever its tax residence, and in its preceding financial year had turnover above two hundred million pounds or a balance sheet above two billion pounds. The figures are aggregated with the other United Kingdom incorporated companies in its fifty one per cent group at the end of that preceding year. Once the group is over the line, every United Kingdom incorporated member qualifies, dormant ones included. A company joining a group is outside the regime for its first financial year in the group if it did not qualify on its own. The officer takes reasonable steps to ensure appropriate tax accounting arrangements, and certifies them. Notification and certificate are due within the accounts filing period, six months for a public company and nine for a private one. Penalties are five thousand pounds, fixed and not reduced.

Second rung, the tax strategy, under Schedule nineteen to the Finance Act twenty sixteen. It applies to groups over two hundred million pounds of turnover or two billion pounds of balance sheet, or in a seven hundred and fifty million euro multinational group. It is published by the head of the group before the end of the financial year, and within fifteen months of the last. Penalties start at seven thousand five hundred pounds and build monthly. Members with different year ends use their latest year ending in the head's year, unapportioned.

Third rung, uncertain tax treatment, under Schedule seventeen to the Finance Act twenty twenty two, an awareness topic. It has the same two hundred million and two billion pound thresholds, aggregated across corporation tax paying members of the fifty one per cent group. There are two triggers, a provision or a departure from H M R C's known position, and a five million pound advantage threshold, with an exemption where H M R C already has the information. Penalties are five thousand, twenty five thousand and fifty thousand pounds.

Fourth rung, the corporate criminal offence, in sections forty five and forty six of the Criminal Finances Act twenty seventeen. There are three stages, evasion, facilitation by an associated person, and failure to prevent. Foreign tax needs dual criminality and a United Kingdom connection. The only defence is reasonable prevention procedures, guided by H M R C's six principles. The fine is unlimited.

Beside the ladder, DOTAS makes promoters disclose hallmarked schemes within five days, with penalties rebuilt by the Finance Act twenty twenty six. Follower notices carry a thirty per cent penalty, and Haworth limits them to cases where the earlier ruling plainly defeats the claim. Accelerated payment notices demand the tax within ninety days. The GAAR uses the double reasonableness test, goes through the Advisory Panel, and carries a sixty per cent penalty.

The chapter's question was who answers for the tax inside a large group. The answer is that the law gives everyone a part. A named officer answers for the systems, the board for the published attitude, the company for its uncertain positions, and the company again, in the criminal courts, for the people who act for it.

Part Two of this book turns from who answers for the tax to how the profit is measured. Chapter five begins where every corporate computation begins, with the accounts.


Part Two: Measuring Profit.

Chapter five: Tax follows the accounts.

In twenty twenty two, the Supreme Court decided a case about money that never moved. A group of companies had recorded a large expense in their accounts for share options granted to their staff. No cash left the companies. The options came from a trust set up by the parent. Yet the accounting standard said the staff's services had been consumed, and their value had to be charged as an expense.

The tax authority, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, or H M R C, said the tax computation should ignore that charge. It argued four separate grounds. It lost on every one. The case was H M R C versus N C L Investments Limited, and the judgment was given by Lord Hamblen and Lady Rose, with whom the other three justices agreed.

So here is this chapter's question. When the accountants change their minds, or their rulebook, does the tax bill change too? And if it does, who decides when the law should step in and say no?

This chapter opens Part Two, on measuring profit. It sits underneath almost every computation the Advanced Technical examiner sets. The impact of accounting standards on taxable profits is a core topic in the syllabus, and so are the general calculation rules that Parliament lays over the top. The Living Law, chapter eleven, taught the adjustment of profits and the line between capital and revenue. This chapter asks why the starting point is the accounts at all, and what happens when the accounts themselves change. We work throughout on the law for the financial year twenty twenty six.

The shadow and the walker.

Start with the statute. The Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act, sets the rule in section forty six. The profits of a trade must be calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting practice, subject to any adjustment required or authorised by law.

That one sentence carries two ideas. The first is that tax begins with the accountant's number. The second is that the law may overrule it, but only where a rule says so. Section forty six also says there is no need to follow company law on accounts, except as to the basis of calculation. The tax computation borrows the method, not the paperwork.

Why build tax on the accounts? Three reasons. Accounts already exist, so a second, separate measurement of profit would double the cost for every company. Large companies' accounts are audited and must give a true and fair view, so they carry their own discipline. And accounting standards are written by people whose whole job is to measure profit over a period, which is exactly the question tax needs answered.

The courts reached the same view long before Parliament wrote it down. In Odeon Associated Theatres versus Jones, decided by the Court of Appeal in nineteen seventy one, the issue was the cost of catching up on deferred repairs to cinemas the company had acquired. Lord Justice Salmon's approach, as H M R C's own manual summarises it, has two steps. Follow the ordinary principles of commercial accounting so far as practicable, and then check that no rule of tax law is broken.

Two later cases pushed further. In Gallagher versus Jones, in nineteen ninety three, a taxpayer leased boats with heavy rents payable at the start. The Court of Appeal held that the rents should be spread across the lease, as the accounts spread them, and not deducted when paid. In Johnston versus Britannia Airways, decided in the High Court in nineteen ninety four, an airline provided each year for the future cost of overhauling its jet engines. The provision was accepted for tax because it reflected accepted accounting practice.

Here is an image to hold. Tax follows the accounts the way a shadow follows a walker. Wherever the accountant goes, the taxable profit goes too, at the same pace. But at certain spots Parliament has nailed the shadow to the floor. The walker moves on, and the shadow stays put. Those nails are the adjustments required or authorised by law.

The precise rule matters more than the image. Accounting practice decides when income and expense are recognised, and how they are measured. It does not decide whether an item is capital or revenue for tax, whether an expense is wholly and exclusively for the trade, or whether a specific statute blocks it. Those are questions of law. Accounting evidence is relevant to them, often persuasive, but never conclusive.

What counts as generally accepted.

Generally accepted accounting practice has a statutory meaning. The Corporation Tax Act twenty ten, which I will call the twenty ten Act, defines it in section eleven twenty seven. In outline, United Kingdom accounting practice means practice for accounts intended to give a true and fair view. The tax definition also embraces international accounting standards where a company uses them.

In practice there are three rulebooks a large group will meet. International financial reporting standards, which accountants call I F R S, are written by an international board and used in the consolidated accounts of every listed group. The Financial Reporting Council writes the United Kingdom standards, the Financial Reporting Standards, or F R S, numbered one hundred to one hundred and five.

Two of them matter most here. F R S one oh one is the reduced disclosure framework. It lets a subsidiary of a listed group use the international recognition and measurement rules, with lighter notes to the accounts. F R S one oh two is the main United Kingdom standard, originally based on the international standard for smaller entities. For tax, the distinction matters because recognition and measurement drive the numbers. A company on F R S one oh one will usually recognise income and expense at the same time as its parent's group accounts.

Our invented group, Tarnmoor, shows the pattern. Tarnmoor P L C is a listed engineering group, invented for this book, and it prepares its consolidated accounts under international standards. Its group policy is that every United Kingdom subsidiary reports under F R S one oh one. That way, each subsidiary's numbers feed straight into the group accounts without a second set of adjustments.

A group that mixes rulebooks can create a tax gap between two companies. Suppose one company uses international standards and its sister uses F R S one oh two. They make a deal with each other. One standard makes the seller recognise income later, while the other lets the buyer take the expense earlier. Across the group, the tax deduction runs ahead of the taxable income.

Parliament closed that gap in section nine hundred and ninety six of the twenty ten Act. Where two companies in a group use different frameworks, and the difference gives a tax advantage on a transaction between them, both are treated as using United Kingdom accounting practice. The rule is narrow and mechanical. It does not ban mixed frameworks. It removes the advantage that mixing would otherwise create.

Where Parliament nails the shadow down.

The adjustments required by law come in layers. The first layer is the case law and general statute that every trader meets, which The Living Law, chapter eleven, covered. Capital expenditure is not deductible. Expenses not incurred wholly and exclusively for the trade are not deductible. Depreciation is replaced by capital allowances.

The second layer is a set of specific rules gathered in Part twenty of the two thousand and nine Act, headed general calculation rules. The examiner treats it as core. It runs from section twelve eighty eight to section thirteen oh nine, and it reads like a list of the places where the accounts are not trusted.

Here is the list in outline. Pay that is charged in the accounts but not paid within nine months of the period end is deductible only when paid, under section twelve eighty eight. Contributions to employee benefit trusts face their own timing rules from section twelve ninety onwards. Business entertainment and gifts are blocked by section twelve ninety eight, with narrow exceptions. Charitable donations are kept out of the computation of income by section thirteen oh one B, because they get their own relief later, against total profits. Penalties and late payment interest on tax are blocked by section thirteen oh three. Payments that are themselves crimes, such as bribes, are blocked by section thirteen oh four. Dividends and other distributions are never deductible, under section thirteen oh five. Chapter seven works through each of these in a full computation.

Parliament still adds to the list. The newest entry is section thirteen oh five B, inserted by the Finance Act twenty twenty six. It concerns assets that a company transfers to a securitisation company but which stay on the transferring group's balance sheet, because the accountants say the risks never really left. The company then shows a liability alongside the asset. The new rule denies deductions on that liability where any party has a main purpose of obtaining a tax advantage, on a just and reasonable apportionment. It applies to accounting periods beginning on or after the twenty sixth of November, twenty twenty five, the date of the Budget that announced it.

The third layer is the most interesting, because it shows the law rejecting accounts that were perfectly correct as accounts. The story is G D F Suez Teesside versus H M R C, decided by the Court of Appeal in twenty eighteen. The company, which had operated the Teesside power station, held claims against companies in the collapsed Enron group. It transferred those claims to a non-resident subsidiary in exchange for shares.

The company's accounts complied with accounting practice, and on that basis the transfer produced no taxable credit that reflected the claims' value. The loan relationship rules of the time, in the Finance Act nineteen ninety six, required the accounting to fairly represent the company's profits and losses. The Court of Appeal held that this requirement could override accounts that were compliant with practice. A credit equal to the value of the claims had to be brought into account, and the company's appeal was dismissed.

The lesson is not that accounts can be ignored at will. The fairly represents test was itself a statutory adjustment, required by law. When the loan relationship rules were reformed from twenty sixteen, Parliament moved them to a simpler footing, which the next section but one describes. The general principle survived the case intact. Tax follows the accounts unless a rule of law says otherwise, and the rule must be found, not assumed.

A debit with no cash.

Now back to the share options. In N C L Investments, the companies employed staff and made them available to other group companies for a fee. The parent's employee benefit trust granted options over the parent's shares to those staff. International standards required the companies to charge the fair value of the options as an expense, because the staff's services had been consumed in return for them. The matching entry was a credit to equity, treated as a capital contribution from the parent.

H M R C argued that the debits should not count. It said the law required an adjustment under section forty six. It said the expense was not wholly and exclusively for the trade. It said the debits were capital. And it said the employee benefit trust rules in section twelve ninety blocked them. The tribunals, the Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court rejected every argument.

The Supreme Court's core reasoning was short. The debits were properly computed under accounting practice. They reflected a real cost of the trade, the consumption of employees' services. No statute required them to be removed. In the words of the Supreme Court, what matters is the character of the Debits, not that of any corresponding credit. A capital credit to equity did not turn a revenue expense into a capital one.

The case is a warning to anyone who thinks a tax deduction needs a cash payment. Under section forty six, it needs an accounting debit that the law does not reject. The burden is on the person who says the accounts should be overridden to find the rule.

There is a twist, and it matters for the exam. N C L concerned accounting periods before the Finance Act twenty thirteen rewrote the rule that now governs most share schemes. For shares and options within the statutory relief for employee share acquisitions, the two thousand and nine Act blocks a deduction for the accounting charge itself, in section ten thirty eight. The company gets a different deduction instead, based on the value of the shares when the employee acquires them. Chapter seven owns that relief. For this chapter, the point is the method. The courts followed the accounts, and when Parliament wanted a different answer, it legislated.

Loan relationships and derivatives follow profit or loss.

The loan relationship rules apply the same philosophy with a sharper edge. Sections three hundred and seven and three hundred and eight of the two thousand and nine Act set the rule. The amounts taxed are those recognised in the company's profit or loss for the period under accounting practice. The derivative contract rules say the same in sections five hundred and ninety five and five hundred and ninety seven.

Two refinements matter. First, amounts that accountants record in other comprehensive income, outside profit or loss, are not taxed when recorded there. They are taxed if and when the accounts recycle them into profit or loss. Second, an entry made directly in equity is not an amount recognised in profit or loss at all. Union Castle Mail Steamship versus H M R C was decided by the Court of Appeal in twenty twenty, under the older rules. It concerned a scheme that tried to turn an equity entry on derivatives into a tax loss of thirty nine point one million pounds. The Court of Appeal held that the amount did not count, and the scheme failed. Today's focus on profit or loss makes that kind of scheme harder still.

The law also overrides the accountant's choice of measurement in places. Any accounting basis that complies with practice can normally be used. But between connected companies, section three hundred and forty nine insists on amortised cost, even if the accounts use fair value. And the Disregard Regulations can take certain fair value swings on hedging derivatives out of the computation, though since twenty fifteen mostly only where the company elects. Chapter twelve teaches all of this in full, including why our invented group's treasury company, which hedges its listed notes with an interest rate swap and has made no election, simply follows its accounts.

Provisions, present obligations and the general reserve.

A provision is an accountant's estimate of a cost the business has become committed to but not yet paid. It is where the shadow most often parts company with the cash. So it is where H M R C looks hardest.

H M R C's view, set out in its Business Income Manual, is that a provision is deductible if four things are true. It is made in accordance with accounting practice. It relates to revenue, not capital, expenditure. It does not conflict with a statutory rule about when the expense is allowed. And it is estimated with sufficient accuracy. Each test does real work.

The accounting test now has teeth of its own. Modern standards allow a provision only where the business has a present obligation from a past event, the payment is probable, and the amount can be reliably estimated. That is why the Britannia Airways case is a lesson in history as much as in law. H M R C's manual points out that today's standards would not allow a provision for overhauling engines on aircraft the company owns, because no present obligation exists until the work is done. The tax law has not changed. The accounts have, and the tax has followed them.

The capital test catches provisions for costs that would themselves be capital, such as a write-down of plant or a provision to demolish a building. The timing test catches provisions that a specific statute overrides, such as unpaid pay beyond nine months or pension contributions, which are deductible only when paid. The accuracy test catches round-sum guesses.

That last test explains an old examination favourite, the general provision. A general provision is a reserve set aside against the risk that some unidentified customers will not pay, often a flat percentage of debtors. It is not an estimate of any particular loss, so it is not deductible. A specific impairment of a named customer's debt, properly estimated, is deductible. For companies, trade debts are money debts, and losses on them come in through the loan relationship rules, as H M R C's manual explains. Chapter twelve takes that further.

Watch the direction. When a general provision goes up, the accounts show an expense that tax will not allow, so you add it back. When it goes down, the accounts show a credit that tax never charged, so you deduct it. The examiners reported, after the May twenty twenty three sitting, that the common mistake in a well answered computation was getting the bad debt provision the wrong way round. Modern expected credit loss accounting blurs the old line between general and specific, and that wider debate is beyond the exam. In an exam question, follow the label the examiner gives you.

Now a moment from our invented case. In Group Year Three, on the fifteenth of June, Calder Valve Engineering announces that it will close its process valves division. Calder is the regional manufacturer The Living Law followed, invented for that book, and by now it is a Tarnmoor subsidiary. The announcement creates a present obligation in the accounting sense, because the staff now have a valid expectation that the closure will happen.

In its nine month accounting period to the thirty first of December, Group Year Three, Calder charges a restructuring provision of one point eight million pounds. The full working is in the reading edition. In round terms, one point two million pounds is redundancy and notice pay. Four hundred thousand pounds is a supply contract for castings Calder can no longer use. And two hundred thousand pounds is outplacement and retraining. By the year end, one point three million pounds has been paid. The other five hundred thousand pounds is still a provision.

Graham Pike, Calder's finance director, asks Tom Hesketh, Tarnmoor's head of tax, whether the half million still in the provision is deductible now. Both are invented characters. Tom's analysis follows H M R C's four tests. The provision complies with the standard. The costs are revenue, because Calder's trade continues in its other divisions. The amounts are specific and carefully estimated. The redundancy payments still owed are paid in March of the next year, within nine months, so no timing rule bites. The whole one point eight million pounds is deductible in the nine month period. Dan Hartley's own package, the one The Living Law, chapter nine, followed from his side, is part of it.

When the accountants change their minds.

Accounting policies change. A new standard arrives, a group imposes its own rulebook on a company it buys, or a company decides a different policy gives a truer picture. Each time, income or expense can fall between two stools. It may be taxed twice, once under the old basis and again under the new. Or it may never be taxed at all.

Chapter fourteen of Part three of the two thousand and nine Act, sections one hundred and eighty to one hundred and eighty seven, exists to stop both outcomes. It applies when a company changes the basis on which it calculates its trading profits from one period of account to the next. Both bases must have been valid, meaning each accorded with the law and practice for its own period.

A change of basis covers two things. The first is a change of accounting policy, and the law says expressly that this includes moving from United Kingdom practice to international standards, or back again. H M R C's manual treats any switch of accounting framework as a change of policy. The second is a change in the tax adjustments the company makes, including a change of view about what the law requires.

Two things are not a change of basis. A change made to comply with new legislation that did not apply to the earlier period is excluded. Parliament deals with its own changes through its own transitional rules. And correcting a fundamental error is not a change of basis either, because the old basis was never valid. An error belongs to the period it affected, and is put right there, through the normal routes for correcting returns.

The mechanics come in two steps, in section one hundred and eighty two. Step one totals the understatements, such as income that fell out of the old periods without being taxed, or expenses deducted twice. Step two totals the overstatements, such as income taxed twice or expenses never deducted. The net figure is the adjustment.

Then comes the rule that surprises people. Under section one hundred and eighty one, a positive adjustment is treated as a receipt, and a negative one as an expense. Either way, it arises on the first day of the first period of account on the new basis. There is no general spreading for corporation tax. The whole adjustment lands in a single period.

There are three softer edges. If an expense already deducted under the old basis would be deducted again under the new, section one hundred and eighty three simply denies the second deduction. Where the change comes from a tax adjustment about stock or depreciation, section one hundred and eighty four defers the adjustment until the asset is realised or written off. And where a company moves its trading stock from cost to fair value, the receipt waits until the stock is realised, with an election to spread it over six periods instead. That election must be made within twelve months of the end of the first period on the new basis.

Calder changes its rulebook.

Back to our invented case, a year earlier. Tarnmoor bought Calder on the first of April in Group Year One. Calder kept its thirty first of March year end for now, and its accounts for its first year in the group were still prepared under F R S one oh two. From the first of April in Group Year Two, group policy applies, and Calder reports under F R S one oh one.

The switch is a change of accounting policy within Chapter fourteen, because both frameworks were valid for their periods. In our invented case, applying the group's revenue policies, as the international rules require, brings forward revenue on part completed installation contracts. Revenue that Calder's old policy would have recognised in the new period has already been earned, on the new view, in the old one. So it would never be taxed at all unless the law caught it.

The net adjustment is a positive four hundred thousand pounds. Under section one hundred and eighty one it is a receipt arising on the first of April in Group Year Two, the first day of the new basis. It is taxed in full in Calder's accounting period to the thirty first of March, Group Year Three. It is not spread.

At twenty five per cent, the extra tax is one hundred thousand pounds. Calder is now a very large company in a large group, so it pays its tax in quarterly instalments during the period itself, in months three, six, nine and twelve. Chapter three explains the thresholds. Each of the four instalments rises by twenty five thousand pounds, the first of them due on the fourteenth of June, Group Year Two. Graham Pike's cash forecast had assumed the change cost nothing, because the group's consolidated accounts were unaffected. The tax function's job is to spot the gap before the first instalment, not after it.

Leases come onto the balance sheet.

For decades, a tenant's accounts showed rent as an expense, and the tax computation deducted it. Then the accounting changed. Under the international leasing standard, I F R S sixteen, which took effect for periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty nineteen, a lessee no longer separates finance leases from operating leases. Almost every lease goes onto the balance sheet. The tenant shows a right-of-use asset and a matching lease liability. The rent disappears from the profit and loss account, replaced by depreciation of the asset and interest on the liability.

The United Kingdom standard has now followed. The Financial Reporting Council's amendments to F R S one oh two, from its periodic review, apply to accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. They bring leases onto the balance sheet in the same way, with exemptions for short leases and leases of low value items. In our invented case, Calder adopted the amended standard in the year The Living Law followed it through, its first year beginning after that date.

Parliament's first instinct, years earlier, had been to freeze the shadow. The Finance Act twenty eleven, in section fifty three, said that changes in lease accounting standards would be ignored for tax. When the international standard finally arrived, the Finance Act twenty nineteen took the opposite view. Schedule fourteen to that Act repealed the freeze and let tax follow the new accounts, with one important cushion.

The cushion is spreading. When a change of accounting policy first brings a right-of-use asset onto the balance sheet, the transition adjustment is not taxed or relieved on day one. It is spread over a spreading period, which is the weighted average remaining term of the leases concerned. Each lease's share of the total adjustment is multiplied by its remaining term, and the results are added up. The amounts are then apportioned by days. The rule is not tied to the international standard by name, so it applies automatically to companies adopting the amended F R S one oh two.

For this example, suppose Calder's transition left a net expense of ninety thousand pounds. Sixty thousand pounds came from a warehouse lease with eight years to run, and thirty thousand pounds from a fleet of forklift trucks with two years left. Two thirds of the adjustment carries a weight of eight years, and one third a weight of two. The weighted average is six years. So Calder deducts fifteen thousand pounds a year for six years, instead of ninety thousand pounds at once.

Beyond the transition, the underlying tax law is unchanged. H M R C's guidance says the twenty nineteen changes were designed to give no tax advantage or disadvantage to lessees. H M R C's view is that, in practice, the tenant deducts the depreciation and the interest instead of the rent. Capital elements inside the right-of-use asset, such as a premium paid for the lease or stamp duty land tax, are not deductible as part of that depreciation and must be stripped out. And every lease must still be tested against the long funding lease rules, which chapter nine explains. A lease of plant that counts as a long funding lease gives the tenant capital allowances instead.

The corporate interest restriction also notices. The Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales reads the rules this way. Interest on a lease liability counts as interest for that regime only where the lease would have been a finance lease under the old accounting test. So the old classification survives in the tax records, even though the accounts no longer show it. Chapter twenty eight picks this up.

The spreading myth.

Here is a belief that costs real money. People assume that when an accounting standard changes, the tax effect can be spread over several years. Usually it cannot. They believe it because the most famous recent change, the leasing one, was spread. And the loan relationship rules also spread some transition amounts. So the exception is mistaken for the rule.

The rule is Chapter fourteen's. A change of basis in a trade is taxed or relieved in full on the first day of the new basis. That includes the big revenue change that came with the amended F R S one oh two, which moved United Kingdom revenue recognition onto a five step model aligned with the international standard. The same Institute warned, in March twenty twenty six, that the transition profit could push a company into quarterly instalments in a single year. It could also push profits over the five million pound allowance for using carried forward losses.

There are only three established routes to spreading. First, the lease transition, under Schedule fourteen to the Finance Act twenty nineteen. Second, the election for a move of trading stock to fair value, over six periods. Third, prescribed loan relationship and derivative amounts under the change of accounting practice regulations. As H M R C's manual describes them, those regulations bring prescribed amounts into account at one tenth a year over ten years. A special five year pattern applies to certain changes in the accounting for a company's own credit risk, at forty, twenty five, fifteen, ten and ten per cent. The amended regulations are not shown in their current form on the official legislation website, so the manual is the working source.

Outside those routes, the loan relationship rules have their own transition mechanism in sections three hundred and fifteen and three hundred and sixteen. Suppose a change of policy means the tax carrying value of a loan at the end of one period differs from its value at the start of the next. The difference is brought in as a credit or debit in the later period. Again, a change made only to comply with new legislation is excluded.

So the honest answer to a finance director who asks whether a change of standard can be spread is a question back. Which change, and under which rule?

Accounts in another currency.

The accounts follow the business, and some businesses do not think in pounds. A United Kingdom company that buys, sells and borrows mainly in euros may find that its accounts measure everything in euros. Its functional currency, in the accountant's language, is the currency of the main economic environment in which it operates.

The tax law starts from sterling. Section five of the twenty ten Act sets the basic rule that profits are calculated in sterling. Sections six to eight then follow the accounts. If a company's accounts are in a foreign currency but its functional currency is sterling, the profits are worked out in sterling, as if the accounts had been kept in sterling. If its functional currency is not sterling, the profits are worked out in that functional currency. And a company whose accounts are kept in a foreign currency outside those two cases works in the accounts currency.

Either way, the final figure is turned into sterling under section eleven. H M R C's manual says the translation uses an average rate for the period or an appropriate spot rate, and that an average rate will usually be right. Losses carried back or forward between periods have their own translation rules.

For this example, suppose a United Kingdom subsidiary with a euro functional currency makes taxable profits of four point six million euros. Using the book's assumed story rate of one point one five euros to the pound, invented for illustration, that is four million pounds. Tax at twenty five per cent is one million pounds. The point is not the arithmetic. It is that exchange movements on the company's own euro assets and debts largely drop out, because tax is measured in euros too. Its sterling items now produce the exchange differences instead.

Investment companies have an extra choice. An investment company's functional currency is often its parent's currency, which may not match its assets. Section nine A of the twenty ten Act lets a United Kingdom resident investment company elect a designated currency, if conditions are met. One condition, as H M R C reads it, is that a significant proportion of the company's assets and liabilities are in that currency. The election has applied to periods of account beginning on or after the first of April, twenty eleven.

Exchange gains and losses on loans are part of the loan relationship rules, with one carve out worth knowing. Translation differences that the accounts record in other comprehensive income, when a business's results are translated into another currency, are left out. The Advanced Technical syllabus names profits accounted for in a foreign currency and the functional currency election, so expect them as add-on marks rather than a whole question.

The tax function and accounting change.

For a group tax function, accounting change is a project, not a footnote. Four tasks recur.

First, get a seat at the table early. When a group moves a subsidiary onto its policies, as Tarnmoor did with Calder, the tax team should model the Chapter fourteen adjustment before the first day of the new basis. A positive adjustment is taxed at once, through instalments that may start in month three.

Second, quantify the cash effect separately from the accounting effect. A change that leaves the consolidated accounts untouched can still move a subsidiary's tax, its instalments, its use of carried forward losses, and the group's corporate interest restriction. Chapter six adds the deferred tax side.

Third, document provisions as they are made. The four tests are factual. A board paper showing the announcement date, the people affected and the basis of each estimate is the evidence that wins an enquiry years later.

Fourth, connect accounting judgements to governance. A provision against an uncertain tax position can itself trigger notification under the uncertain tax treatment rules, which chapter four explains. And the senior accounting officer's certificate depends on accounting systems that get these adjustments right.

There is a judgement call too. A company may face a choice of accounting policy that happens to defer tax. Choosing a policy because it is the truer picture is ordinary. Choosing one only for the tax, especially across group companies, invites the mixed framework rule, the loan relationship purpose tests, and the question every adviser should ask about professional conduct.

How the examiner tests it.

The impact of accounting standards on taxable profits is core, and so are the general calculation rules in Part twenty. Neither usually appears as a whole question. Instead, accounting items run through every computation the examiner sets, and they cost candidates marks in predictable places.

The examiners have reported the same errors across sittings. A general bad debt provision taken in the wrong direction, in May twenty twenty three. Capitalised revenue expenditure handled badly, in November twenty twenty three. Errors of direction when adjusting the accounting profit, in May twenty twenty six. Impairments that need sorting between a trade debt and a loan to a fellow subsidiary, in November twenty twenty four.

Two of those deserve a sentence each. Impairing land, as in May twenty twenty five, is a capital write-down, so it is added back. And a loan to a fellow subsidiary is a connected loan relationship, so writing it off gives no debit, while a trade debt owed by an outside customer does.

The Chartered Institute of Taxation's prospectus for the paper says candidates are expected to understand current accounting issues relevant to tax, naming deferred tax, profit recognition and share schemes. Profit recognition is this chapter. The functional currency material sits inside the core row on calculating the liability, which, reading the syllabus grid, is not limited to sterling for this paper.

The style is technical prose and computation, never a letter. Marks come at half a mark or a mark per valid point, so a short reason beside each adjustment is worth more than a paragraph at the end. In a computation, start from the profit before tax, and label every adjustment with its reason. When you meet a change of accounting standard, say whether Chapter fourteen applies, when the adjustment arises, and whether any spreading rule applies. Usually none does. The reading edition sets out the past appearances and the traps in full.

What to take away.

The chapter asked whether the tax bill changes when the accountants change their minds. Mostly, yes. Tax follows the accounts, and that is a choice Parliament made deliberately, because accounts are already prepared, audited and built to measure profit over time. But the law nails the shadow down wherever it chooses to.

Here are the rules to keep.

Section forty six of the two thousand and nine Act. Trading profits are calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting practice, subject to any adjustment required or authorised by law. The accounts decide timing and measurement. The law decides capital or revenue, wholly and exclusively, and anything a statute blocks.

The cases. Odeon, Gallagher and Britannia Airways built the accounting principle. N C L Investments, in the Supreme Court in twenty twenty two, held that a properly computed accounting debit counts unless a statute removes it, cash or no cash. G D F Suez Teesside, in the Court of Appeal in twenty eighteen, showed a statutory test overriding accounts that were correct as accounts.

Part twenty of the two thousand and nine Act. Unpaid pay beyond nine months, employee benefit contributions, entertaining and gifts, charitable donations, penalties, crime-related payments, distributions, and from the Finance Act twenty twenty six, losses on non-derecognition liabilities in securitisations.

Loan relationships and derivatives. Amounts in profit or loss are taxed. Other comprehensive income is taxed only when recycled. Connected companies use amortised cost.

Provisions. In H M R C's view, a provision is deductible if it follows accounting practice, is revenue, meets any statutory timing rule and is accurately estimated. A general provision is not deductible. Watch the direction of any movement. Calder's one point eight million pound restructuring provision is deductible in its nine month period.

Change of basis. Chapter fourteen of Part three. A change of accounting policy, or of view of the law, but not a change forced by new legislation, and not the correction of an error. The adjustment arises on the first day of the new basis. No general spreading. Calder's move to F R S one oh one produced four hundred thousand pounds, taxed in full, adding one hundred thousand pounds of tax and twenty five thousand pounds to each instalment.

The three spreading routes. Lease transitions under Schedule fourteen to the Finance Act twenty nineteen, over the weighted average remaining lease term. The six period election for trading stock moved to fair value. And prescribed loan relationship amounts, at one tenth a year, with a five year pattern for own credit changes. Everything else lands at once.

Leases. The amended F R S one oh two applies to periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. Right-of-use assets do not change the underlying tax law, but they change the numbers and the records.

Mixed frameworks. Section nine hundred and ninety six of the twenty ten Act treats both companies as using United Kingdom practice where the mix gives a tax advantage between them.

Currency. Profits are calculated in sterling, or in the functional currency where that is not sterling, then translated into sterling, usually at an average rate. Investment companies may elect a designated currency.

The accounts give tax its profit. Chapter six turns to the other side of the same page, the tax charge the accounts must show, and the deferred tax that measures what the timing differences will cost in years to come.


Chapter six: Deferred tax and the tax charge.

After the November twenty twenty five sitting of this paper, the examiners wrote a sentence that every candidate should hear before the exam. A question had asked for the total tax charge in the profit and loss account, current and deferred. In the examiners' words, only a small number of candidates calculated the deferred tax charge. Most wrote about balances, and many forgot whole categories of difference.

So here is the question this chapter answers. Why does a company that owes H M R C seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds report a tax charge of nine hundred and fifty thousand pounds? And why is the higher figure, not the lower one, the honest number for a shareholder to read?

This is the second chapter of Part Two, on measuring profit. Chapter five showed that taxable profit starts from the accounts. This chapter runs the other way, and shows how the accounts report the tax. Deferred tax is a core topic on the Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups paper. The Living Law signposted deferred tax but never taught it, so we start from first principles and go to Advanced Technical depth.

Two numbers for one year.

Every company's profit and loss account carries one line for tax. Behind that line sit two numbers. The first is current tax. That is the corporation tax the company expects to pay H M R C for the period, computed on taxable total profits, plus any adjustment for earlier periods. The second is deferred tax. That is an accounting measure of the tax effects of items that the accounts and the tax computation recognise in different periods.

Add the two together and you have the total tax charge, the number analysts divide by profit before tax and the examiner asks you to compute.

Our running case is the invented Tarnmoor group, a listed engineering group whose companies, people and figures are all made up for teaching. In Group Year One, Tarnmoor bought Calder Valve Engineering, the invented manufacturer from The Living Law. Calder kept its thirty first of March year end. Its first year end inside the group is the thirty first of March of Group Year Two.

For that year, in our invented case, Calder's taxable total profits are three million pounds. At twenty five per cent, its corporation tax is seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds. Its research and development expenditure credit of four hundred thousand pounds is set off against that liability, so the cash it actually sends H M R C is three hundred and fifty thousand pounds. Yet Calder's accounts show a tax charge of nine hundred and fifty thousand pounds.

Here is the misconception this chapter sets out to kill. Many people think deferred tax is tax you owe H M R C, a hidden liability the taxman will one day demand. It is not. H M R C never assesses deferred tax and never refunds a deferred tax asset. Deferred tax exists only in the accounts. It measures how today's transactions will change tomorrow's tax bills.

The gap between the two figures is two hundred thousand pounds of deferred tax. By the end of this chapter you will be able to build it from the ground up.

This chapter applies the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, with a main rate of twenty five per cent.

Why the accounts need deferred tax.

Accounting rests on matching. Income and the costs of earning it belong in the same period. Tax is a cost of earning profit. So the tax charge should broadly follow the profit that produced it.

Corporation tax does not cooperate. The tax computation recognises many items in a different year from the accounts. A machine is depreciated over ten years in the accounts but written off in one year for tax under full expensing. A bonus is charged in the accounts this year but deducted for tax only when paid, if payment comes more than nine months after the year end. A pension contribution accrued this year is deducted for tax only when paid. If the tax line showed only current tax, the reported tax rate would swing wildly from year to year for reasons that have nothing to do with how profitable the company really is.

Picture deferred tax as the bill in the post. The timing difference has already happened. The profit has been earned, or the cost has been spent. The tax consequence has not yet landed, but it is on its way, and its amount is known with reasonable confidence. A prudent householder who knows the gas bill is in the post does not pretend the winter was free. The accounts record the bill when the gas was burned, not when the envelope arrives.

Now the precise rule. A deferred tax liability records tax that will become payable in future periods because of differences that exist at the balance sheet date. A deferred tax asset records tax that will be saved in future periods. The movement in those balances during the year is the deferred tax charge or credit. It sits in profit or loss when the underlying item went through profit or loss, and in other comprehensive income or equity when the underlying item went there.

That last point matters for the examiner. The deferred tax charge is a movement, not a balance. The November twenty twenty five question asked for both, the charge and the closing balance. Always compute the opening position, the closing position, and the difference between them.

There is a cash story here too. A large deferred tax liability tells a reader that the company has paid less tax so far than its profits suggest, and will pay more later. Lenders and analysts read the deferred tax note for exactly that reason.

Temporary differences and timing differences.

There are two accounting languages for deferred tax in the United Kingdom, and a group tax adviser must speak both.

The first is International Accounting Standard twelve, Income Taxes, which practitioners call I A S twelve. A listed group such as Tarnmoor prepares its consolidated accounts under international standards, so I A S twelve governs the group accounts. A subsidiary that uses the reduced disclosure framework, Financial Reporting Standard one oh one, also measures its tax under I A S twelve, because that framework takes international recognition and measurement with lighter disclosure. Chapter five explained Calder's move to it.

I A S twelve looks at the balance sheet. For each asset and liability, it compares the carrying amount in the accounts with the tax base, which is broadly the amount that will be deductible for tax in future. The gap is a temporary difference. If an asset is carried at more than its tax base, recovering it will generate taxable profit, so there is a taxable temporary difference and a deferred tax liability. If an asset is carried at less than its tax base, or a liability is carried that will be deductible when paid, there is a deductible temporary difference and potentially a deferred tax asset.

The second language is Financial Reporting Standard one oh two, Section twenty nine. Calder used it until the thirty first of March of Group Year Two. It looks at the profit and loss account instead. It recognises deferred tax on timing differences, which are gains and losses recognised in the accounts in a different period from the tax computation. It then adds some items that are not strictly timing differences, such as deferred tax on fair value adjustments in a business combination and on revaluations. The Association of Chartered Certified Accountants calls this the timing differences plus approach.

Both languages ignore permanent differences. A regulatory fine is never deductible. Depreciation on a building that qualifies for no allowance is never relieved against income. Those items change the effective tax rate permanently, and no deferred tax arises on them.

For most items in a trading company, the two languages give the same answer. Plant, unpaid bonuses and pension accruals work the same way in both. The languages part company mainly at the edges, such as share schemes and the initial recognition of some assets.

For the exam, read which standard the question names. A new company reporting under international standards, as in the May twenty twenty six deferred tax question, is an I A S twelve question. Use its vocabulary, carrying amount and tax base.

Liabilities always, assets only when probable.

The recognition rules are deliberately asymmetrical. Under I A S twelve, a deferred tax liability is recognised for all taxable temporary differences, subject to a short list of exceptions. Under Section twenty nine the same is true of timing differences. Liabilities are not optional. A company cannot decline to book one because it hopes the difference will never reverse. The examiners' report on the May twenty twenty six sitting made the same point. Liabilities are always provided.

Assets are different. A deferred tax asset is recognised only to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available to absorb the deduction. Section twenty nine applies the same idea. That is a judgement, and it is where the auditors spend their time.

I A S twelve gives two sources of comfort. The first is taxable temporary differences. If the same company has deferred tax liabilities, owed to the same tax authority, that will reverse in the same periods as the deductible differences, or in periods to which a loss can be carried, those reversals will create the taxable profit the asset needs. That is the point the May twenty twenty six examiners wanted. A tax loss can be recognised as an asset to offset a liability from accelerated capital allowances.

The second source is forecast profit. Here the standard is stern. Its guidance says the existence of unused tax losses is strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available. A company with a recent history of losses needs convincing other evidence, not hope.

Three exceptions to the liability rule matter for this paper. First, no deferred tax liability is recognised on the initial recognition of goodwill. Second, I A S twelve has an initial recognition exception for some assets and liabilities acquired outside a business combination where the transaction affects neither accounting nor taxable profit. In May twenty twenty one the International Accounting Standards Board narrowed that exception, for annual periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty three, so that it no longer applies where a single transaction creates equal taxable and deductible differences. Leases are the main example. A lessee now books deferred tax on both the right-of-use asset and the lease liability. Third, the Pillar Two exception, which has its own section later.

Two measurement rules complete the picture. Deferred tax is never discounted, however far away the reversal. And deferred tax assets and liabilities may be offset in the balance sheet only where they relate to the same tax authority and there is a legal right to set them off.

Which rate, and when.

Deferred tax is measured at the rate expected to apply when the difference reverses, but only using rates and laws enacted or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date. Both standards use that test.

In the United Kingdom, a rate is substantively enacted when the bill containing it has completed its passage through the House of Commons. The logic is constitutional. Once the Commons has finished with a Finance Bill, the House of Lords can debate a tax rate but cannot change it. A resolution with statutory effect under the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act nineteen sixty eight also counts.

The best real illustration came in twenty twenty one. The government announced that the main rate would rise from nineteen per cent to twenty five per cent from the first of April, twenty twenty three. The Finance Bill completed its Commons stages on the twenty fourth of May, twenty twenty one, and received Royal Assent on the tenth of June. Groups with a balance sheet date on or after the twenty fourth of May had to remeasure their deferred tax at the new rate, to the extent the differences were expected to reverse after the first of April, twenty twenty three. A deferred tax liability built up at nineteen per cent jumped by almost a third overnight, and the increase went straight through the tax charge.

For the financial year twenty twenty six, the position is calm. The Finance Act twenty twenty six, which received Royal Assent on the eighteenth of March, twenty twenty six, sets the main rate at twenty five per cent for the financial year twenty twenty seven, with the small profits rate at nineteen per cent and the marginal relief fraction at three two hundredths. So for a large company, twenty five per cent is enacted for every reversal the examiner is likely to set you. Use it, and say why.

A company expecting to pay at the small profits rate, or within marginal relief, measures at the rate it expects to pay. Every Tarnmoor company pays the main rate, so the point never arises in our story.

The Finance Act twenty twenty six also cut the main pool writing down allowance from eighteen to fourteen per cent. That does not remeasure existing deferred tax, because the rate of tax has not changed. It only changes how quickly differences reverse.

The fixed asset difference.

In most trading companies, the largest deferred tax balance comes from capital allowances. Take the net book value of the assets that qualify for capital allowances, and deduct their tax written down value. The difference, at twenty five per cent, is the deferred tax liability.

The trap is the word qualifying. Land never attracts capital allowances, so including it in net book value creates a phantom difference. The May twenty twenty five examiners reported that some candidates did exactly that. A building that qualifies for no allowance is also outside the comparison, because its depreciation is never relieved.
