Haymarket was a value added tax case about the sale of a television studio site, not a capital allowances case, but the going concern question is the same. Buying the assets is not the same as succeeding to the business.

For connected parties, market value is often the wrong answer. If the predecessor and successor are connected, and both are within the charge to United Kingdom tax on the activity, they may jointly elect, within two years of the succession, for the plant to pass at its tax written down value. That is the connected-party succession election in sections two hundred and sixty six and two hundred and sixty seven. There is no balancing adjustment for the predecessor, and the successor steps into its shoes, taking over its pools and its history. The election is not available to a dual resident investing company, or where the cross-border transfer rule in section five hundred and sixty one applies.

Suppose, for this example, connected companies transfer a trade whose plant has a tax written down value of two million pounds and a market value of three million pounds. Without the election, the predecessor has a balancing charge of one million pounds, and the successor starts with three million pounds of expenditure but no first-year allowance. With the election, neither side has a balancing adjustment, and the successor continues from two million pounds.

Inside a group, a stronger rule often takes over. Where a trade passes between companies under common ownership, Part twenty two, Chapter one, of the twenty ten Act can apply automatically. Section nine hundred and forty eight then says allowances continue as if the successor had always carried on the trade, and the transfer itself gives no allowances or charges. Chapter nineteen owns Part twenty two. In our invented case, when Tarnmoor Engineering hives its actuators trade down into Tarnmoor Actuators in Group Year Six, the plant passes at tax written down value under that rule, with no balancing charge and no election needed.

Connected parties, cross-border transfers and the Act's toolbox.

Not every transfer is a succession. A group company may simply sell plant to a fellow group company. The Capital Allowances Act treats buyer and seller as connected, using the connected persons test in its final provisions, and section two hundred and fourteen brings in the connected-party rules. The buyer gets no annual investment allowance and no first-year allowance, under section two hundred and seventeen. Its qualifying expenditure is capped at the seller's disposal value, or, if the seller had none, the lower of market value and the original cost to the seller or a connected person, under section two hundred and eighteen. The aim is to stop a group generating fresh allowances by selling plant to itself at a high price.

For assets outside plant and machinery, sections five hundred and sixty seven to five hundred and seventy do a similar job. Where the buyer and seller are under common control, or the sole or main benefit of the sale is a tax advantage, the sale is treated as made at market value. If control is the only reason and there is no tax advantage, the parties may elect for an alternative amount, broadly the lower of market value and the unrelieved balance. That election is barred where the buyer is a dual resident investing company. Within the syllabus they matter mainly for research and development allowances, which chapter ten covers. Section five hundred and seventy A denies a balancing allowance where a tax avoidance scheme has reduced the proceeds.

Then there are the cross-border transfer rules in sections five hundred and sixty one and five hundred and sixty one A. They follow the Gains Act's rules for transferring a business between companies of different states, and for cross-border mergers. Where they apply, there are no allowances or charges on the transfer, and the transferee stands in the transferor's shoes, provided it is resident in the United Kingdom or carries on the business through a permanent establishment here. These rules were built for the European Union. How far they still reach after Brexit is not clear from the sources opened for this book, and their scope is flagged as unsettled. In an exam, recognise them, state the effect and say that the conditions turn on the definition of a relevant state.

Finally, the Act's toolbox, its final provisions in sections five hundred and seventy one to five hundred and eighty one. These hold the definitions the rest of the Act leans on, including the rule that treats certain transfers as sales, in section five hundred and seventy three, and the meaning of connected persons, in section five hundred and seventy five. Along with section five hundred and sixty two on apportionment, they are core on the syllabus because they answer three questions every transaction raises. Was there a sale? At what price? Between whom?

Contributions and grants.

Capital allowances relieve the cost a business bears. So when someone else pays, the law asks who really bore the cost. The general rule, in section five hundred and thirty two, is that expenditure is treated as not incurred by a person to the extent that it is met, directly or indirectly, by a public body or by another person. The rule applies across the Act, including the structures and buildings allowance.

There are exceptions. Insurance money and compensation do not count as a contribution. More important for groups, where the contributor is not a public body and cannot get allowances or a deduction for its contribution, the recipient is treated as having incurred the expenditure after all, under section five hundred and thirty six. The relief is not lost. It stays with the company that owns the asset.

The contributor may get relief of its own. A contributor that pays towards another person's capital expenditure for the purposes of its own trade or other qualifying activity can claim contribution allowances, as if it owned the asset, provided the two are not connected. That is sections five hundred and thirty seven and five hundred and thirty eight, with a version for the buildings allowance in section five hundred and thirty eight A. Notice the group consequence. Two companies in the same group are connected, so a group company that pays towards a fellow member's building cannot claim contribution allowances. The recipient keeps the allowances instead, because the contributor could not claim them. For a group, that is usually the right place for them anyway.

In our invented case, in Group Year Three, Tarnmoor Estates builds a concrete flood wall to protect a riverside site it lets to Tarnmoor Engineering. The wall costs five hundred thousand pounds and is in use from the first of January in Group Year Three. The local authority pays a grant of two hundred thousand pounds towards it. A local authority is a public body, so the general rule applies. Tarnmoor Estates' qualifying expenditure is three hundred thousand pounds, not five hundred thousand pounds. The wall is a structure, so it earns the structures and buildings allowance at three per cent, nine thousand pounds a year. Chapter twenty eight comes back to the grant, because its accounting treatment touches the corporate interest restriction.

Anti-avoidance and the special tax sites.

Two awareness topics close the technical part of the chapter.

The first is allowance buying. When a company has more tax written down value in its plant than the plant is worth in its balance sheet, it holds latent allowances. A buyer with profits could acquire the company and enjoy those allowances. The Finance Act twenty ten inserted Chapter sixteen A into Part two of the Capital Allowances Act to stop this, with effect from the twenty first of July, two thousand and nine. It applies where there is a qualifying change in the ownership of a company that has a relevant excess of allowances, meaning tax written down value above balance sheet value. Amendments in twenty thirteen added thresholds. The rules bite where the excess is fifty million pounds or more, where it is two million pounds or more and not insignificant compared with the benefits of the change, or, for a smaller excess, where the change has an unallowable purpose. When they bite, the excess allowances are restricted, so that a change of ownership cannot be used to put them to work for the new owners. The twenty ten Act also has separate rules on the sale of lessor companies. At awareness level, recognise the pattern. Tax value above book value, plus a change of ownership, means check the allowance buying rules.

The second is the special tax sites. Freeports in England, Scotland and Wales, and investment zones, contain designated tax sites. A company investing in new plant for use primarily in a special tax site can claim a one hundred per cent first-year allowance, and the plant must stay primarily in use in the site for five years. A building in a special tax site earns an enhanced structures and buildings allowance of ten per cent a year over ten years, instead of three per cent over thirty three and a third. These reliefs end on sunset dates. According to the government's guidance, the enhanced buildings allowance applies to expenditure incurred up to the thirtieth of September, twenty thirty one, for English freeport sites, and the thirtieth of September, twenty thirty four, for Scottish green freeports, Welsh freeports and investment zones. The government's policy paper gives the same dates for the plant allowance, though reliefs vary between investment zones, so check each site before use. Tarnmoor has no site in a freeport. In an exam, a scenario that mentions a freeport is inviting you to mention these reliefs.

The tax function's checklist, and the examiner's.

Every property or plant transaction in a group raises the same short list of questions, and most have a deadline.

On buying a building, split the price on a just and reasonable basis. Separate the land, the structure, the integral features, other plant and any non-qualifying costs. Ask whether the seller is a developer, a non-developer or a past user, because that decides the structures and buildings allowance. Obtain the allowance statement and warranties on the construction contract date. Make the section one nine eight election within two years, and check that the seller pooled. Write all of this into the sale contract, because the seller's cooperation ends at completion.

On selling a building, remember the gains add-back for the buildings allowance and the disposal value for fixtures. Agree the fixtures figure with the buyer, and pass on the allowance statement.

On leasing, classify every lease of plant at inception. A ten year finance lease is likely to be a long funding lease, and the return must treat it as one. For an exam answer, the machine goes in the pool its nature decides.

On reorganisations, decide whether a transfer is a succession, a Part twenty two transfer or a simple connected sale. Use the connected-party succession election within two years where it helps. When plant moves between group companies, expect no first-year allowance and a cost capped at the seller's disposal value.

On grants and contributions, net public grants off the qualifying cost, and remember that a group company paying for a fellow member's asset gets no allowance itself.

The examiner tests these topics often, usually embedded in a larger question. In May twenty twenty six, a fifteen mark question on capital allowances included a warehouse bought from a developer and an office built in twenty ten with later alterations. In May twenty twenty five, a computation included the buildings allowance on second-hand buildings with conversion costs, and the examiners reported that qualifying expenditure was weak. In November twenty twenty five, a new company's buildings allowance had to be time apportioned by twelfths. In May twenty twenty three and November twenty twenty five, property questions included fixtures elections. The examiners reported candidates deducting fixtures values from gains, and few dealing with the election at all. In November twenty twenty five, long funding lease machinery belonged in the main pool. The answers are technical prose with computations in the conventional columns. They are never letters or reports.

What to take away.

A building is a bundle of tax assets. Land earns nothing. The structure earns the structures and buildings allowance. Integral features and other fixtures are plant. A just and reasonable apportionment splits the price, whatever the contract says.

The structures and buildings allowance is three per cent a year of qualifying construction cost, for thirty three and a third years, starting from the later of first non-residential use and the date of the expenditure. The construction contract must date from the twenty ninth of October, twenty eighteen, or later. For an older building, only later alterations and extensions qualify. Land, land alterations and plant are excluded. A building bought unused from a developer qualifies on the price paid. One bought unused from anyone else qualifies on the lower of price and construction cost. One bought used carries on at three per cent of the original cost. There is no balancing adjustment on sale. The seller adds the allowances it claimed to its sale proceeds for gains. Demolition ends the allowance. No claim can be made without an allowance statement.

For Tarnmoor's distribution centre, the structure of three point four million pounds earns one hundred and two thousand pounds a year, and thirty four thousand pounds for the four months of Group Year Three. The land of one point two million pounds earns nothing. The integral features of nought point six million pounds go to the special rate pool.

Fixtures follow the building. A buyer can claim only if the past owner pooled its expenditure and the value was fixed, usually by a joint section one nine eight election within two years. The elected figure cannot exceed the seller's original cost. Miss either requirement and the claim is nil for every later owner. The election affects allowances, not the gains computation, except that a loss is restricted by net allowances. Tarnmoor Estates' office fixtures were fixed at four hundred thousand pounds, all covered by the annual investment allowance.

A long funding lease is a funding lease of more than seven years. It meets the finance lease test, the eighty per cent payments test or the sixty five per cent useful life test. The lessee claims the allowances on the present value of the payments, and its rental deduction is limited to the finance charge. Tarnmoor Engineering's machine adds one point five million pounds to the main pool.

On a succession, plant passes at market value with no first-year allowance, unless connected parties elect within two years for tax written down value, or Part twenty two passes it at tax written down value automatically. Connected sales of plant give no annual investment or first-year allowance, and the cost is capped at the seller's disposal value.

Public grants reduce qualifying expenditure. Connected contributors get no contribution allowance. Tarnmoor Estates' flood wall qualifies on three hundred thousand pounds.

Allowance buying and the freeport reliefs are awareness topics. Recognise them and state the rule.

Next, chapter ten turns from buildings and machines to ideas, and to research and development.


Chapter ten: Research and development.

In our invented case, it is a grey morning in early April of Group Year Two, and Graham Pike, the finance director of Calder Valve Engineering, is reading a checklist from the group tax team. Calder is the invented valve maker from The Living Law, now owned by our invented group, Tarnmoor. Its first year inside the group has just ended, on the thirty first of March. Calder has spent two million pounds developing a valve that can sense its own wear. Item four on the checklist asks a simple question. Has Calder made a research and development claim in the last three years? Graham checks the files. Calder has never claimed at all.

That one fact sets a clock running. If Calder does not tell H M R C, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, that it intends to claim, within six months of the end of that year, the claim is invalid. Not reduced. Invalid. A credit worth four hundred thousand pounds would be lost for want of a short online form.

This chapter is about the relief that pays companies to invent, and about the machinery around it, which is now as much about proof and procedure as about rates. It sits in Part Two of this book, on measuring profit, because the relief works inside the trading computation. All three syllabus rows it covers are core for the paper. They are the research and development expenditure credit, research and development intensive companies, and research and development allowances. The Living Law, chapter twenty one, introduced the merged scheme and the intensive relief at Taxation Knowledge level. Here we go deeper, into the payment steps, group surrender, the size tests that catch a start-up the day a large group buys it, the overseas restriction, and the claim notification trap that Graham has just found.

The law is the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, under the Finance Act twenty twenty six. The main rules live in Part thirteen of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act, and the allowances in Part six of the Capital Allowances Act two thousand and one, which I will call the Capital Allowances Act.

Why the state pays for ideas.

Start with the problem the relief solves. When a company discovers something, it cannot keep all of the value. Competitors learn from its products, its engineers move on, and other firms build on what it has shown is possible. Economists call this a positive externality. The company bears the whole cost but captures only part of the benefit, so left alone it invests less in research than would be best for the economy as a whole.

The government says exactly this. Its guidance on the merged scheme gives the policy aim as supporting and incentivising research and development, helping overcome a market failure, a positive externality, which causes underinvestment. The relief is a subsidy delivered through the tax system, and it is a large one. H M R C's statistics published in September twenty twenty six give a provisional figure of eight point two billion pounds of relief claimed for twenty twenty four to twenty five, on about forty thousand three hundred claims. The number of claims fell by about seventeen per cent in a year, driven by fewer claims from smaller companies.

Does the subsidy work? The evidence says it buys extra research, though by how much depends on the scheme. An H M R C working paper in twenty fifteen estimated that each pound of tax forgone stimulated between one pound fifty three and two pounds thirty five of extra research spending. H M R C's evaluation of the expenditure credit, published in November twenty twenty, put the figure for that scheme at between two pounds forty and two pounds seventy for each pound of relief. Those estimates count only extra spending by companies already claiming, not wider spillovers.

The other side of the story is abuse. During the years of easy claims, a market grew up of advisers who promised refunds for routine work and took a share of the cash. H M R C later revised its estimate of error and fraud for twenty twenty to twenty one to sixteen point seven per cent of the cost of the reliefs, about one point one three billion pounds. In the old small company scheme the figure was twenty four point four per cent, almost one pound in every four. Those numbers explain almost every procedural rule in this chapter, from the advance notification the additional information form to the restriction on overseas work and the cap on payable credits by reference to the company's payroll taxes.

So the policy debate has two sides, and both are serious. One side says research relief is among the most effective things the tax system does, and that complexity and compliance burdens deter the honest small firms who need it most. The other says a relief paid in cash to loss-making companies will attract fraud unless it is fenced, and that the fences are the price of keeping the relief at all. The law today reflects the second view tempered by the first. As a larger company adviser, you will meet both. There is the group that under-claims because nobody joined up the engineers and the tax team, and there is the boutique adviser who offers to find a refund that is not there.

What counts as research and development.

Before any rate applies, the activity must be research and development. The tax definition starts from generally accepted accounting practice and is then shaped by guidelines issued by the government department responsible for science, which tax law adopts. The heart of the test is that a project seeks an advance in science or technology, by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty. The guidelines also ask whether a competent professional working in the field would regard the advance as one, rather than as routine development. Work that merely applies known techniques, however clever or commercially valuable, is not research and development for tax.

The courts have tested this line twice in recent years, both times in the First-tier Tribunal, so neither decision binds other tribunals. In Get Onbord Limited versus H M R C, decided in twenty twenty four, a company had built an artificial intelligence tool for know your client checks. H M R C refused the claim, saying the project did not advance overall knowledge or capability. The tribunal allowed the company's appeal. It accepted the company's evidence and said that, once a taxpayer has shown enough to suggest an overall advance, H M R C needs some material of its own to show the advance was only routine.

In Tills Plus Limited versus H M R C, decided in the same year, the result went the other way. The company's software project was found to combine existing technology and products rather than to develop something new. The tribunal found no evidence of an advance achieved by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty, and the claim failed. One commentary noted that an expert report put forward for the company lacked evidence and reasoning.

Read together, the two cases make one lesson. The test is the same. Evidence decides it. A claim stands or falls on contemporaneous records that show what was uncertain, why a competent engineer could not simply look the answer up, and what the team tried.

Now to our invented case. Calder's Project Ashlar is a smart process valve. Sensors inside the valve body measure vibration and seal wear, so that a refinery can replace a valve before it fails rather than on a fixed timetable. The uncertainty is real. Nobody knew whether sensors and their wiring could survive the pressure and heat inside the valve body, or whether a signal could pass reliably through thick steel. Dan Hartley, the invented chartered engineer whose life we followed in The Living Law, spends sixty per cent of his time on Ashlar in Calder's first group year. His design notes and failed prototypes are exactly the evidence that a tribunal looks for.

Here is a misconception worth clearing early. People assume research must happen in a laboratory, with white coats. It need not. The workshop where Dan's team cracks open a failed prototype qualifies, if the project seeks a genuine advance. Equally, the shiniest laboratory in the group does not qualify for work that is routine testing of a known product.

The merged expenditure credit.

For many years the United Kingdom ran two schemes side by side. Small and medium-sized companies received an enhanced deduction, and loss makers could swap losses for cash. Larger companies received an expenditure credit, shown in the accounts above the line, like a grant. In the Autumn Statement of the twenty second of November, twenty twenty three, the government announced that the two would be merged. Schedule one to the Finance Act twenty twenty four enacted the merged scheme, alongside a separate enhanced relief for loss-making small companies that are research intensive. The start date was fixed by regulations. The merged scheme applies for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty four.

The merged scheme's credit is called the research and development expenditure credit, which practitioners say as R D E C. The rate is twenty per cent of qualifying expenditure. A higher rate of forty nine per cent applies to ring fence oil and gas trades, which this paper does not examine. Any trading company can claim, whatever its size, including a small company that is not research intensive enough for the enhanced relief.

Three features set the credit apart from the old enhanced deduction.

First, the credit is taxable. It is treated as a trading receipt of the period. The company deducts its research spending in full, as normal trading expenses, and then adds the credit back as income. That is why the credit appears above the line.

Second, the net value is lower than the headline. For a company paying corporation tax at twenty five per cent, a credit of twenty per cent is worth twenty per cent less a quarter of itself, which is fifteen per cent of the spending. For a company taxed at nineteen per cent, the net value is sixteen point two per cent.

Third, the credit is used through a fixed set of payment steps, which first pay the company's own corporation tax, and only at the end produce cash. Those steps are where the examiners have caught candidates, and we take them slowly in a moment.

Calder shows how the credit runs through a computation. In its year to the thirty first of March of Group Year Two, Calder's qualifying expenditure is two million pounds. Its credit is twenty per cent of that, four hundred thousand pounds. Before the credit, Calder's adjusted trading profit is two point six million pounds, after deducting the two million pounds of research costs as ordinary expenses and after capital allowances. Add the credit as a trading receipt and the taxable total profits become three million pounds. Corporation tax at twenty five per cent is seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds.

The credit then pays four hundred thousand pounds of that tax, leaving three hundred and fifty thousand pounds to pay. The group's real benefit is four hundred thousand pounds of credit less one hundred thousand pounds of tax on it, three hundred thousand pounds, which is the fifteen per cent we expected.

Qualifying expenditure.

The credit is twenty per cent of qualifying expenditure, so the next question is which costs qualify. The law lists categories, and a cost outside them does not count, however closely it relates to the project.

Staffing costs come first and are usually the largest. They are the salaries, employer's national insurance contributions and employer pension contributions of staff directly and actively engaged in the research. Where a person works only partly on research, the cost is apportioned on a just and reasonable basis. Dan Hartley's employment costs are about one hundred and twenty thousand pounds a year. Sixty per cent of his time goes on Ashlar, so seventy two thousand pounds of his cost qualifies.

Externally provided workers are people supplied by an agency or another company who work under the claimant's direction. Contractor payments are payments for research that another business carries out under contract. For both, the qualifying amount from an unconnected provider is restricted to sixty five per cent of the payment. Connected providers, or providers who jointly elect to be treated as connected, are measured differently, by reference to the provider's own relevant costs.

Calder subcontracted part of the sensor design to an invented start-up called Brackenwell Sensors, paying four hundred thousand pounds. Brackenwell was unconnected throughout Calder's year, so sixty five per cent qualifies, two hundred and sixty thousand pounds.

Then come consumable items, such as materials used up or transformed in prototypes. Calder burns through castings, seals and sensors worth one hundred and eighty thousand pounds. Software, data licences and cloud computing services qualify too, so far as they are used directly in the research. Data and cloud costs qualify for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty three. Calder's are sixty thousand pounds. Its remaining staffing costs for the engineers and technicians on the project are one point four two eight million pounds. Add them up and Calder's qualifying expenditure is two million pounds exactly. The full working is in the reading edition.

Every category also has a payment condition. No amount can be claimed until it has actually been paid.

Notice what is missing. Repairs to the test bay are not research, even if the bay is used for research, and the November twenty twenty five examiners criticised candidates who put repairs into a claim. Rent, rates and general overheads do not qualify. Nor does capital expenditure. When Calder spends half a million pounds on a test rig, that cost does not enter the credit at all. It gets a capital allowance of its own, which we come to later in the chapter.

The categories are also a test of judgement. A cost is either in a category or out. The adviser's job is to resist the temptation to stretch a category to cover something that feels like research but is not, and to make sure that genuine costs, such as cloud processing of test data, are not left out because nobody told the tax team they existed.

Who claims, and research done abroad.

When research is done under a contract, two companies might want to claim the same work. The merged scheme answers with a simple principle. The company that decides to undertake or initiate the research claims it. The company that merely does the work to order cannot claim for it, where the customer intended or contemplated the research when the contract was made.

So Calder claims for the Ashlar sensor design, sixty five per cent of what it paid Brackenwell. Brackenwell, which did the work, cannot also claim for that work, even though it was the company whose engineers solved the problem. Its own claims rest on research it decided to undertake for itself. This is the cure for an old weakness, where both parties sometimes claimed the same project under different schemes.

Then there is the overseas restriction, in section eleven thirty eight A of the two thousand and nine Act. Since accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty four, contractor payments for research carried out abroad, and the costs of externally provided workers who are not subject to United Kingdom payroll taxes, are excluded from both the merged scheme and the intensive relief. There is one exception. The research qualifies if conditions that are necessary for it are not present in the United Kingdom, are present where the work is done, and it would be wholly unreasonable to replicate them in the United Kingdom. The conditions may be geographical, environmental, social, legal or regulatory. The law says expressly that the cost of workers and the availability of workers are to be disregarded.

Suppose, for this example only, that Calder had paid a laboratory in Vallaria, an invented country, to run the pressure tests because it was cheaper. That spending would be excluded, because cheaper labour is exactly the reason the law disregards. Suppose instead that the tests needed a natural geological condition found only in Vallaria. Then the exception might apply. The May twenty twenty five paper tested this rule, with a company that subcontracted work overseas.

The Finance Act twenty twenty six made one small change here, in section thirty four. A separate relaxation lets Northern Ireland companies claiming the intensive relief escape the overseas restriction, because of the Windsor Framework. The Act confirms that this relaxation applies only to the intensive relief, and the change has effect for claims made on or after the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty four. In other words, it is retrospective. It will rarely matter in a paper about large groups, but it is a good illustration of how a technical correction can reach back in time.

Seven steps to cash.

Now the hard part, slowly. The credit is not simply paid out. It flows through seven steps set out from section ten forty two I of the two thousand and nine Act onwards. Picture a waterfall. The credit first fills the company's own tax pool. What spills over loses a splash to notional tax. Then it meets a weir set by the company's payroll taxes. Only what passes all of that flows on to other periods, other group companies, other taxes, and finally to the company's bank account.

Before the steps begin, any step two amount brought forward from an earlier period is used to pay the current period's corporation tax.

Step one. The credit discharges the company's corporation tax liability for the period of the claim. Calder stops here. Its credit of four hundred thousand pounds is less than its tax of seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds, so all of it is used at step one.

Step two is the notional tax deduction. If any credit is left after step one, it is reduced by notional tax. The rate is the main rate of twenty five per cent if the company's profits are chargeable at the main rate, and that includes a company in the marginal relief band. Otherwise the rate is the small profits rate of nineteen per cent, which covers small profit companies and loss-making companies. The lower rate for loss makers is the main design concession in the merged scheme. The amount deducted is called the step two amount, and it is not lost. It can be surrendered to another company in the group, or carried forward to pay the company's corporation tax in later periods.

Why notional tax at all? Because the credit is taxable. A loss-making company pays no tax on its credit this year, but the credit reduces its loss, and so its future relief. The notional tax deduction stops the company taking cash today for the tax element of the credit.

Step three is the pay as you earn cap. Cash from the credit is limited to twenty thousand pounds plus three hundred per cent of the company's relevant pay as you earn and national insurance liabilities for the period. Anything above the cap is carried forward as credit of the next period. The cap does not apply if the company is exempt. Broadly, H M R C's guidance says the company is exempt if its staff are creating or managing intellectual property it can exploit, and no more than fifteen per cent of its qualifying expenditure goes on connected subcontractors and externally provided workers. The cap targets claims by shell companies with no real payroll, which is where much of the fraud sat.

Step four. What remains discharges the company's corporation tax for any other accounting period.

Step five. A company in a group may surrender the whole or part of what remains to another group member, which uses it to pay its own corporation tax.

Step six. What remains can discharge the company's other liabilities to H M R C, such as value added tax or pay as you earn.

Step seven. Only then is any balance paid to the company in cash, and H M R C need not pay while the company is not a going concern or while its return is under enquiry.

The May twenty twenty four examiners reported that candidates confused step one, the set off against the period's own tax, with step two, the notional tax restriction. Learn the order as a sentence. Own tax, notional tax, payroll cap, other periods, group, other taxes, cash.

Surrender inside the group.

Step five is where a large group finds value, and Brackenwell shows how.

In our invented case, Tarnmoor buys Brackenwell Sensors on the first of July of Group Year Two. Brackenwell is the loss-making sensor developer founded by Doctor Asha Varma, who stays on as its chief technology officer. In Group Year Two, which for Brackenwell is the year to the thirty first of December, its qualifying expenditure is three million pounds. As we shall see in a moment, Brackenwell is no longer a small company that year. So it claims the merged credit, twenty per cent of three million pounds, six hundred thousand pounds.

Run the steps. At step one, Brackenwell has no corporation tax to pay, because it is making losses. Nothing is used. At step two, it is a loss maker, so notional tax is at nineteen per cent. Nineteen per cent of six hundred thousand pounds is one hundred and fourteen thousand pounds, and four hundred and eighty six thousand pounds remains. At step three, Brackenwell's relevant payroll taxes are about nine hundred thousand pounds, so its cap is twenty thousand pounds plus two point seven million pounds, two point seven two million pounds. The cap does not bite. At step four, there is no other period's tax to pay.

At step five, Tom Hesketh, the group's head of tax, has a choice. Brackenwell could go on to take the four hundred and eighty six thousand pounds in cash. Or it could surrender it to a group company that pays tax. Tarnmoor Engineering, the main trading company, has a corporation tax bill of two million, two hundred and twenty six thousand, two hundred and fifty pounds for Group Year Two. Brackenwell surrenders the four hundred and eighty six thousand pounds to it. It also surrenders the one hundred and fourteen thousand pound step two amount, which would otherwise sit idle in a company that will make losses for years. Together the two surrenders pay six hundred thousand pounds of Tarnmoor Engineering's tax. The surrendered credit discharges Tarnmoor Engineering's liability when Brackenwell's claim is made. Its instalments are still based on its full liability.

Does the group lose anything? The credit is taxable income for Brackenwell, so its loss for the year is six hundred thousand pounds smaller. Because the year's loss is split by time, half of that reduction falls on the loss Brackenwell surrenders to Tarnmoor Engineering after the acquisition, and half on its restricted loss from before it. Valued at twenty five per cent throughout, that costs one hundred and fifty thousand pounds, leaving a net benefit of four hundred and fifty thousand pounds, fifteen per cent of three million pounds. Since the earlier half may never be usable, the real cost is probably lower. The steps move cash around. The rate decides value.

Next, the money between the companies. Tarnmoor Engineering pays Brackenwell for the credit it received, so that each company's accounts show what it gave up and what it gained, which matters to its directors and its creditors. Here the Finance Act twenty twenty six helps. Section thirty one inserts new subsections into section ten forty two N. A payment for surrendered credit, made under an agreement between the companies and not exceeding the credit surrendered, is ignored in computing both companies' profits, and is not a distribution. It applies to payments made on or after the twenty sixth of November, twenty twenty five. So Tarnmoor Engineering's payment of six hundred thousand pounds is tax neutral. Pay more than the credit, and the excess falls outside the protection.

Research and development intensive companies.

Now the second relief. Alongside the merged credit, the law keeps an enhanced relief for one kind of company only, a small or medium-sized enterprise that is loss-making and research intensive. Practitioners call it enhanced R and D intensive support, or E R I S.

Start with size. For research relief, a small or medium-sized enterprise is defined by the European Commission's recommendation of two thousand and three, with the ceilings doubled. The company must have fewer than five hundred staff, and either turnover of no more than one hundred million euros or a balance sheet total of no more than eighty six million euros. The recommendation's own ceilings are two hundred and fifty staff, fifty million euros and forty three million euros. The twenty twenty six exam tax tables set out the definition, so you need to know how to apply it rather than memorise every figure.

The recommendation does not look at the company alone. A linked enterprise, broadly one that controls or is controlled by the company, usually through more than half of the voting rights, is added in full. A partner enterprise, broadly a holding of between twenty five and fifty per cent, is added in proportion to the holding.

Next, intensity. The company's relevant research expenditure must be at least thirty per cent of its total relevant expenditure, with the figures of connected companies brought in. A company that met the test in its previous twelve month period, with a valid claim, gets one year's grace if it dips below.

Then the relief. The company deducts its qualifying expenditure in full and takes an extra deduction of eighty six per cent, one hundred and eighty six per cent in all. If that leaves a loss, it may surrender part of the loss for a payable credit at fourteen point five per cent. The surrenderable loss is the lower of the unrelieved trading loss and one hundred and eighty six per cent of the related qualifying expenditure. The unrelieved loss is the loss left after any relief against the company's other profits of the period. The credit is not taxable, unlike the merged credit, and the loss surrendered is gone. At best, a company receives one hundred and eighty six per cent of fourteen point five per cent, almost twenty seven pence in cash for each pound of qualifying spending. The pay as you earn cap applies here too, as does the exemption. Companies in Northern Ireland meet one further limit, under section eleven twelve J, which caps their extra relief at the level of de minimis State aid.

Brackenwell, before Tarnmoor bought it, is the model case. In its year to the thirty first of December of Group Year One, it had forty five staff and was independent, owned by its founders and venture investors. Its relevant research spending was three point five million pounds out of total relevant expenditure of five million pounds, an intensity of seventy per cent. Its qualifying expenditure was three point five million pounds, so the extra deduction was three point zero one million pounds. Its trading loss of four point two million pounds grew to seven point two one million pounds.

The cap on the surrenderable loss is one hundred and eighty six per cent of three point five million pounds, six point five one million pounds. That is less than the loss, so Brackenwell surrenders six point five one million pounds, and its credit is fourteen point five per cent of that, nine hundred and forty three thousand nine hundred and fifty pounds. Its payroll tax cap, at two point seven two million pounds, does not bite. The remaining loss of seven hundred thousand pounds is carried forward.

That credit was due to Brackenwell for a year when it was independent. It matters in the deal. A buyer who pays for a company with a large research credit pending must decide whether the price includes it, and the sale agreement should say who benefits if H M R C reduces it. Chapter twenty, on buying and selling companies, picks that up.

Linked enterprises and the cliff edge of acquisition.

Here is this chapter's main misconception. Many people think a small subsidiary of a large group can claim the intensive relief because the subsidiary itself is small. It cannot. Size is tested across linked enterprises. The moment Tarnmoor owns Brackenwell, the group's thousands of staff and its revenue of more than a billion pounds are added to Brackenwell's own. Brackenwell is no longer a small or medium-sized enterprise. It can claim only the merged credit.

The May twenty twenty four paper turned on exactly this. A parent and its research subsidiary were linked enterprises, so the size tests had to be applied to both together, and the examiners reported that most candidates missed it.

The next question is timing. The recommendation normally lets a company keep its status until it crosses the thresholds in two consecutive years, a cushion against a single good or bad year. H M R C's view is that the cushion does not apply when a company is taken over by a large group. In H M R C's view, the company is treated as large for research purposes for the whole accounting period in which it is acquired, including the months before the takeover.

That is why Brackenwell's Group Year Two claim is a merged credit claim on all three million pounds of spending, including the half year before the first of July. The point is H M R C's guidance rather than settled law, but it is how claims are processed and a well advised buyer plans around it. Advisers sometimes suggest that the target's accounting period should end at completion, so that the pre-acquisition months form a separate period that can still be tested as a small company. In our invented case, nobody thought of that until too late. The lesson is to put research status on the due diligence list before the sale agreement is signed.

The size test also works in reverse. A small company that is part owned by an investor holding between twenty five and fifty per cent must include a share of the investor's own figures. Before acquisition, the question was whether Brackenwell's venture investors made it a partner of anything larger. The recommendation has special rules for some kinds of investor, and in our invented case they were satisfied. In real work you would check them against the text in H M R C's manual.

Telling H M R C first.

Back to Graham Pike and his clock. Two procedural requirements now guard every claim.

The first is claim notification. Section eleven forty two A of the two thousand and nine Act requires a company to notify H M R C in advance if it is claiming for the first time, or if it has not made a claim in the three years ending with the last day of the notification period. The notification period begins on the first day of the period of account and ends six months after the period of account ends. Without a notification, a claim made after that period ends is invalid. Regulations made in twenty twenty three set out what the notification must contain, and H M R C's directions require it online, naming the company officer responsible.

For Calder, the period of account ends on the thirty first of March of Group Year Two, so the notification must be in by the thirtieth of September of Group Year Two. Graham files it in April. Brackenwell does not need to notify for Group Year Two, because it claimed the intensive relief for Group Year One, within the three year window.

Note the trap in the wording. The window runs from the period of account, not the accounting period. Where a long period of account is split into two accounting periods, the six months run from the end of the period of account. And a company whose last claim was more than three years ago is treated like a first time claimant.

The second requirement is the additional information form. For claims made on or after the eighth of August, twenty twenty three, every claim must be supported by a form giving the projects, the costs by category and the people involved, submitted before the claim in the return. H M R C has power to remove a claim from a return where the company failed to meet a requirement for making it, such as the form.

The ordinary time limit then applies. A research claim can be made, amended or withdrawn within two years from the end of the period of account, in the company return rules in Schedule eighteen to the Finance Act nineteen ninety eight.

For a large group, this becomes a calendar. Tom Hesketh's team keeps a list of every company that does research, its period of account, whether it has claimed in the last three years, and the notification deadline. A company that joins the group, a newly formed subsidiary, or a company that pauses its research for a few years, is exactly the kind that falls through the gaps. Losing a claim through a missed form is not a technical failure that H M R C can overlook. The law simply says the claim cannot be made.

Research and development allowances.

Not all research spending is revenue. Calder's half million pound test rig is plant used for research. Capital expenditure never enters the merged credit or the intensive relief. Instead, Part six of the Capital Allowances Act gives a research and development allowance of one hundred per cent.

The allowance applies to capital expenditure on research and development related to the trade, undertaken by the trader or on its behalf. The meaning of research and development follows the same accounting based definition and guidelines as the credit. Land does not qualify. The allowance is given for the chargeable period in which the expenditure is incurred, or for the period in which the trade starts if the spending comes first, and the company may claim less than the full amount. When the asset is later sold, its disposal value brings a balancing charge.

Why does the allowance exist at all? Without it, research buildings and equipment would be relieved slowly, or not at all, and the incentive would favour research done with people and materials over research that needs heavy kit. The allowance gives the whole cost at once, which matches the way the credit treats revenue spending.

Calder's rig gets a five hundred thousand pound allowance in its year to the thirty first of March of Group Year Two. In our invented case, that allowance sits inside Calder's capital allowances of one point eight million pounds for the year, alongside one point three million pounds of ordinary plant and machinery allowances.

Why choose the research allowance over full expensing? For a company, new plant may already get full expensing at one hundred per cent, and chapter eight covered it. The research allowance has one big advantage. It covers capital spending on buildings used for research, which full expensing never does. Against that, a disposal triggers a balancing charge. The November twenty twenty five paper had a new subsidiary with research equipment, and the examiners reported that few candidates mentioned the research allowance at all. A new company may incur research capital spending before it starts to trade. The allowance then waits for the period in which the trade begins, and the timing affects when the company's tax and any instalments fall due.

Where the regimes meet.

Research relief does not live alone, and the examiner likes the joins.

First, the corporate interest restriction, which chapter twenty eight owns. The restriction allows interest deductions by reference to tax E B I T D A, short for earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, computed on tax figures. The law excludes from tax E B I T D A both the merged credit and the intensive relief deductions. So the credit does not increase a company's capacity for interest, and capital allowances, including research allowances, do not reduce it. That is why Calder's tax E B I T D A for its first group year is four point four million pounds, before both its allowances and its credit.

Second, the accounts. The merged credit is designed to sit above the line, in operating profit, like a grant, and it is taxable. The intensive relief payable credit is not taxable, and in practice it is often shown in the tax charge. Chapter six, on deferred tax, explains why the difference affects the effective tax rate the group reports.

The same chapter covers deferred tax on the allowance itself. Calder's rig is written off at once for tax but depreciated over its life in the accounts. That temporary difference creates a deferred tax liability, which unwinds as the rig is depreciated.

Third, intellectual property. Ashlar's patents, filed in Group Year Two, will later earn Calder the Patent Box's ten per cent rate. The Patent Box rewards research done by the company itself more than acquired research or work bought from connected parties. Chapter eleven explains how.

Fourth, transfer pricing. When research is done in one group company for the benefit of another, the price must be at arm's length. The November twenty twenty three paper asked candidates to price a research centre, and the cost plus method was the answer expected. Chapter twenty seven takes this further, and shows how the location of research functions affects where the group's intangibles profits are taxed. One contrast is worth noting now. If Brackenwell does research for Calder after the acquisition, both companies are in the United Kingdom, and the Finance Act twenty twenty six exemption for transactions between United Kingdom companies will usually take the work out of transfer pricing, subject to conditions that chapter twenty seven explains. But for the research credit, Calder and Brackenwell are now connected, so the sixty five per cent rule no longer applies to Calder's payments, and the connected party measure takes over.

Fifth, groups. Surrender of the credit is a group matter, governed by the payment steps and the Finance Act twenty twenty six payment rule. It is separate from group relief for losses, which chapter fifteen owns, though the two interact, as Brackenwell's reduced loss showed.

Going further, the tax function's work.

In a large group, the tax function's job is to make sure that every genuine claim is made, and that no claim is made that should not be.

The first task is finding the research. Engineers do not think in tax categories. In a group of Tarnmoor's size, research happens in places the tax team never visits, such as a product team improving a pump seal, a software group building control systems, or a start-up bought last year. A group needs a process that reaches the people who run projects, asks them what was uncertain, and records the answers when the work happens, not two years later. Dan Hartley's project notes are worth more than any adviser's narrative written after the event. If H M R C opens an enquiry, the questions will be about the project. What was the uncertainty, who resolved it, and how do you know? A group that can answer from its own records is in a strong position. A group that relies on a narrative assembled by an outside firm two years later is not.

The second task is the calendar, which we have seen, with its claim notification deadlines, additional information forms, and return deadlines, company by company.

The third task is location. The overseas restriction means research done abroad through contractors will usually not qualify. A group that is choosing where to place a laboratory needs that fact on the table, alongside the transfer pricing consequences of putting valuable functions in one country rather than another.

The fourth task is acquisitions. Due diligence on a research company must ask whether it has claimed correctly, whether its size status is right, whether credits are pending, and whether the acquisition will end its intensive relief.

The fifth task is ethics. In our invented case, a firm offers to review the group's claims for a share of any extra refund it finds. Tom Hesketh asks it to explain each additional project in technical terms. It cannot. He declines. The professional conduct rules, which chapter four discusses, expect an adviser to stand behind every claim filed. H M R C's compliance work in recent years has been aimed squarely at claims built on vague narratives and contingent fees.

How the examiner tests it.

Research and development has appeared three times in the last seven papers. In May twenty twenty four, a ten mark question turned on a parent and research subsidiary that were linked enterprises, and on the payment steps. Answers were poor. In May twenty twenty five, a computation included the merged scheme with overseas subcontracting and cloud and software costs, and the examiners marked the research part leniently because the law had just changed. In November twenty twenty five, a full computation again included the merged scheme, and repairs were wrongly included by some candidates. In the same sitting, a question on a new subsidiary expected a mention of research allowances.

The pattern is clear. The examiners rarely set a whole question on research alone, though May twenty twenty four did, for ten marks. More often, research is a few marks inside a fifteen or twenty mark computation, where the credit, its rate and its use at step one each earn half a mark or a mark. Those marks are cheap if you know the steps, and expensive in time if you have to think them out in the exam. So expect research to arrive inside a computation more often than on its own. The credit is a trading receipt, so add it to the adjusted profit, then use it at step one against the tax. Show the rate you use at step two, and say why. Test size across linked enterprises before you decide which relief applies. Strip out capital items, repairs and overseas contractor costs from the qualifying expenditure, and give the research allowance for the capital items. And if the scenario mentions a company that has not claimed before, say the words claim notification.

Remember too that the exam's tax tables give the credit rate, the extra deduction and the payable credit rate, and the size definition. What they do not give you is the order of the steps, the notional tax rates and their reasons, or the claim notification rule. Those you must carry in your head.

All three rows are core on the twenty twenty six grid, which this book follows for the twenty twenty seven sittings. From twenty twenty eight, the reformed syllabus drops research intensive small companies from this paper, but that is after the twenty twenty seven sittings.

What to take away.

Research relief exists because ideas leak, so the state shares the cost. Fraud and error followed, and almost every procedural rule is a fence built in response.

For accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty four, the merged scheme gives a research and development expenditure credit of twenty per cent of qualifying expenditure. The credit is a taxable trading receipt. Its net value is fifteen per cent for a company paying twenty five per cent, and sixteen point two per cent at nineteen per cent.

Qualifying expenditure is staffing costs, externally provided workers, contractor payments, consumables, software, data and cloud costs. Unconnected contractors and externally provided workers count at sixty five per cent. Every cost must have been paid. Capital spending is out of the credit, and gets a one hundred per cent research and development allowance under Part six of the Capital Allowances Act instead. Repairs and overheads are out. Contractor work done abroad is out, unless the conditions needed are not present in the United Kingdom and it would be wholly unreasonable to replicate them, with cost and availability of workers ignored. The company that decides to undertake the research claims it.

The credit runs through seven steps. Own tax. Notional tax at twenty five per cent, or nineteen per cent for small profit and loss-making companies, with the step two amount surrendered or carried forward. The payroll cap of twenty thousand pounds plus three hundred per cent of pay as you earn and national insurance, unless exempt. Other periods. Group surrender. Other taxes. Cash. A payment for surrendered credit, up to the credit surrendered, is ignored for tax and is not a distribution, under the Finance Act twenty twenty six.

Enhanced R and D intensive support is for loss-making small or medium-sized enterprises only. That means fewer than five hundred staff, and turnover up to one hundred million euros or a balance sheet up to eighty six million euros, with linked enterprises added in full and partners in proportion. Intensity must be at least thirty per cent. The relief is an eighty six per cent extra deduction, one hundred and eighty six per cent in all, and a fourteen point five per cent payable credit on the lower of the unrelieved loss and one hundred and eighty six per cent of the qualifying expenditure. A subsidiary of a large group cannot claim it, and H M R C's view is that a company acquired by a large group is large for the whole period of the acquisition.

A first claim, or a claim after three years without one, needs claim notification within six months of the end of the period of account, or the claim is invalid. Every claim needs the additional information form.

In our invented case, Calder's credit of four hundred thousand pounds pays more than half of its seven hundred and fifty thousand pound tax bill, leaving three hundred and fifty thousand pounds to pay. Brackenwell's intensive credit before acquisition was nine hundred and forty three thousand nine hundred and fifty pounds. Its merged credit after acquisition was six hundred thousand pounds, all surrendered to pay Tarnmoor Engineering's tax.

Ashlar's work has produced something valuable, and the law treats valuable knowledge as an asset of its own. The next chapter follows the patents and the know-how into the regime for intangible assets and intellectual property.


Chapter eleven: Intangible assets and intellectual property.

On the thirtieth of September, in Group Year Three of our invented group, Tarnmoor, Dan Hartley clears his desk at Calder Valve Engineering. His division is closing. The next morning, the first of October, Calder sells that division's customer contracts and its manufacturing know-how to the group's Vallarian subsidiary, Tarnmoor Vallaria, for six million pounds. Vallaria, like everything else in this story except Ireland, is invented.

Think about what was sold. Not a building. Not a machine. The machines went separately. What crossed the border was a set of promises from customers and a body of knowledge, much of it written down in the weeks before, from interviews with engineers like Dan. You cannot drop it on your foot. Yet it was worth six million pounds, and the tax system has to decide three things about it. Is the money income or a capital gain? What was it worth, when the buyer and the seller answer to the same board? And when the buyer is abroad, what stops the know-how leaving the United Kingdom's tax net at a bargain price?

This chapter answers those questions. It sits in Part Two, on measuring profit, because the intangibles code is the clearest case of tax following the accounts. Intangible fixed assets are core for the paper, grade one. The Patent Box is awareness, grade three. The Living Law, chapter twenty one, introduced the regime at the level of a company buying and writing off an asset. Here we go deeper, into goodwill, reinvestment, groups, degrouping, related parties, the twenty twenty six move to arm's length pricing, and the Patent Box. Everything is taught on the law for the financial year twenty twenty six.

Why intangibles got their own code.

Before April two thousand and two, a company's intangible assets lived in an awkward place. Goodwill and most other intangibles were capital assets. A company that bought goodwill got no deduction as it wore away. When it sold, it had a chargeable gain. Patents and know-how had their own small capital allowance codes. Trade marks and brands, in general, got nothing. The result was a patchwork that bore little relation to how the accounts treated the same assets, and it fitted badly with an economy whose value was moving from factories to ideas.

The answer was a single code, introduced by Schedule twenty nine to the Finance Act two thousand and two, and now rewritten as Part eight of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act. Its central idea is simple. For a company, an intangible fixed asset is taxed as income, not as capital. The amortisation and impairment in the accounts are deductions. Receipts and profits on sale are taxable credits. Losses on sale are deductions. Tax follows the accounts, with a few deliberate departures that are where most of the exam marks sit.

The code is symmetrical, and that is its purpose. A company that gets a deduction as an asset is written down must give the deduction back if it later sells for more. Think of it as a meter running in both directions. Every pound of relief is metered out, and if the asset turns out to have kept its value, the meter runs back.

There is a boundary. Part eight applies to assets created on or after the first of April, two thousand and two, and to assets acquired from an unrelated party after that date. Older assets, held before the regime began, stayed in the capital gains world. From the first of July, twenty twenty, any asset acquired from that date comes into Part eight whoever the seller is. The detailed rules for the older assets, in Chapter sixteen of Part eight, are outside the syllabus. You need only spot that an asset is old and say that it sits outside the code.

For a large group the code matters in four ways. It gives relief for bought intangibles. It taxes the sale of home-grown ones, often at far more than their book value. It lets assets move around a group without tax, but polices them when a company leaves. And it decides the price when an intangible crosses a border to a related company.

What counts as an intangible fixed asset.

The definition starts with the accounts. An intangible asset has its meaning under generally accepted accounting practice. The statute then widens it. It includes intellectual property, which covers patents, trade marks, registered designs, copyright and design right. It also covers any idea, information or technique not protected by such a right. That is how know-how gets in. Goodwill is expressly included.

The word fixed matters. The asset must be acquired or created for use on a continuing basis in the company's activities. Know-how bought to be resold quickly is not a fixed asset.

Next come the exclusions. Rights over land and over tangible movable property are out. Financial assets are out. So are shares and rights in companies and trusts. Shares are the big one. When a group buys a company, it buys shares, and the goodwill inside that company never becomes the group's intangible asset for tax. A company may also elect to keep capital spending on computer software within the capital allowance rules instead.

An asset inside the code is called a chargeable intangible asset. Each one is either used in a trade, held for a property business, or held for some other purpose. Credits and debits on trading assets go straight into the trading profit. Everything else is non-trading, and pools into a non-trading gain or loss on intangibles. We come back to that pool shortly.

In our invented case, the customer contracts and know-how Calder sold were trading assets. They were also home-grown. Calder had built them up over decades, and the cost of building them had always been charged in the accounts as it was spent. So they had no cost on the balance sheet and no cost for tax. Hold on to that, because it decides how big the tax bill on the sale will be.

The same is true of most intellectual property a group creates for itself. When Calder's engineers worked on Project Ashlar, the cost of their research was charged in the accounts as it was spent, and relieved through the research and development expenditure credit that chapter ten explains. The patents that came out of that work carry only a small capitalised cost, such as filing fees. That is a fair result. The research has already been relieved once. But it means that when home-grown intellectual property is sold, almost all of the price is taxable. Groups that think of their patents as capital assets, protected by the substantial shareholding exemption, are often surprised. The exemption protects a sale of shares, never a sale of the assets themselves.

Writing down by the accounts, or at four per cent.

The default rule is that the tax deduction follows the accounts. If a company amortises an intangible, or writes it down for impairment, the amount in the profit and loss account is the deduction. Where the tax cost differs from the accounting value, the statute scales the accounting write-off by the ratio of tax written down value to accounting value. A later reversal of an impairment is a taxable credit.

Following the accounts creates a problem. Some intangibles are never amortised. Under international accounting standards, goodwill and intangibles with an indefinite useful life are not amortised at all. They are only tested for impairment. Under F R S one oh two, by contrast, every intangible, goodwill included, is treated as having a finite life and is amortised. So two identical acquisitions can produce very different tax deductions, depending on the accounting framework.

The fixed-rate election is Parliament's fix. A company may elect to write an asset down at four per cent of its cost each year, whatever the accounts do. The debit is the lower of four per cent of cost and the remaining tax written down value. At four per cent, the cost is relieved over twenty five years.

The conditions are strict. The election is made in writing to H M R C, which is His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, within two years after the end of the accounting period in which the asset was created or acquired. It covers all the capitalised spending on that asset. And it is irrevocable.

When does it help? Take a labelled example, not part of the story. Suppose Tarnmoor Engineering buys a registered trade mark for five million pounds and its accounts give it an indefinite life, so there is no amortisation. Without an election, there is no deduction unless the brand is impaired. With the election, there is a deduction of two hundred thousand pounds a year, worth fifty thousand pounds of tax a year at twenty five per cent. For a long-lived asset that the accounts will never amortise, the election is usually worth making. For an asset the accounts write off over five years, it would slow relief down. The skill is choosing asset by asset, inside the two-year window.

There is one twist for goodwill. As we will see, goodwill and customer-related assets that qualify for relief at all are written down at a fixed six point five per cent, not four per cent, and not by the accounts.

Realisation, when an intangible leaves.

A realisation is the event that ends, or reduces, the company's ownership. In general it is a transaction that causes the asset to cease to be recognised on the balance sheet, or would do so if it had a balance sheet value. A sale is the obvious case. A part disposal is a part realisation.

The arithmetic depends on the asset's history. If the asset has been written down for tax, the credit is the proceeds less the tax written down value. If it has not been written down, the credit is the proceeds less the cost recognised for tax. If the proceeds are lower, there is a debit instead. Proceeds are the amount recognised in the accounts, less incidental costs of the realisation. Where the consideration is not in money, it is treated as money equal to what it would reasonably have fetched in the open market. On a part realisation, only a matching proportion of the cost is set against the proceeds.

An asset that was never on the balance sheet is treated as if it had a balance sheet value. That is the rule that catches home-grown assets. Their cost was expensed long ago, so their tax cost is nil, and the whole of the proceeds is a credit.

Now return to the first of October, in Group Year Three. Calder sells its process-valve customer contracts and know-how to Tarnmoor Vallaria for six million pounds. The cost for tax is nil. So the realisation credit is the full six million pounds. Because the assets were used in Calder's trade, the credit is a trading credit. It lands in Calder's nine-month accounting period to the thirty first of December, Group Year Three. At twenty five per cent, it carries one point five million pounds of corporation tax.

Notice what has not happened. There is no capital gain, no indexation, no capital loss to set against it, and no substantial shareholding exemption. It is income, taxed as trading profit. The related plant, sold for one point four million pounds, follows the capital allowance rules of chapter eight, not these.

Also notice the price. Six million pounds is what Calder and Tarnmoor Vallaria agreed. Both are owned by Tarnmoor. Later in this chapter we will see that the law does not simply accept that figure. It asks what independent parties would have paid. In our invented case, H M R C will later argue for nine and a half million pounds, and the dispute will settle years afterwards at eight million. Chapter twenty seven tells that story. Here the point is only that a realisation credit is only as good as the price behind it.

Non-trading debits, credits and losses.

Not every intangible is used in a trade. A holding company might own a brand and license it to its subsidiaries. An investment company might hold a patent portfolio. For those assets, the credits and debits do not go into a trading profit. They are pooled. Royalty income, amortisation, and realisation credits and debits on non-trading assets net off to give a single non-trading gain or loss on intangible fixed assets for the period.

A net gain is simply taxed as part of total profits. A net loss gives three choices. The company may claim to set it against its total profits of the same period. It may surrender it to another group company as group relief, under the rules chapter fifteen covers. Or it may carry it forward, where it is treated as a non-trading debit of the next period and joins that period's pool.

Two classic exam points sit here. First, a debit that the goodwill rules deny as an ordinary write-down may still arise on realisation, and then it is a non-trading debit even if the asset was used in the trade. That rule stops a company turning a blocked deduction into a trading loss. Second, change of ownership rules in Part fourteen of the Corporation Tax Act twenty ten, which I will call the twenty ten Act, can block the carry forward of a company's non-trading intangibles losses, just as they block other carried-forward reliefs. Chapter fourteen has the detail.

For a trading group like Tarnmoor, most intangibles are trading assets, and the non-trading pool is small. But in the exam, a holding company with a licensing arm is a favourite way of moving an intangible out of the trade and into this pool. Read the facts for who uses the asset, not who owns it.

A labelled example shows the pool at work. Suppose a holding company owns brands that it licenses to the group's trading companies. In a year it receives royalties of one million pounds, writes its brands down by three hundred thousand pounds, and sells one brand at a loss of two hundred thousand pounds. None of these is a trading item. The pool nets them to a non-trading gain of five hundred thousand pounds, taxed as part of the holding company's total profits. Had the loss on sale been larger than the royalties, the net loss could have been set against other profits of the year, surrendered to a group company, or carried forward.

Goodwill, a door that opened, slammed and reopened.

Goodwill is the most valuable intangible most businesses own, and its tax history is a saga. Picture a door. In two thousand and two, it opened. Companies buying a business could write off purchased goodwill against profits, following their accounts. Then it slammed shut. For acquisitions from the eighth of July, twenty fifteen, relief for goodwill and customer-related intangibles was withdrawn. And in April twenty nineteen it reopened, but only for visitors carrying intellectual property.

Why slam it? The Treasury's policy paper of twenty fifteen gave the reason. Relief was available only when a company bought a business directly, not when it bought the shares of a company owning the business. That distorted deals in favour of asset purchases. The paper said that removing the relief would bring the regime into line with other major economies, reduce distortion and level the playing field for mergers and acquisitions. Why reopen it? Because the government then wanted to support investment in intangibles and the United Kingdom's attractiveness for business. The compromise of twenty nineteen is the law today, in Chapter fifteen A of Part eight.

Here is how it works. The rules apply to relevant assets. Those are goodwill, information about customers or potential customers, customer relationships, unregistered trade marks and other signs used in a business, and licences of any of these. For a relevant asset acquired or created on or after the first of April, twenty nineteen, the asset is written down at a fixed six point five per cent a year.

Then come three restrictions. First, an asset caught by the old twenty fifteen rules stays caught. Second, if the relevant asset was not acquired as part of acquiring a business, or the business acquired included no qualifying intellectual property assets, there are no write-down debits at all. Qualifying intellectual property means patents, registered designs, copyright, design right and plant breeders' rights, and their foreign equivalents and licences. Third, if the asset was acquired from a related individual or a firm, typically when a sole trader incorporates, relief is denied unless a third-party acquisition condition is met.

Finally, the cap. Where the business does include qualifying intellectual property, relief on the relevant assets is limited to six times the spending on that intellectual property. If the relevant assets cost more than that, the debits are scaled down in proportion.

Take a labelled example. Suppose a group company buys a business for twenty million pounds, with patents of two million pounds and goodwill and customer relationships of fifteen million pounds. Six times two million is twelve million. So only twelve fifteenths, which is four fifths, of the six point five per cent write-down is allowed. The annual debit is seven hundred and eighty thousand pounds, worth one hundred and ninety five thousand pounds of tax a year.

Now the story. In Group Year Two, Tarnmoor Ireland, then still resident in the United Kingdom because its board met in Leeds, bought an Irish distributor's business, including its customer list, for three million pounds. The distributor had no patents, designs or copyright to speak of. So the customer list is a relevant asset acquired with a business that had no qualifying intellectual property. There are no debits at all. Its tax value stays at its cost of three million pounds. That matters later, when Tarnmoor Ireland moves its management to Dublin and the list is deemed sold at market value, which is chapter twenty two's story.

The myth of relief for bought goodwill.

Here is the misconception of this chapter. Goodwill bought with a business always gets tax relief. Many people believe it because it was true from two thousand and two to twenty fifteen, because accountants amortise goodwill under F R S one oh two, and because the word acquisition sounds like a purchase of assets.
