It is wrong in at least four ways. First, buying shares gives no relief at all. The goodwill is the subsidiary's, or appears only in the consolidated accounts, and Part eight never sees it. Most large acquisitions are share deals, so most purchased goodwill gets nothing. Nor can a group fix that afterwards by hiving the business up from its new subsidiary into another group company. The intra-group transfer is tax-neutral, as we will see, so the transferee takes over the subsidiary's own tax cost, which for home-grown goodwill is usually nil, not the price the group paid for the shares. Second, an asset deal with no qualifying intellectual property gives no debits, as Tarnmoor Ireland found. Third, even with intellectual property, the six times cap limits relief. Fourth, a purchase from a related individual, typically an incorporation, is blocked.

And when relief is due, it is at six point five per cent, not the accounts rate. That means just over fifteen years to relieve the whole cost.

The myth has a planning consequence. A buyer will often prefer an asset deal, to get relief on the intellectual property and, within the cap, on goodwill. A seller usually prefers a share sale, because a company selling a trading subsidiary can often use the substantial shareholding exemption, which I will call the shareholding exemption, and pay no tax on the gain. That tension is at the heart of every negotiation in chapter twenty, on buying and selling companies. Price usually settles it.

The examiner tested this ground in November twenty twenty three, question four. A loss-making retailer had acquired goodwill and registered designs in twenty nineteen, inside a full computation. The registered designs were qualifying intellectual property, which opened the door for the goodwill. A candidate who said no relief for goodwill, without checking for qualifying intellectual property and the date, lost the marks. A candidate who gave relief on the full cost of the goodwill without testing the cap risked losing them too.

Reinvestment relief.

Suppose a company sells an intangible at a profit and uses the money to buy another. Should it be taxed on the first sale? The capital gains code has long said no, through roll-over relief. The intangibles code has its own version, called reinvestment relief, in Chapter seven of Part eight.

The conditions mirror roll-over. The old asset must have been a chargeable intangible asset throughout the company's ownership. The proceeds of realisation must exceed its cost recognised for tax. The company must spend on other chargeable intangible assets in a window running from twelve months before the realisation to three years after it, a window H M R C may extend. The new spending must be capitalised in the accounts. And the company must claim.

The arithmetic has a familiar shape. If the company reinvests at least the full proceeds, the relief is the proceeds less the old asset's cost. If it reinvests less than the proceeds, the relief is the amount reinvested less the old asset's cost, and nothing if that is negative. Either way, the realisation credit is reduced by the relief, and so is the tax cost of the new asset.

Notice what is never relieved. Any write-downs already given are clawed back in full. Reinvestment relief defers only the profit above original cost.

Take a labelled example. Suppose a company bought a brand for one million pounds, wrote it down for tax to six hundred thousand, and sells it for three million pounds. The realisation credit is two point four million. It spends two and a half million on a new patent within the window. That is less than the proceeds, so the relief is two and a half million less the original cost of one million, giving one and a half million. The taxable credit falls to nine hundred thousand pounds. That is the four hundred thousand of clawed-back write-downs plus the half a million not reinvested. The new patent's tax cost is one million pounds. The full working is in the reading edition.

Groups can share this relief. Spending by another company in the same intangibles group counts, on a joint claim. And if a group company buys control of a company that owns chargeable intangibles, the underlying assets can count as reinvestment, even though the group bought shares.

In our invented case, Tom Hesketh, the group head of tax, looks at whether Calder's six million pound credit could be deferred. Calder's know-how had no tax cost, so the potential relief is large. But it needs capitalised spending on new intangibles by Calder or a group company inside the window, and a claim would cut the new asset's tax cost by the same amount. Tom finds nothing that would make a claim worth having. In our invented case, no claim is made, and Calder pays the tax.

Tax-neutral transfers inside a group.

A group often wants to move an intangible from one company to another. A brand migrates to a new brand-owning company. Patents follow a business into a new subsidiary before a sale. If each move were a taxable realisation at market value, groups would be stuck. So the code makes intra-group transfers tax-neutral.

First, the group. Part eight uses a group definition built on the same lines as the capital gains group. A principal company and its seventy five per cent subsidiaries, and their seventy five per cent subsidiaries, so long as each is an effective fifty one per cent subsidiary of the principal company. Non-resident companies can be members.

The rule in section seven hundred and seventy five of the two thousand and nine Act has three conditions. Both companies are members of the same group at the time of transfer. The asset is a chargeable intangible asset of the transferor immediately before the transfer. And it is a chargeable intangible asset of the transferee immediately after. If so, the transfer is tax-neutral. The transferor has no credit or debit. The transferee steps into its shoes, as if it had held the asset all along and done everything the transferor did. And the transfer pricing rules do not apply to it.

The third condition is the one that matters across borders. Tarnmoor Vallaria is a member of the Tarnmoor intangibles group. But after the sale, the know-how is not a chargeable intangible asset of Tarnmoor Vallaria, because Tarnmoor Vallaria is not within the charge to United Kingdom corporation tax on it. So the October sale fails the test. It is a realisation at the transfer price, taxed in Calder. Tax neutrality is only for assets that stay inside the United Kingdom net.

There are exclusions too. For example, a transferor that has elected for the foreign branch exemption cannot pass on neutrally an asset used in its exempt foreign branch.

Now a transfer that passes. In Group Year Six, Tarnmoor Engineering hives down its actuators business into a new subsidiary, Tarnmoor Actuators. Among the assets are Tarnmoor Engineering's actuator patents, with a tax written down value of one point two million pounds and a market value of four million pounds. Both companies are in the group and in the charge to corporation tax. The patents pass at no tax cost. Tarnmoor Actuators simply takes over the tax written down value of one point two million pounds. Chapter nineteen covers the hive-down of the trade itself.

The degrouping charge and its switch-off.

Tax neutrality invites a game. Move an asset into a subsidiary at no tax cost, then sell the subsidiary's shares. The group has sold the asset, but no realisation has happened. The degrouping charge stops that game.

The law says that where a company leaves a group within six years of acquiring an asset in a tax-neutral transfer, and still holds the asset when it leaves, it is treated as having realised and immediately reacquired the asset at its market value at the time of the original transfer. The resulting credit, or debit, is brought into account immediately before the company leaves the group. There is a related rule where an associated company that leaves at the same time holds the asset.

Two features differ from the capital gains degrouping charge in section one seven nine of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act nineteen ninety two, which I will call the Gains Act. First, the intangibles charge falls on the company leaving the group, not on the seller of its shares. Second, until twenty nineteen there was no equivalent of the twenty eleven gains reform, which adds the degrouping gain to the share sale proceeds so that the shareholding exemption can cover it. That left a gap. A share sale fully exempt for gains could still carry an intangibles charge inside the company being sold, which its buyer would then inherit.

The Finance Act twenty nineteen closed the gap with section seven hundred and eighty two A of the two thousand and nine Act, for degroupings on or after the seventh of November, twenty eighteen. Where a company leaves a group because of a disposal of shares by another group company, and that disposal would qualify for the shareholding exemption, the degrouping charge simply does not apply. H M R C's manual describes the purpose as stopping degrouping adjustments from impeding genuine commercial disposals of trading businesses. Think of it as the twin of the gains rule, reached by a different road. The gains rule moves the charge into an exempt sale. The intangibles rule switches it off.

Back to the story. On the thirty first of December, Group Year Six, Tarnmoor Engineering sells Tarnmoor Actuators to an invented American buyer, Brennock Industries, eleven months after the hive-down. Chapter twenty explains why the sale qualifies for the shareholding exemption, even though Tarnmoor Engineering has held the new company's shares for less than twelve months. Because it qualifies, the patents' degrouping charge is switched off.

What would it have cost? Ignoring any write-downs since the transfer, Tarnmoor Actuators would have been treated as selling and buying back the patents at four million pounds. Less the one point two million of tax written down value, that is a credit of two point eight million pounds, and seven hundred thousand pounds of tax at twenty five per cent. Switched off, the charge is nil. But note the price of the switch-off. With no deemed reacquisition, the patents keep their low tax value of one point two million pounds in Tarnmoor Actuators' hands. The buyer gets no uplift, which a well-advised buyer will reflect in the price.

Where the switch-off does not apply, the group has tools. The degrouping credit can be reallocated to another group company by election, it can be matched against reinvestment, and unpaid tax can be recovered from other group companies or a controlling director. In the exam, the first question is always whether the share sale qualifies for the shareholding exemption.

Related parties and the arm's length turn of twenty twenty six.

The group rules deal with transfers inside the United Kingdom net. The related party rules deal with everything else between people who are not at arm's length. Without them, a company could sell an intangible to a friendly party cheaply, or buy one dearly, and shift profit with a stroke of a pen.

A related party, for this code, includes a company that controls or is controlled by another, two companies under common control, and a company in which another has a major interest. Participators and their connected individuals are also related to a close company. Between related parties, a transfer of a chargeable intangible asset is treated as made at market value. The rule does not apply to a tax-neutral group transfer, which has its own rules.

Market value has a cousin, the arm's length price under the transfer pricing rules in Part four of the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act. The two can differ. Market value asks what the asset would fetch in an open market. Transfer pricing asks what independent enterprises would have agreed in the same circumstances, looking at each party's functions, assets, risks and realistic options. For a cross-border transfer, both tests could apply, with different answers.

The Finance Act twenty twenty six chose one. Paragraphs twenty five and twenty eight of its Schedule six say that the market value rule does not apply to a cross-border transfer that is subject to transfer pricing. Such a transfer is treated as made at the arm's length price. For other related party transfers, market value still applies. The new rule covers transfers and grants made on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, unless they were made under a contract that became unconditional before that date.

Take a labelled real-calendar example. Suppose a United Kingdom company sells a brand to its French sister company on the fifteenth of February, twenty twenty six. That is a cross-border transfer subject to transfer pricing, so it is priced at arm's length, not at market value. If the same sale had been under a contract that became unconditional in December twenty twenty five, the old market value rule would still govern.

In our invented case, every story period falls under this law. So Calder's sale to Tarnmoor Vallaria is priced at arm's length. The six million pounds came from a valuation report. Whether it was the arm's length price is a transfer pricing question about who really controlled the development and use of the know-how. That is where Dan's interviews come back, in chapter twenty seven.

The Patent Box, a ten per cent rate for inventions.

The last tool in this chapter is a reward, not a restriction. The Patent Box, in Part eight A of the twenty ten Act, lets a company elect to have profits from patented inventions taxed at an effective rate of ten per cent. It is awareness for the paper, grade three. You need the principles, not the full computation.

Why does it exist? It is an incentive. By cutting the tax on profits from patented inventions, it makes the United Kingdom a more attractive place to own and exploit them, not just to do the research. The regime began on the first of April, twenty thirteen, phased in so that the full benefit applied from the first of April, twenty seventeen. It was then reshaped by an international agreement through the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the O E C D, that preferential regimes for intellectual property must reward real research done by the company itself. That is the nexus approach, which applies to elections made after the thirtieth of June, twenty sixteen.

The conditions in outline. The company must be within the charge to corporation tax and must elect. It must hold qualifying patents, granted by the United Kingdom Intellectual Property Office, the European Patent Office or certain other European states, or an exclusive licence of them. It must meet the development condition, which means it, or a group company, did qualifying development on the invention. If the development was done by another group company, the holder must actively manage its portfolio.

The mechanism is a deduction, not a different rate. The deduction is the relevant intellectual property profits, multiplied by the main rate less ten per cent, divided by the main rate. At a twenty five per cent main rate, that is fifteen twenty fifths, or three fifths, of the relevant profits.

Finding relevant profits is the hard part. In outline, income is streamed between income from the patented inventions and other income. A routine return of ten per cent of certain costs is taken out, because ordinary manufacturing profit is not a reward for invention. A return for marketing assets, such as brands, comes out too. A simplified route exists for small claims. Then the nexus fraction applies. It is the company's own research spend plus research subcontracted to unconnected parties, times one point three, divided by the total research spend including connected-party subcontracting and the cost of acquiring the intellectual property. It is capped at one.

Now the story. Calder filed patents on Project Ashlar's valve design in Group Year Two. They were granted in Group Year Four. Calder elects into the Patent Box from Group Year Four and licenses the patents to Tarnmoor Vallaria for a royalty of six per cent of its Ashlar valve sales. That royalty is one point two million pounds a year. Calder did the development itself, with some work subcontracted to Brackenwell Sensors before Tarnmoor bought it, when it was unconnected. So the nexus fraction is one.

In a simplified illustration, the relevant intellectual property profits are nine hundred thousand pounds. The deduction is three fifths of that, five hundred and forty thousand pounds. The remaining three hundred and sixty thousand pounds is taxed at twenty five per cent, which is ninety thousand pounds. That is ten per cent of the nine hundred thousand. Without the box, the tax would have been two hundred and twenty five thousand. The real computation streams the profits and tests every step, and the reading edition shows the shape.

The election must be made within twelve months after the filing date of the return for the first period it is to cover. A company that revokes cannot come back in for five years.

The tax function's work, and the other regimes.

An intangibles question rarely stands alone. For a large group, the tax function's work runs across several regimes at once.

Start with acquisitions. On an asset deal, the purchase price must be allocated between goodwill, customer relationships, intellectual property, plant and stock. The allocation drives everything. It decides how much is qualifying intellectual property, how much goodwill can be relieved within the six times cap, and what capital allowances and stamp duty land tax follow. The tax team works with the valuers before the accounts are finalised, and diarises every four per cent election inside its two-year window.

Next, internal moves. Before any hive-down, check that the tax-neutral rule applies, and record the market value at the date of transfer, because that is the value the degrouping charge would use within the next six years. Before any share sale, check whether the shareholding exemption applies, because that decides whether the switch-off applies.

The calendar matters as much as the analysis. A four per cent election must be made within two years after the end of the period of acquisition. A Patent Box election must be made within twelve months after the filing date of the return for the first period it covers. A reinvestment claim must be made within the ordinary time limit for claims, with a provisional declaration possible where the reinvestment is still planned. Each of these is easy to miss in a busy group, and each is lost if missed.

Then cross-border transfers. Since the first of January, twenty twenty six, a transfer to an overseas group company is priced at arm's length. That means a functional analysis, a valuation, and transfer pricing documentation prepared at the time, as Tarnmoor's chapter twenty seven shows. A restructuring that moves know-how abroad is exactly the kind of transaction H M R C reviews.

Royalties raise their own questions. A United Kingdom company paying a royalty for intellectual property to a non-resident must normally deduct income tax at the basic rate, unless it reasonably believes a treaty lower rate applies, as chapter twenty three explains. Calder's royalty from Vallaria bears Vallarian withholding of five per cent, sixty thousand pounds a year, and the credit for it, and its limit when the Patent Box has already cut the United Kingdom tax, is chapter twenty four's business.

Finally, the corporate interest restriction in chapter twenty eight. Its measure of taxable earnings, tax E B I T D A, which stands for earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, ignores Patent Box deductions. It also ignores intangibles amortisation, including four per cent write-downs, and losses on disposals of intangibles. Realisation credits are treated more narrowly. A credit is left out only so far as it claws back earlier tax debits, which means up to the asset's cost less its tax written-down value. Think of it as amortisation in, amortisation out. H M R C's own summary sounds wider, but the statute is the test. Calder's know-how and customer contracts had no tax cost and no past debits, so its six million pound credit is a gain over cost. It raises both taxable profit and interest capacity. Chapter twenty eight works through the effect on Tarnmoor's figures.

How the examiner tests it.

Intangible fixed assets are core in the twenty twenty six grid, grade one, after moving up from non-core. They have not appeared as a standalone question in the sittings from May twenty twenty three to May twenty twenty six. They appear inside computations, as in November twenty twenty three, question four. In the twenty twenty eight grid they fall back to non-core, but your sitting uses the current grid. Patent Box is grade three and has not appeared recently.

The style is technical prose and computation, with marks of half a mark to one mark per point. A typical requirement says calculate, with explanations, the tax-adjusted trading profit, and an acquisition of a business with goodwill and intellectual property is dropped into the facts. The marks come from explaining each adjustment. Say why the goodwill qualifies, or why it does not. State the six point five per cent rate and its source. Test the cap with a short calculation. Show whether the amortisation in the accounts is added back, and what is deducted instead. The examiners reported that question four of November twenty twenty three was very well answered overall, so the marks in this area are there to be banked by those who know the rules exactly.

For Patent Box, awareness means you should be able to spot that an election would help a company with profits from patents, state the ten per cent effective rate and how the deduction works, and name the main conditions. You will not be asked to stream profits.

The traps are predictable. First, the three goodwill restrictions and the six times cap, and the six point five per cent rate, not four per cent and not the accounts. Second, the four per cent election deadline, two years after the end of the period of acquisition, and that it is irrevocable. Third, tax-neutral transfers need the asset to be chargeable in both companies. Fourth, the degrouping charge falls on the leaving company, uses market value at the time of the transfer, and is switched off by a share sale qualifying for the shareholding exemption, the twin of the gains rule. Fifth, a realisation of a home-grown asset taxes the whole proceeds. And since the Finance Act twenty twenty six, a cross-border related party transfer uses the arm's length price.

What to take away.

Intangible fixed assets are taxed as income, following the accounts. That is Part eight of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, for assets created or acquired from April two thousand and two, and for all acquisitions from the first of July, twenty twenty.

Write-downs follow the accounts, unless the company elects for four per cent a year. The election must be made within two years after the end of the period of acquisition, and it is irrevocable. It helps most for assets the accounts never amortise.

A realisation gives a credit of the proceeds less the tax written down value, or less cost if the asset was never written down. A home-grown asset has no tax cost, so the whole of the proceeds is taxed. In our invented case, Calder's sale of know-how and customer contracts to Tarnmoor Vallaria gave a credit of six million pounds and one point five million pounds of tax.

Goodwill and customer-related assets acquired from April twenty nineteen are relieved at six point five per cent a year, but only if acquired with a business that includes qualifying intellectual property, and only up to six times that intellectual property spend. There is no relief where the business had no qualifying intellectual property, as for Tarnmoor Ireland's three million pound customer list. Buying shares never gives relief for the goodwill inside.

Reinvestment relief defers the profit above original cost where proceeds are reinvested in capitalised intangibles from twelve months before to three years after. Write-downs are always clawed back.

Inside a seventy five per cent group, a transfer is tax-neutral only if the asset is chargeable in both companies' hands. A transfer to an overseas company outside the United Kingdom net is a realisation.

If a company leaves the group within six years holding such an asset, it bears a degrouping charge at the market value at the time of the transfer. The charge is switched off where it leaves through a share sale that qualifies for the shareholding exemption. That saved Tarnmoor Actuators a two point eight million pound credit on its patents.

Between related parties, transfers are at market value. Since the first of January, twenty twenty six, cross-border transfers subject to transfer pricing are at the arm's length price instead.

The Patent Box taxes relevant intellectual property profits at an effective ten per cent, through a deduction of three fifths of those profits at the twenty five per cent main rate. For Calder, nine hundred thousand pounds of relevant profits gave a deduction of five hundred and forty thousand pounds and tax of ninety thousand pounds.

All of this is the law for the financial year twenty twenty six.

The intangibles code showed tax following the accounts for things you cannot touch. Chapter twelve, on loan relationships and derivatives, follows the accounts for the most intangible thing of all, money owed and money promised.


Chapter twelve: Loan relationships and derivatives.

Between the eleventh of April and the thirteenth of June, twenty twenty four, the Court of Appeal decided three corporation tax cases about interest. In each one, a group had lent money from one of its companies to another. In each one, the group said the borrowing served a commercial end. And in each one, H M R C won. That October, the Supreme Court refused permission to appeal in all three.

Those cases are the sharp end of a much larger body of law. Every company that borrows or lends, issues a bond, pays an arrangement fee, writes off a loan or hedges a price with a derivative is inside it. So this chapter asks a plain question. The tax system follows the accountant on debt. When does it stop following?

This is the financing chapter of Part Two. Loan relationships are core material on the Advanced Technical paper, and derivatives and the special relationships treated as loans are non-core. The Living Law, chapter twenty one, introduced the basic code. Here we take it to the depth the examiner expects, with the groups, the cases and the traps.

The nineteen ninety six bargain.

Start with the problem the code was built to solve. Before nineteen ninety six, the tax treatment of company debt turned on labels. Was a payment interest, or a premium? Was a loss on a loan capital, or revenue? The answers decided whether anything was taxed or relieved at all, and clever drafting could move a return from one label to another.

The Finance Act nineteen ninety six replaced the labels with a single idea for companies. Debt is income. Every profit, loss, interest payment and cost connected with lending money is a credit or a debit in computing income, and the amounts come from the accounts. The courts have noted that origin. The Court of Appeal's judgment in Greene King, in twenty sixteen, sets out the original nineteen ninety six provisions. The rules now live in Part five of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act.

A quick recap from The Living Law. A loan relationship is a money debt, owed to or by a company, that arises from a transaction for the lending of money. Trading debits are those on borrowing for the trade. Trading credits arise only where lending is integral to the trade, as for a bank. Everything else goes into a non-trading pot, which produces either a non-trading profit or a non-trading deficit.

Now the Advanced Technical layer. The law says the matters taxed are the profits and losses on the relationships and related transactions, the interest, and the expenses incurred directly in bringing a relationship into existence, in related transactions, in making payments, or in securing receipts. Costs of a loan that never happens, and costs incurred before a loan is made, are also brought in by a separate rule.

The amounts are those recognised in profit or loss under generally accepted accounting practice. Amounts that the accounts put in other comprehensive income are left out until they are recycled into profit or loss. Where the accounting period and the period of account differ, the amounts are time-apportioned.

The accounts can measure a loan at amortised cost, using the effective interest method, or at fair value. Tax usually accepts whichever basis the accounts properly use. The important exception is that connected companies must use amortised cost, which we will come to.

So the starting rule is simple. Find the debt, find the amounts in profit or loss, and tax them as income. The rest of this chapter is about where Parliament stops the accountant at the door. Think of three bouncers. The first is the connected-party rules, which make a group's two sides of a debt mirror each other. The second is the unallowable purpose rule, which turns away debits that exist for a tax advantage. The third is the Disregard Regulations, which decide how derivatives that hedge risks are let in. Each bouncer has its own guest list, and the examiner tests all three.

What goes into the pot.

The pot holds more than interest. Discounts and premiums accrue over the life of a loan under the effective interest method. Profits and losses on selling or repaying a loan are credits and debits. Fees and other costs of raising finance are debits, spread as the accounts spread them. And exchange gains and losses on a loan go in too.

Fees are the classic examination point. When a company borrows to buy a business, the arrangement fee is not part of the cost of the shares, and for an investment holding company it is not a management expense either. It is a loan relationship debit. The examiners reported, after the May twenty twenty three sitting, that some candidates missed exactly this.

Our invented group, Tarnmoor, shows how it works. Tarnmoor plc, the listed parent, drew thirty million pounds on a revolving credit facility from its bank on the first of April in Group Year One, to buy Calder Valve Engineering. It drew twenty four million pounds more on the first of July in Group Year Two, to buy Brackenwell Sensors. In our invented case, each drawing carried an arrangement fee of three hundred thousand pounds, so six hundred thousand pounds in all.

The accounts spread each fee over the expected life of its drawing using the effective interest method. The group expected to pay most of the facility down quickly, which it did, so the fees are front-loaded. The debits that follow are two hundred and fifty thousand pounds in Group Year One, two hundred and fifty thousand pounds in Group Year Two, and one hundred thousand pounds in Group Year Three. They are non-trading debits of Tarnmoor plc, because Tarnmoor plc does not trade. Chapter thirteen explains its management expenses. These fees are kept apart from them.

Exchange movements follow the same logic. The law brings exchange gains and losses on loan relationships into account, except translation differences that the accounts take to other comprehensive income. Suppose, for this example only, that a British company lent euros to a foreign subsidiary, and over a year the pound value of the loan rose by two point four million pounds. That is a taxable exchange gain of two point four million pounds, and six hundred thousand pounds of tax, even though no cash moved.

Groups manage this in two ways. They hedge the currency, which brings in the derivative rules later in this chapter. Or, where a company borrows in a foreign currency to fund a holding of shares in that currency, the Disregard Regulations can match the loan's exchange movements with the shares, so that the movements are left out of income. The matching rule exists because the shares are capital assets whose exchange movement is not taxed as it accrues.

Tarnmoor's treasury.

For the financial year twenty twenty six, the law we apply throughout, Tarnmoor's debt sits mainly in one company. In our invented case, Tarnmoor Finance Limited is the group treasury company. Before the story begins, it issued five hundred and fifty million pounds of listed notes paying five point five per cent. That is thirty point two five million pounds of interest a year. Because the notes are listed and pay interest, they are quoted Eurobonds, so the interest can be paid without deducting income tax. Chapter twenty three explains that rule.

Tarnmoor Finance lends every pound on at six per cent. Two hundred million pounds goes to Tarnmoor Engineering, the main trading company. Forty million goes to Tarnmoor Water Systems, seventy million to Tarnmoor Estates, the property company, and one hundred and twenty million to the parent. A final one hundred and twenty million pounds goes to Tarnmoor Vallaria, the subsidiary in the invented country of Vallaria. Its interest income is thirty three million pounds a year.

Take away the thirty point two five million pounds paid on the notes and six hundred thousand pounds of running costs. Tarnmoor Finance is left with taxable profits of about two point one five million pounds a year. Its lending is not a trade of banking, so its credits and debits sit in the non-trading pot. The pot is in profit, and the profit is taxed.

Now look at the borrowers, because the same interest can be trading for one company and non-trading for another. Tarnmoor Engineering borrows for its trade, so its twelve million pounds of interest is a trading debit. It reduces the trade profit. Tarnmoor Water Systems' two point four million pounds is a trading debit for the same reason. Tarnmoor Estates is a property investment company, so its four point two million pounds is a non-trading debit. Tarnmoor plc's seven point two million pounds is non-trading too.

That distinction matters three times over. It decides where a deficit goes. It decides which debits the corporate interest restriction disallows first. And it decides whether a loss is trading or non-trading when the group plans its claims.

Two more features complete the picture. Tarnmoor Finance has an interest rate swap, designated in its accounts as a fair value hedge of the notes. Its net settlements are left out of the book's figures for simplicity. And the loan to Tarnmoor Vallaria crosses a border, so transfer pricing applies to it, as chapter twenty seven explains. The loans between British companies fall within the exemption for wholly domestic transactions, which applies for chargeable periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six.

When both sides belong to the group.

Here is the first bouncer. Inside a group, one board controls both sides of a debt. Left to the accounts, the creditor could write a loan down and claim a debit, while the debtor kept the full liability and recognised no income. The group would have a deduction with no matching receipt. The connected companies rules stop that by forcing the two sides to mirror each other.

The test is connection, and connection means control. Two companies are connected if one controls the other, or both are under the control of the same person. The law asks whether there was a connection at any time in the accounting period, and if there was, the relationship is connected for the whole period. It also reaches indirect connections through a series of loans. Every loan from Tarnmoor Finance to a group company is a connected companies relationship.

Three consequences follow. First, a connected companies relationship must be accounted for on an amortised cost basis. If the accounts use fair value, tax ignores them and uses amortised cost instead. So a group cannot put an intra-group loan at a falling market value and claim the fall.

Second, related transactions are disregarded where they would reduce credits or increase debits. A creditor cannot sell or assign a connected loan in a way that produces a tax result worse for H M R C than if the transaction had not happened.

Third, and most examined, the rules on impairment and release, to which we turn next.

Why does the law accept the cost of all this rigidity? Because the alternative is an open invitation. If a group could choose the measurement basis for loans between its own companies, it would choose whichever one gave a debit today and a credit never. The amortised cost rule means the debtor's liability and the creditor's asset are measured on the same footing, so what one side loses the other gains.

A small example shows the effect. Suppose, for this example only, that a parent lends ten million pounds to a subsidiary at a fixed rate, and market interest rates then rise. At fair value, the loan asset would fall in value, and an unconnected lender using fair value would book a loss. Between connected companies, tax ignores that fall. The creditor recognises interest at the effective rate on its amortised cost, the debtor deducts the same, and the two figures match year after year. The connected rules do not stop the group from using fair value in its accounts. They stop the group from taxing it.

There is one practical warning. Connection is about control, not about the seventy five per cent test for group relief, or the fifty one per cent test for group payment arrangements. The examiner likes a company owned at, say, sixty per cent. It is outside group relief, but it is connected for loan relationship purposes.

No bad debt, no free release.

The creditor side first. The law says that a company with a connected creditor relationship brings in no impairment loss and no release debit. If Tarnmoor Engineering lent money to a struggling fellow subsidiary and wrote the loan down, the write-down would be added back. If it then forgave the loan, the release would be added back too.

There are two exceptions. One is a debt-for-equity swap, where the creditor releases the debt in exchange for ordinary shares in the debtor. The other is where the creditor itself is insolvent. Exchange losses are not affected by the bar.

Now the debtor side. A debtor in a connected relationship, using amortised cost, brings in no credit when the debt is released. Put the two sides together and the result is symmetry. The creditor gets no debit, the debtor pays no tax, and the group is left where it started. This is the bargain that makes intra-group rescues tax-neutral.

The examiner tests this constantly. In May twenty twenty four, a twenty mark computation contained an intra-group debt write-off that had to be reversed, and the examiners reported that candidates were weaker on that point. In November twenty twenty four, a computation set an impairment of a trade debt beside an impairment of a loan to a fellow subsidiary. The trade debt was deductible. The loan to the fellow subsidiary was not.

The misconception to clear away here is a natural one. People assume a bad debt is a bad debt, and that relief follows the loss. Between connected companies, relief does not follow the loss, because the matching income never arises either.

Outside a group, the rules are different. When an unconnected lender releases a debt, the debtor normally has a taxable credit. That is the point of following the accounts. But the law lifts the credit in five situations. The release is part of a statutory insolvency arrangement. The release is in exchange for ordinary shares in the debtor. The debtor is in insolvent liquidation, administration or a similar process, and the relationship is not connected. The release is under the bank resolution regime. Or, the fifth condition, the corporate rescue exception, which H M R C's guidance says applies to releases on or after the first of January, twenty fifteen. It applies where, without the release, there would be a material risk that within twelve months the company would be unable to pay its debts.

A related rule covers a debt that is substantially modified, or replaced, when the company is in the same distress. No credit arises on the change in carrying value.

Why the generosity? Because taxing a distressed company on the very debts it cannot pay would kill the rescue the creditors are trying to achieve. The tax bill would simply become one more debt the company could not meet.

Buying the debt cheaply.

The connected companies symmetry has a gap, and the deemed release rule closes it. Imagine a group that wants to buy a struggling company. The target owes ten million pounds to outside lenders, and the debt trades at four million pounds because the market doubts it will be repaid. The group buys the debt for four million pounds, buys the shares, and then releases the debt.

Without a special rule, the result would be extraordinary. Once the group owns both, the debtor and the creditor are connected. The release produces no credit for the debtor. A six million pound debt has vanished, and nobody has paid tax on that gain. Had the outside lenders released it themselves, the debtor would normally have been taxed.

The deemed release rule answers this. Where a company acquires a debt for less than the debtor's carrying value, and immediately afterwards the creditor and the debtor are connected, the creditor is treated as releasing the shortfall at that moment. The debtor then brings in a credit for the difference, before the connected companies protection can take effect. In the example, that is six million pounds.

The law then allows two exceptions, in the form given to these rules by the Finance Number Two Act twenty fifteen. H M R C's guidance says the rescue exception applies to acquisitions of impaired debt on or after the eighteenth of November, twenty fifteen.

The first is the equity-for-debt exception. The acquisition is at arm's length, and the only consideration is ordinary shares in the acquiring company or a company connected with it. The creditors swap debt for equity, which is the classic restructuring.

The second is the corporate rescue exception, and its conditions are worth learning word for word. The acquisition must be at arm's length. The new creditor, or a company connected with it, must release the debt within sixty days of acquiring it. And it must be reasonable to assume that, without the release and the arrangements around it, there would be a material risk that at some time within the next twelve months the debtor would be unable to pay its debts.

A parallel pair of rules deals with companies that become connected while the creditor already holds an impaired debt. There too a deemed release can arise, with a matching corporate rescue exception.

The design is careful. The law is not against groups buying distressed debt. It is against a group using the connected companies rules to make a commercial gain disappear. Where the purchase is part of a genuine rescue, and the group follows through quickly by releasing the debt, the law lets the rescue proceed without a tax charge on money the company never had.

Brackenwell's notes.

Here the story supplies a case. Brackenwell Sensors, in our invented case, was a loss-making sensor developer founded by Dr Asha Varma. Before Tarnmoor bought it, its venture investors held three million pounds of its convertible notes. On the first of July in Group Year Two, Tarnmoor plc bought Brackenwell's shares, and on the same day it bought the notes from the venture investors for one point eight million pounds.

The investors were unconnected, and the price was negotiated at arm's length. But immediately afterwards Tarnmoor plc and Brackenwell were connected, and Tarnmoor plc had paid one point eight million pounds for a debt carried at three million pounds. That is the deemed release rule's exact target. Unless an exception applied, Brackenwell would be treated as released from one point two million pounds and would bring in a credit of that amount. At twenty five per cent, that is three hundred thousand pounds of potential tax. Whether Brackenwell's old losses could have absorbed it is a question for chapter fourteen, and the group did not rely on them.

Tom Hesketh, Tarnmoor's head of tax, built the deal timetable around the corporate rescue exception. Tarnmoor plc released the notes within sixty days, by the twenty ninth of August in Group Year Two. The board minutes recorded the evidence for the third condition. Brackenwell's cash flow forecasts showed that, without the release, there was a material risk it could not pay its debts within twelve months. The rescue exception applied. There was no deemed release credit.

Then the actual release. Tarnmoor plc's notes, carried at one point eight million pounds, were written off in its accounts. That is a connected creditor relationship, so no debit is allowed. Brackenwell's liability of three million pounds was released, and the accounts showed a gain. That is a connected debtor relationship, so no credit arises either. The result is symmetry again, and the rescue was tax-neutral, as Parliament intended.

Three practical lessons come from those few weeks. First, the sixty-day clock starts on acquisition, so the release has to be planned before completion, not after it. Second, the material risk condition is a matter of evidence, and the evidence should be made at the time, in board papers and forecasts. Third, the exceptions are conditions, not elections, so if they fail, the credit arises whether or not anyone notices. The book treats the notes as plain debt in Tarnmoor plc's hands. Their conversion rights fell away with the release.

It is worth asking what the alternatives would have looked like. Had Tarnmoor plc paid the venture investors in its own ordinary shares rather than in cash, the equity-for-debt exception would have been available instead, and the sixty-day release would not have been needed. Had Tarnmoor plc kept the notes outstanding and released them six months later, neither exception would have applied, and the one point two million pound credit would have arisen in Brackenwell on the first of July. And had the investors released the notes themselves before the sale, Brackenwell would have faced a release credit from unconnected lenders, relieved only if one of the five conditions for unconnected releases applied. Much the same commercial result, three different tax outcomes. That is why the tax function sits at the deal table.

Interest paid late.

For years, one of the most common traps in company tax was late-paid interest. The rule's aim was sensible. A debtor company accruing interest it did not pay could take a deduction year after year, while a creditor outside the charge to corporation tax paid nothing until the cash arrived, if it ever did. So in certain cases the debtor's deduction was deferred until payment.

The general rule still exists. If interest is not paid within twelve months after the end of the accounting period in which it accrues, and the creditor does not bring the full amount into account as it accrues, the debtor gets relief only when the interest is paid. But the rule now applies only in two kinds of case.

The first is the close company case. The debtor is a close company, and the creditor is a participator, an associate of one, or a company controlled by or with a major interest held by a participator. There are carve-outs for certain small company and collective investment cases. And where the creditor is itself a company, the rule applies only if that company is resident in a non-qualifying territory, essentially a territory without a suitable tax treaty with the U K.

The second is a loan by the trustees of an occupational pension scheme to the employer company, or to certain connected companies.

The cases that once caught groups, interest owed to a connected company and interest owed to a company with a major interest, were removed by the Finance Act twenty fifteen. So the old reflex of treating every unpaid intra-group interest balance as relieved only on payment is now wrong. Connected British companies accrue interest in the normal way.

For Tarnmoor, the point is quickly answered. A subsidiary controlled by a widely held listed parent is not a close company. None of Tarnmoor's companies is close, so the late interest rules do not apply to its intra-group debts. The examiner still sets owner-managed scenarios on other papers, but on this one, recognising when the rule does not apply is the skill.

Where the rule does apply, the mechanics are short. The debtor's debit is taken out of the period in which the interest accrues and allowed in the period in which it is paid. Nothing is lost, only delayed. In an answer, the marks come for three steps. Identify the close company and the participator link. Check the twelve-month payment window. Then, if the creditor is a company, check where it is resident before applying the deferral at all.

The purpose test.

Now the second bouncer, and the most powerful. The rule is in section four hundred and forty one of the two thousand and nine Act, which practitioners call section four four one. If a loan relationship has an unallowable purpose in an accounting period, the debits for that period are disallowed so far as they are attributable to that purpose on a just and reasonable apportionment.

A purpose is unallowable if it is not among the company's business or other commercial purposes. Two refinements make the test bite. First, a tax avoidance purpose counts as a business purpose only if it is not the main purpose, or one of the main purposes, for which the company is a party to the loan. Second, a tax avoidance purpose means any purpose of securing a tax advantage for the company or for any other person. That last phrase means a group's advantage counts, not just the borrower's. The law also says that the purposes of activities outside the charge to corporation tax are not business purposes for this test.

Notice what the test examines. It asks about the purpose of being a party to the loan, period by period. A loan taken for good reasons can acquire an unallowable purpose later, if it is restructured for tax. And the apportionment is not mechanical. The tribunal decides how much of the debits is attributable to the bad purpose, and the answer can be all of them.

The leading earlier case is Fidex Limited versus H M R C, decided by the Court of Appeal in twenty sixteen. It concerned a scheme, known as Project Zephyr, that used the move to international accounting standards to produce a debit on bonds. It was decided under the predecessor rule in the Finance Act nineteen ninety six. The scheme failed. In the words of the Court of Appeal, but for this tax avoidance scheme there would have been no debit at all. Once a debit exists only because of the scheme, all of it is attributable to the scheme.

That but for reasoning became the template. If you strip away the tax avoidance purpose and the debit disappears, the debit belongs to the unallowable purpose. The hard question, and the one the twenty twenty four cases answered, is what happens when there is a real commercial transaction in the picture too.

Two more features of the rule deserve attention before the cases. The first is that it is applied loan by loan and period by period. A company with ten loans can have one tainted loan and nine clean ones, and a tainted loan can become clean again when its purpose changes. The second is that the apportionment is a matter of judgement for the tribunal, not a formula. The law says just and reasonable, and the courts have accepted that, on some facts, the just and reasonable answer is every pound of the debits. The rule disallows debits. It does not tax the lender's matching credits any less, which is why a failed plan inside a group usually costs more than doing nothing.

Three cases in nine weeks.

The first was BlackRock HoldCo Five versus H M R C, decided by the Court of Appeal on the eleventh of April, twenty twenty four. The prologue told its story. An American group bought a business, and a British resident company in the group took on about four billion dollars of intra-group loans. The company won on transfer pricing, because the loans could have been made at arm's length. But it lost on unallowable purpose. The court held that the loans had a main tax avoidance purpose and that, on the facts, all the debits were attributable to it.

The second was Kwik-Fit Group versus H M R C, decided on the third of May, twenty twenty four. As the reported facts describe it, one group company held about forty eight million pounds of old non-trading deficits that could only be used against its own non-trading profits. The group expected them to take about twenty five years to use. It reorganised its intra-group loans so that interest income would flow into that company and the losses would be used in about three years. Other group companies took on new loans, or higher interest rates, and claimed the debits.

The Court of Appeal upheld the tribunal's view that the debits on the new loans were attributable to an unallowable purpose. As commentators read the judgment, the tax advantage was the deductions made available to the paying companies, while the receiving company's income was sheltered. Kwik-Fit also adds a time dimension. H M R C accepted that once the target losses had been used, continued denial would no longer be just and reasonable.

The third was J T I Acquisition Company twenty eleven Limited versus H M R C, decided on the thirteenth of June, twenty twenty four. A British company was set up by an American group to buy an American business, LeTourneau Technologies, and borrowed from a group company to do so. The interest was surrendered as group relief against the group's British profits. The acquisition was real. But the tribunal had found that the British company's own part in the deal, as borrower, had no commercial purpose. The Court of Appeal would not disturb that finding. The tax advantage had been bolted on to a commercial deal, and the debits could be attributed wholly to it.

In October twenty twenty four, the Supreme Court refused permission to appeal in all three cases.

Here is the chapter's misconception. People say interest on money borrowed to buy a company must be deductible, because buying a company is commercial. The Court of Appeal has now closed that argument. The test looks at the borrower's purpose in being party to the loan, not at the purpose of the acquisition. A commercial deal can carry a loan whose own purpose is tax.

The debate is not quite over. The profession argues that this leaves groups uncertain, because ordinary acquisition finance with a tax benefit attached is common, and the line between a tax-efficient structure and a main purpose is not easy to draw. H M R C's view is that the rule asks a factual question, and the tribunals answer it. One case is still running. In Syngenta Holdings versus H M R C, the First-tier Tribunal found for H M R C in twenty twenty four, and in October twenty twenty five the Upper Tribunal gave permission to appeal on some grounds. Commentators report that the main question is whether a genuine business purpose must lead to apportionment rather than total disallowance. No Upper Tribunal decision had been published by October twenty twenty six.

The plan Tarnmoor turned down.

In our invented case, the test arrived at Tarnmoor in Group Year Two, a few months after the Brackenwell deal. The idea came from Calder's own finance team, whose results were measured on Calder's profit after tax. Tarnmoor plc would sell Brackenwell to Calder for twenty four million pounds, and Calder would borrow the price from Tarnmoor Finance at six per cent.

The arithmetic looked attractive from Calder's desk. Interest of one point four four million pounds a year would cut Calder's taxable profits, and its corporation tax by three hundred and sixty thousand pounds a year.

Tom Hesketh wrote the analysis for the board. He made three points.

The first was commercial. Brackenwell already supplied sensors to Calder and to Tarnmoor Engineering, and owning it from Calder changed nothing about how that supply worked. Calder had no need of the money and no business reason to borrow it. On any honest reading, the only purpose of Calder becoming a debtor was the deduction.

The second was the group view. Tarnmoor Finance would receive the same one point four four million pounds as taxable interest. The group's tax bill would barely move. What would move was Calder's own bill, and that is still a tax advantage, for Calder. The law counts an advantage for the company or any other person, and, as commentators read Kwik-Fit, it shows that deductions made available to one company can be the advantage even where the receiving side is not better off. The rule asks what the company was trying to do, not whether the group came out ahead.

The third was the case law. On the reasoning of J T I and Kwik-Fit, a tribunal would very likely find that being party to the loan had a main tax avoidance purpose, and would attribute all the debits to it. Calder's deduction would be disallowed, while Tarnmoor Finance's interest income stayed taxable. The plan would turn a neutral position into a loss for the group.

The board declined, and minuted why. The episode also shows the tax function's quieter job. Purpose is a question of fact, decided years later from documents. Groups that borrow for good reasons should say so at the time, in board papers that explain the business case. Groups that are offered plans whose only case is tax should be able to show that they said no.

Notice also what did not save the plan. The loan was between two British companies, so the domestic exemption meant transfer pricing would not have questioned the six per cent rate. The interest restriction is measured across the whole worldwide group, so moving debt between British companies would have changed nothing there either. Neither rule stood in the way. The purpose test did. That is the role Parliament gave it, a backstop for cases that pass every mechanical rule.

When the debits outrun the credits.

When a company's non-trading debits exceed its non-trading credits, it has a non-trading deficit. For deficits of accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty seventeen, the law offers four routes.

First, the company can claim to set the deficit against any profits of the same period. Second, it can claim to carry it back twelve months, but only against non-trading loan relationship profits of that earlier period. Both these claims must be made within two years after the end of the deficit period.

Third, a deficit of the current period can be surrendered as group relief to another group company. Chapter fifteen covers the mechanics.

Fourth, whatever is not claimed or surrendered is carried forward. In a later period, the company can claim to set it against its total profits, within two years after the end of that later period. Carried-forward deficits can also be surrendered to the group, and they count towards the restriction that limits carried-forward reliefs to the five million pound allowance plus half of the profits above it. If the company has ceased its investment business, carried-forward deficits are confined to non-trading profits.

Two warnings follow. The carry-back is narrow. A deficit carried back cannot touch trading profits of the earlier year. And even the current-year set-off needs a claim. A deficit nobody claims simply rolls forward. The examiners set a twenty mark question in November twenty twenty five on a new subsidiary that included the options for relieving non-trading deficits, so these routes are live examination material.

Deficits from before April twenty seventeen were stuck under the old rules, usable only against the company's own later non-trading profits. That is exactly the kind of trapped deficit that sat behind Kwik-Fit.

Tarnmoor's numbers show the routes at work. In Group Year One, Tarnmoor plc's non-trading debits were eight point eight million pounds. They were seven point two million pounds of interest to Tarnmoor Finance, one point three five million pounds of interest on the bank facility, and the two hundred and fifty thousand pound fee. The corporate interest restriction disallowed two point two one million pounds of them, and the default order hits non-trading debits first. Chapter twenty eight explains why. That left a deficit of six point five nine million pounds, which Tarnmoor plc surrendered to Tarnmoor Engineering. In Group Year Two, the debits were nine point nine seven million pounds, the disallowance two point three million, and the surrender seven point six seven million.

Tarnmoor Estates is the other pattern. Its four point two million pounds of non-trading interest exceeds its non-trading credits, so it claims to set the deficit against its own rental profits in the same period.

In the examination, lay the deficit out in steps. Total the non-trading credits and debits, including fees, exchange movements and any non-trading derivative amounts. Take out any disallowed amounts, under the purpose rule or the interest restriction. Then state the deficit and walk through the options in order, with the time limit for each claim. The examiners reward a clear statement of what each option would achieve, such as saving tax at twenty five per cent this year against a refund for last year, more than a list of section numbers.

Debts that are not loans.

Part six of the two thousand and nine Act extends the loan relationship rules to things that are not loans in the ordinary sense, and it is non-core for this paper. The idea behind it is simple. The same economic return should get the same tax treatment, whatever its legal form.

The most practical chapter covers relevant non-lending relationships. A money debt that does not arise from lending, a trade debt for example, is brought into the loan relationship rules where interest is payable on it, where exchange gains or losses arise on it, or where an impairment loss or release debit arises on certain unpaid business payments. So interest charged on an overdue customer balance, or an exchange gain on a dollar trade debt, is a loan relationship credit.

The second is disguised interest. Where a company is party to an arrangement that produces a return economically equivalent to interest, the return is taxed as a loan relationship profit on an amortised cost basis. A return is economically equivalent to interest if it is reasonable to regard it as a return on an investment of money at a reasonably commercial rate, reflecting the time value of money, and there is no practical likelihood that it will cease. There are exclusions, including where the return is otherwise taxed and where there is no tax avoidance main purpose. The target is a share or contract dressed up to turn interest into an untaxed or capital receipt.

Three more chapters can be named in a line each. Transferred income streams catch a company that sells a right to income, such as interest, for a lump sum, and tax the lump sum as the income it replaces. Alternative finance arrangements give finance structured to comply with Islamic principles the same treatment as interest. And shares with guaranteed returns treat shares that are designed to produce an interest-like return as if they were a creditor relationship.

In the examination, Part six usually appears as a recognition point. A scenario mentions an overdue debt with interest, a preference share with a fixed redemption premium, or a sale of a stream of payments, and the marks come for naming the rule and saying it brings the return into the loan relationship regime.

Suppose, for this example only, that Tarnmoor Engineering charges interest on customer accounts paid more than sixty days late. The customer balances are trade debts, not loans. But because interest is payable on them, the rules treat them as relevant non-lending relationships, and the interest is a loan relationship credit rather than a sales receipt. The same company's dollar receivables, revalued at the year end, produce exchange gains and losses that are also brought in under these rules.

Derivatives and the hedging rules.

Derivatives are the third bouncer's territory, and on this paper they are non-core. The rules are in Part seven of the two thousand and nine Act. A derivative contract is, broadly, an option, a future or a contract for differences that meets an accounting condition, which in essence means the accounts treat it as a derivative. Some contracts are excluded because of what they are based on. Interest rate swaps, currency contracts and commodity futures are the everyday examples.

The default is familiar. Credits and debits are the amounts recognised in profit or loss. Trading derivatives go into trading profits. Non-trading derivatives join the non-trading loan relationship pot. Derivatives are usually at fair value in the accounts, so a company that holds them without hedge accounting is taxed on fair value movements as they occur.

The courts have patrolled the edges. In Union Castle Mail Steamship Company versus H M R C, decided by the Court of Appeal in twenty twenty, a group used a scheme to produce a tax debit of about thirty nine million pounds on derivative contracts, from amounts recognised in equity rather than in profit or loss. The appeal failed. H M R C's manual explains that, since twenty sixteen, the rules have focused firmly on amounts in profit or loss.

Now the Disregard Regulations, made in two thousand and four. The problem they solve is a mismatch. A company hedges a risk, say the price of a commodity it buys, with a derivative. The derivative is at fair value and its movements hit profit or loss now. The hedged purchase affects profit only later. Tax that follows the accounts would tax the derivative's swings before the matching cost arrives.

Since twenty fifteen, the regulations no longer apply automatically. H M R C's guidance says the default is to follow the accounts. A company that wants the hedging rules elects into them, and the election can cover currency contracts, commodity and debt contracts, and interest rate contracts. Where an election applies, the fair value movements on the hedging derivative are left out. For currency, commodity and debt contracts they are brought back into account in line with the hedged item. For interest rate contracts they are brought in on an appropriate accruals basis. A company new to fair value accounting has an extended window to elect, and an election then locks in for a period.

H M R C's guidance lists several automatic cases, and its list is not closed. The one to know is where the hedged item is not itself taxed in line with the accounts, connected company debt being the usual example. Then the hedging rules apply without an election. There is also an anti-avoidance rule where a main purpose of arranging matters is to avoid the regulations.

Tarnmoor shows both sides. In our invented case, Tarnmoor Engineering buys copper and hedges the price with copper futures. When it first used derivatives, before the story begins, it made the election. Suppose, for this example only, that at a year end its futures showed a fair value gain of four hundred thousand pounds. With the election, that gain is left out and brought in when the hedged copper purchases reach profit or loss. Without it, the gain would be taxed now, adding one hundred thousand pounds to that year's tax.

Tarnmoor Finance's swap is different. It is designated as a fair value hedge of the external notes. In a fair value hedge the accounts already adjust the notes for the hedged risk, so the two movements offset in profit or loss. Tarnmoor Finance has made no election. On H M R C's guidance, none is needed. Tax simply follows the accounts.

Notice too how the two derivatives are classified. Tarnmoor Engineering's futures hedge purchases for its trade, so their credits and debits are trading items. Tarnmoor Finance's swap hedges the notes of a company that does not trade, so its amounts are non-trading and sit in the same pot as the interest. Timing also matters for the election itself. The law gives a company that is new to fair value accounting six months from key dates, such as the start of its first relevant period or the date it first holds a fair-valued derivative, and a company with no senior accounting officer obligations can have longer. Miss the window and the election works only for later periods.

The examiner set this in November twenty twenty three. A company held a fuel future without hedge accounting, and the examiners reported that only a minority of candidates mentioned the Disregard Regulations. The marks came for saying that fair value movements are taxed as they arise unless the company has elected.

Financing the group.

Step back from the rules to the job. A group tax function lives with financing decisions every week, and the examiner's narrative syllabus names common financing transactions as part of this paper. Here is how the pieces fit.

Debt or equity is the first choice. Interest on debt is, in principle, deductible, while dividends on shares are not. That asymmetry is why every regime in Part Four exists. The corporate interest restriction in chapter twenty eight limits net interest to a share of taxable earnings. Transfer pricing in chapter twenty seven asks whether an independent lender would have lent that much on those terms. The hybrid rules in chapter twenty nine deny deductions where the other side is not taxed. And the unallowable purpose rule sits underneath them all. Each looks at the same interest from a different angle, and a debit can survive one and fall to another. BlackRock won on transfer pricing and lost on purpose.

Acquisition finance is the second. The arrangement fee is a loan relationship debit, spread as the accounts spread it. The interest follows the accounts, subject to the purpose test. Where the target owes debt to outsiders, the group must decide before completion whether to buy that debt, refinance it, or release it, because the deemed release rule and its sixty-day rescue window turn on the timetable.

Bonds are the third. Listed bonds that pay interest are quoted Eurobonds and can pay interest gross. Interest paid on other debt to lenders abroad may need income tax deducted. For twenty twenty six to twenty seven, the rate on yearly interest is twenty per cent. Coming next, enacted by the Finance Act twenty twenty six, is twenty two per cent from twenty twenty seven to twenty eight. Chapter twenty three covers the withholding rules in Part fifteen of the Income Tax Act two thousand and seven.

Cash pooling is the fourth. In a physical pool, balances are swept into a header account each day, so each participating company has a loan relationship with the header company. Those are connected companies relationships. The pool's interest must be at arm's length where a border is crossed, and the balances can generate exchange movements when currencies differ.

Then the calendar. Claims to use non-trading deficits are due within two years. A hedging election must be made in its window. A rescue release must happen within sixty days. And the board minutes must show purpose at the time.

The tax function's role in all of this is coordination as much as calculation, which is exactly the skill the paper claims to test. Treasury decides the funding. The accountants decide the measurement basis and whether to designate hedges. Lawyers draft the loan terms and the release deeds. Corporate finance runs the acquisition timetable. Each of those choices has a tax answer, and the tax team's job is to see the answer before the choice is made. When Tarnmoor's treasury team proposed a new intra-group loan, Tom Hesketh's checklist asked five questions. Is the relationship connected? Is the purpose documented? Does it cross a border? How will it affect the interest restriction? Will any payment need income tax deducted?

One trap from the examiners deserves a last word. In May twenty twenty three, candidates facing a loan from an American company wasted time on diverted profits tax. The examiners reported that it does not apply to loan relationships. That tax has since been repealed and replaced, as chapter thirty explains, but the lesson stands. On a financing question, think loan relationships, transfer pricing, the interest restriction and withholding first.

What to take away.

The loan relationship code, since the Finance Act nineteen ninety six, treats company debt as income. Interest, discounts, fees, profits and losses on loans, and exchange movements are credits and debits. The amounts are those in profit or loss under generally accepted accounting practice. Amounts in other comprehensive income wait until they are recycled. Trading debits arise on borrowing for the trade, and everything else goes into the non-trading pot.

The first bouncer is the connected companies rules. Connection means control at any time in the accounting period. Connected relationships must use amortised cost. The creditor gets no impairment or release debit, except in a debt-for-equity swap or if the creditor is insolvent. The debtor brings in no release credit. The result is symmetry, and reversing an intra-group write-off is a favourite examination point.

Buying a debt cheaply and becoming connected triggers a deemed release, taxed on the debtor, unless the equity-for-debt exception or the corporate rescue exception applies. The rescue exception needs an arm's length acquisition, a release within sixty days, and a material risk of insolvency within twelve months. Outside a group, a released debt is normally taxable on the debtor, but five conditions lift the credit, including corporate rescue. Brackenwell's notes, bought for one point eight million pounds against three million, would have produced a deemed release of one point two million pounds. The release inside sixty days and the board's evidence meant no credit, and Tarnmoor plc got no debit.

Late-paid interest now matters only for close company participators, with corporate creditors caught only in non-qualifying territories, and for pension scheme loans. Tarnmoor is not close.

The second bouncer is section four four one. Debits are disallowed so far as attributable to an unallowable purpose, and a tax advantage for any person counts. Fidex gave us but for. BlackRock, Kwik-Fit and J T I, all decided in twenty twenty four, showed that a commercial acquisition does not save a loan whose own purpose is tax, and that all the debits can be disallowed. Syngenta is still pending. Tarnmoor turned down a twenty four million pound debt pushdown that would have saved Calder three hundred and sixty thousand pounds a year, because it had no purpose but the deduction.

Non-trading deficits since April twenty seventeen can be set against current profits, carried back twelve months against non-trading profits only, surrendered to the group, or carried forward against total profits. Each route needs a claim within two years.

The third bouncer is the Disregard Regulations. Derivatives follow profit or loss. Since twenty fifteen, the hedging rules apply only by election, or automatically where the hedged item is not taxed in line with the accounts, or in the other automatic cases H M R C lists. Tarnmoor Engineering's copper futures are under an election. Tarnmoor Finance's fair value hedge simply follows the accounts.

And the grades are these. Loan relationships are core. Derivatives and the relationships treated as loans are non-core.

One kind of company sits at the centre of all this borrowing, and its costs are among the most misunderstood on the paper. Chapter thirteen turns to companies with investment business.


Chapter thirteen: Companies with investment business.

Two and a half million pounds of advice.

On the sixteenth of July, twenty twenty four, the Supreme Court gave judgment in a case about a bundle of invoices. The company was Centrica Overseas Holdings Limited, the overseas investment arm of the energy group Centrica. In two thousand and five the group had bought Oxxio, a Dutch energy supplier. The investment failed. By the middle of two thousand and nine, Centrica had resolved to sell Oxxio, and it instructed advisers to make it happen. Deutsche Bank, the accountants P W C and the Dutch law firm De Brauw worked on the disposal until it completed in March twenty eleven. Their fees came to just over two and a half million pounds.

The holding company claimed those fees as expenses of management. H M R C refused. The case climbed through every tier of the tax tribunals and courts. Five Justices decided it in the end. They were Lord Hodge, the Deputy President, with Lord Stephens, Lady Rose, Lord Richards and Lady Simler. By then everyone accepted that the fees were expenses of management. But the Supreme Court held that they were also capital. So nothing could be deducted.

That outcome holds the whole of this chapter in miniature. A company that holds investments, rather than trading, gets a special deduction for the cost of running itself. But the deduction has edges. It stops at capital. It stops at costs that belong to someone else's trade. It stops at expenses that the company cannot use, and it can be frozen when the company changes hands. The question for this chapter is simple to ask. When the parent of a large group spends money, which of its costs does the tax system recognise, and when?

This is chapter thirteen, the last but one chapter of Part Two, on measuring profit. Companies with investment business are a core topic on the Advanced Technical paper, and so is the change of ownership rule for them. The Living Law, chapter eleven, drew the line between trading and investing for individuals and companies. Here we take the investing side to Advanced Technical depth. Throughout, we apply the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, under the Finance Act twenty twenty six.

A business of making investments.

The relief belongs to a company with investment business. The Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act, defines it in section twelve eighteen B. It is any company whose business consists wholly or partly in the making of investments. Credit unions are excluded.

The words wholly or partly matter, and they are newer than they look. Before the first of April, two thousand and four, the relief belonged only to an investment company, a company whose business consisted wholly or mainly of making investments. The Finance Act two thousand and four relaxed that test. H M R C's manual explains that the change helped so-called hybrid companies, which held investments but could not claim because they also ran a substantial trade. Since then, one company can be both a trader and an investor. Its trade is taxed under the trading rules, and the costs of managing its investment business are management expenses.
