Penalties are flat. A late return costs five hundred pounds if it is within three months of the filing date, and one thousand pounds otherwise. Finance Act twenty twenty six added a new one thousand pound penalty where a company submits a return without having been appointed. There is no penalty if the company is appointed within eighteen months of the end of the period, if it told H M R C unprompted, or if it has a reasonable excuse.

In our invented case, Tarnmoor's head of tax, Tom Hesketh, treats the appointment as part of the year-end routine. The parent's board paper lists every eligible United Kingdom company, each company's board authorises the parent, and the parent files a full return every year. It needs to. It has disallowances to allocate in Group Years One and Two, and a reactivation to claim in Group Year Three. Once the return is in, each company's own corporation tax return must reflect its allocated disallowance or reactivation, and any difference is corrected by amendment.

Infrastructure.

Some businesses are financed almost entirely by debt by design. A toll road, a power network or a hospital built under a public contract borrows against decades of predictable income. Thirty per cent of earnings would cripple them, and the debt is not the kind of base erosion the rule was aimed at. The public infrastructure exemption takes them out.

A company can elect to be a qualifying infrastructure company. Broadly, all or all but an insignificant part of its income must come from public infrastructure assets, and the same must be true of its assets. It must be fully within the charge to United Kingdom tax. Interest it pays to third parties is then left out of tax-interest, provided the lender's recourse is limited to the company's own income, assets, shares or debt. Loans between qualifying infrastructure companies can qualify too. In return, the company's tax E B I T D A is treated as nil. The logic is a trade. The company gives up any contribution its earnings would have made to the group's capacity, and in exchange its own qualifying interest stops counting against that capacity. Some older loans made before the thirteenth of May, twenty sixteen, are protected by transitional rules.

On H M R C's guidance the election must be made before the end of the accounting period it is to cover. Once made, it cannot be revoked with effect for a period beginning within five years of the start of the first period it covered.

Here is the point that cost marks in May twenty twenty six. When a qualifying infrastructure company sits inside a larger group, both sides of the computation change. Its interest comes out of the group's net interest. Its earnings come out of tax E B I T D A.

Suppose, for this example, that after Tarnmoor takes control of Helmside in Group Year Five, its hydrogen plant met the statutory tests, and Helmside elected. Suppose it paid two point eight million pounds of interest on limited recourse bank debt and had tax E B I T D A of six million pounds. The group's net interest would fall by two point eight million. Its earnings would fall by six million, and its thirty per cent allowance by one point eight million. Net headroom would improve by one million pounds. Whether a real plant meets the tests is a question of fact, and this one is purely an illustration.

Where the restriction meets other rules.

The interest restriction comes last. Transfer pricing first fixes the arm's length amount of each loan and its interest. The unallowable purpose rule then removes debits that serve a tax avoidance purpose. The hybrid rules counteract mismatches. What survives is the tax-interest the restriction tests. Disallowed amounts under those earlier rules are simply not brought into account, so they never reach the group's net interest. The transfer pricing code makes the order explicit from the other side. In deciding whether there is a potential United Kingdom tax advantage, the interest restriction is disregarded.

Then there is the trap the examiners reported after May twenty twenty six. Very few candidates adjusted both figures correctly. The rule is this. A transfer pricing adjustment to interest changes tax-interest, so it moves the group's net interest, but it does not change tax E B I T D A, which excludes interest anyway. A transfer pricing adjustment to a service charge changes ordinary profit, so it does move tax E B I T D A.

Tarnmoor has examples of both. In Group Year One Tarnmoor plc charged the Vallarian company one point six million pounds for head office services that should, at arm's length, have cost two point one million. The five hundred thousand pound adjustment raised the parent's taxable profit, so it raised tax E B I T D A by the same amount, and the allowance by one hundred and fifty thousand pounds. The adjustment cost one hundred and twenty five thousand pounds of tax. It also shrank the disallowance from what would have been two point three six million pounds to two point two one million. Looking ahead, Tarnmoor plc's twenty million pound interest-free loan to its Irish company becomes cross-border when the Irish company migrates in Group Year Four. Transfer pricing then imputes interest at six per cent. That is tax-interest income for the parent. It reduces the group's net interest, six hundred thousand pounds for the second half of Group Year Four and one point two million a year after that, and leaves tax E B I T D A untouched.

Leases are the next join. Since twenty nineteen, lessees have brought most leases onto the balance sheet, and Parliament adjusted this regime to match. Chapter five reported the profession's reading of the result. A lease's financing cost is tax-interest where the lease would have been a finance lease under the old accounting classification, and not where it would have been an operating lease. Tarnmoor Engineering's machining centre lease is a finance lease on any view, which is why its ninety thousand pounds counted in Group Year Three.

Flood defences show the newest exclusion at work. Chapter nine followed the property company's flood wall. Its structures and buildings allowance is a capital allowance, so it never touched tax E B I T D A, and nor did the local authority's grant. Now suppose, for this example, that Tarnmoor Engineering instead contributed three hundred thousand pounds to an Environment Agency flood scheme protecting its works. That contribution is deductible under the special rule for flood and coastal erosion projects. Before Finance Act twenty twenty six it would have cut tax E B I T D A, and so the allowance, by ninety thousand pounds. Now it is excluded.

Two more joins in a sentence each. The finance company exemption in the controlled foreign company rules looks at the same group net interest figure, as chapter twenty six explains. And deferred tax follows any carried-forward disallowance, as we saw.

Finally, the regime has its own anti-avoidance rule. Where one of the main purposes of arrangements is to obtain a tax advantage, and the advantage comes from leaving tax-interest out of account, reducing a restriction, increasing a reactivation or shifting either into a different period, the advantage is counteracted by just and reasonable adjustments. H M R C's guidance adds that the rule does not apply if another rule already neutralises the advantage.

How the examiner tests it.

The corporate interest restriction is core on the twenty twenty six grid, which governs Kian's likely sitting in May twenty twenty seven, and it has appeared at four of the last seven sittings. It falls to non-core only from twenty twenty eight.

May twenty twenty six was the big one. Question one, for twenty marks, combined a merger forming a new worldwide group, the administration of the reporting company and the return, the public infrastructure exemption, and a fixed ratio calculation with transfer pricing adjustments and a qualifying infrastructure company to carve out. The administration was answered adequately but padded. The calculation was poor. Very few candidates adjusted the group's net interest and tax E B I T D A correctly. Some computed the group ratio when told not to. Some wrongly adjusted tax E B I T D A for the disallowed interest.

May twenty twenty four set a calculation inside a twenty mark question about a parent company, with an interest-free loan, transfer pricing and reactivation of a brought-forward disallowance, plus administration. A minority mixed up the group's tax-interest figure with its external interest figure. The same sitting put an allowance brought forward into a computation question. November twenty twenty four gave three and a half marks, inside a question on a newly acquired company, for saying that there was probably no restriction but that a return could protect the position, with a reporting company and an abbreviated return. May twenty twenty three set transfer pricing and the interest restriction together on a loan from an American company, and the examiners noted that time was wasted on diverted profits tax.

The style is technical prose and computations, half a mark to a mark per point. The layout the marker wants follows the statutory steps. Group net interest, company by company. Tax E B I T D A, company by company. Thirty per cent. Debt cap. Allowance, capacity, the two million pound floor. Disallowance or reactivation. Allocation. The reading edition sets out the template.

The traps follow from what we have covered. The two million pounds is a floor, not a bonus. Disallowed interest waits forever, but unused allowance dies after five years and needs full returns. An interest transfer pricing adjustment moves the net interest figure, not the earnings figure. Under Finance Act twenty twenty six the appointment is per period, with no deadline and more than half of the companies. And do not pad. Administration answers lose time, not marks, when they wander.

What to take away.

The corporate interest restriction answers one question. How much net interest should the United Kingdom let a whole group deduct? It is the United Kingdom's version of the O E C D's Action four, and it has applied to periods of account beginning on or after the first of April, twenty seventeen.

The unit is the worldwide group, the ultimate parent and its consolidated subsidiaries, for the group's period of account. Only United Kingdom companies contribute, and a company whose accounting period straddles the group's period contributes the just and reasonable share, usually by time.

The tested figure is the aggregate net tax-interest expense. Tax-interest covers loan relationship amounts, without exchange movements or impairment, interest rate and similar derivative amounts, and the financing cost in finance leases, factoring and service concessions. Interest between United Kingdom companies cancels out. For Tarnmoor it was twenty four point six five million pounds in Group Year One, twenty five point eight two million in Group Year Two and twenty four point four four million in Group Year Three.

The earnings measure is tax E B I T D A, built from taxable profits and excluding interest, capital allowances, intangibles debits and clawback credits, losses from other periods, group relief and qualifying reliefs such as the expenditure credit, charitable donations and the patent box deduction. Since Finance Act twenty twenty six it also excludes capital expenditure deducted under the flood defence and three similar rules. Tarnmoor's was seventy four point eight, seventy eight point four and eighty seven point seven million pounds.

The fixed ratio allowance is the lower of thirty per cent of tax E B I T D A and the debt cap, which is the group's external net interest plus excess debt cap from the previous period. The group ratio is an election for highly geared groups. Interest capacity is the allowance plus unused allowance brought forward, never less than two million pounds.

Tarnmoor lost two point two one million pounds of deductions in Group Year One and two point three million in Group Year Two. Its parent, as reporting company, allocated both to its own non-trading debits, keeping the queue in the company that will stay. In Group Year Three it reactivated one point eight seven million pounds as first filed, and two point four seven million after the revised return, leaving two point zero four million waiting, with no unused allowance created.

Disallowed interest carries forward without limit, unless the business ceases or becomes small or negligible. Unused allowance lasts five years, and only with full returns. Reactivation needs a full return and must be taken at the first opportunity.

Under Finance Act twenty twenty six, for periods of account ending on or after the thirty first of March, twenty twenty six, a reporting company is appointed for each period, with no deadline and no notice, by more than half of the eligible companies. The return is due twelve months after the period ends. Late returns cost five hundred pounds or one thousand pounds, and an unappointed filer can face one thousand pounds.

Transfer pricing and the other interest rules come first. An interest adjustment moves the net interest figure. A services adjustment moves tax E B I T D A. A qualifying infrastructure company comes out of both.

So how much interest should the United Kingdom let one group deduct? About thirty per cent of what the group earns here, never more than it really pays to outsiders, and never less than two million pounds. Everything else is the machinery for counting that fairly across many companies and many years.

The next chapter follows money that tries a different trick. Chapter twenty nine, on hybrid mismatches, deals with payments that two countries see differently, so that one deduction is claimed twice or matched by nothing.


Chapter twenty nine: Hybrid mismatches.

The slide deck arrived in Group Year Four. In our invented story, an outside adviser had a proposal for our invented group, Tarnmoor, and its treasury company, Tarnmoor Finance. It would issue eighty million pounds of perpetual notes to Tarnmoor Capital, the group's finance company in the invented country of Marrovia. The coupon would be seven per cent, five point six million pounds a year.

The adviser's pitch rested on one fact. The United Kingdom would see the notes as debt, so the coupon would be deductible here. Marrovia, under its invented law, would see the same notes as shares, so the coupon would arrive as an exempt dividend. One payment, two readings. A deduction in one country, and nothing taxed in the other. The project even had a name. Project Undertow.

Tom Hesketh, the group's head of tax, read the deck and recognised it at once. This was exactly the kind of arrangement that the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the O E C D, had set out to stop. On the fifth of October, twenty fifteen, it published its final report on neutralising the effects of hybrid mismatch arrangements. The United Kingdom turned that report into law from the first of January, twenty seventeen.

So this chapter asks one question. When two countries describe the same payment differently, which of them gets to tax it, and what happens if neither does?

This is the eighth chapter of Part Four, Across Borders. Hybrid mismatches are core material on the Advanced Technical paper under the current syllabus grid, although they fall to non-core from twenty twenty eight. The Living Law only signposted them, so we build from first principles. The law throughout is that for the financial year twenty twenty six.

One coin, two readings.

Start with the problem. Every tax system has to decide what a payment is. Interest or dividend. A person or a pass-through. Here or there. Each country answers by its own law, and the answers need not match. Before these rules, a well-advised group could sometimes design an instrument so that each country's reading produced the better answer.

Picture one coin tossed between two countries. If both call it heads, both give a deduction for the same expense. If both call it tails, neither taxes the income. A hybrid mismatch is that gap. The rules exist to make one country call the coin fairly.

The O E C D's work came out of its base erosion and profit shifting project, which everyone calls B E P S. Action two of that project dealt with hybrids. Its key choice was to target outcomes, not motives. The rules ask what happened to the payment. Was it deducted here and not included there? Was one expense deducted twice? They do not start by asking why.

The O E C D named two outcomes. The first is the deduction non-inclusion mismatch, which practitioners shorten to D N I. A payment is deductible for the payer, but the payee does not bring it in as ordinary income. The second is the double deduction. The same amount is deductible in two territories.

Its second key choice was a pair of responses. A primary response tells one country to act first, usually the payer's. A secondary response tells the other country to act if the first does not. Whichever country moves, the mismatch is neutralised once, and only once.

The United Kingdom already had rules aimed at this territory. Anti-arbitrage rules arrived in the Finance Number Two Act two thousand and five and were later rewritten into the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act. Those rules did nothing until H M R C served a notice. They were repealed for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty seventeen.

Their replacement is Part six A of the International Act, inserted by the Finance Act twenty sixteen. It applies to payments made on or after the first of January, twenty seventeen. And unlike its predecessor, it needs no notice. A company must apply it in its own return.

That is the shift to remember. From rules that H M R C switched on, to rules that switch themselves on.

The vocabulary of Part six A.

Part six A has its own dictionary, and the exam rewards using it precisely.

Tax, for these rules, means income tax and corporation tax on income in the United Kingdom, and taxes on income abroad. It also includes the controlled foreign company charge, which I will call the C F C charge, and foreign C F C charges. Withholding tax is ignored. So a payment that suffers withholding but is never taxed as income is still not included.

Ordinary income is income brought into account in calculating the profits on which tax is charged. Income that is exempt or excluded is not ordinary income. Income taxed at a reduced rate because of an instrument's terms is included, but under-taxed, and the law scales it.

A hybrid entity is an entity that one territory regards as a person, while another territory treats its income as someone else's. A partnership seen as a company in one country is the obvious case. So is a company that its foreign parent treats as transparent.

Most chapters apply only between related parties, or under a structured arrangement. Two parties are related if they are in the same control group, or if one has a twenty five per cent investment in the other, or a third person has a twenty five per cent investment in both. A control group broadly means companies consolidated together, or linked by the transfer pricing participation test, or by a fifty per cent investment.

A structured arrangement catches unrelated parties. The law asks whether it is reasonable to suppose the arrangement was designed to secure the mismatch, or that its terms share the mismatch's economic benefit between the parties. A commercial objective does not save it. Notice what this means. For related parties there is no purpose test at all.

Dual inclusion income is income taxed in both of the relevant territories. Many responses let a deduction survive only against dual inclusion income, because a deduction set against income taxed twice gives no one a windfall.

Timing gets its own concept. A permitted taxable period is broadly one that begins within twelve months after the end of the payer's period. Income included that late still counts.

Last, the law fixes an order, because one payment can trigger several chapters. Chapter four, on hybrid transfers, goes first, then chapter three, on financial instruments, then chapters five to ten in turn.

A misconception belongs here. People assume the hybrid rules are anti-avoidance rules with a motive test. Between related parties they are mechanical. If the mismatch exists and arises from the hybrid feature, the counteraction follows.

Financial instruments.

Chapter three of Part six A is the one the examiner meets most often, and it is Project Undertow's chapter. It deals with a deduction non-inclusion mismatch arising from the terms or other features of a financial instrument.

The conditions are these. There is a payment under a financial instrument. The payer is within the charge to corporation tax, or the payee is. The mismatch arises because of the instrument's terms or features. And the payer and payee are related, or the arrangement is structured.

There are two cases. In the first, the deduction exceeds the ordinary income that arises to the payee in a permitted taxable period. The classic example is a coupon the payee's country treats as an exempt dividend. In the second, the income is included, but under-taxed, because of the instrument's features.

The primary response falls on the payer. Where the payer is a United Kingdom company, its deduction is reduced by the amount of the mismatch.

The secondary response applies where the United Kingdom is the payee's country and the payer's country has not counteracted. Then the United Kingdom payee is taxed on the relevant amount as income.

Here is the first case in miniature. Suppose, for this example only, a United Kingdom company pays a one million pound coupon to its parent abroad. The parent's country treats the instrument as equity and exempts the receipt. The whole one million pounds is a mismatch. The deduction is denied, and that costs two hundred and fifty thousand pounds of corporation tax.

Now the second case, which is harder. Suppose instead the parent's country taxes the coupon, but at a special rate of five per cent, where its full marginal rate is twenty per cent. The law measures the mismatch by scaling the under-taxed amount. Multiply it by the full rate less the actual rate, and divide by the full rate.

So one million pounds, times fifteen, divided by twenty, gives a mismatch of seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds. The United Kingdom payer keeps a deduction of only two hundred and fifty thousand pounds. The tax cost of the counteraction is one hundred and eighty seven thousand, five hundred pounds. The full working is in the reading edition.

Why scale it that way? Because the income was taxed at a quarter of the full rate. So a quarter of the payment is treated as properly included, and three quarters as not.

Timing can also create a first case mismatch. Suppose the payer accrues interest and deducts it each year, but the payee's country taxes it only when it is paid, many years later. If the income is included in a permitted taxable period, beginning within twelve months after the end of the payer's period, there is no mismatch. If it comes later, the deduction is denied for now. When the income finally arrives, the law lets the position be adjusted, so the relief is delayed, not lost.

Chapter four applies the same thinking to hybrid transfers, such as repos and stock lending. There, two countries disagree about who owns the transferred instrument, so both may give relief, or neither may tax a return. The payer again responds first, and the payee second.

One boundary matters. The mismatch must come from the instrument. If the payee is simply exempt because of who it is, a pension fund or a sovereign body perhaps, the shortfall is not a hybrid mismatch.

When the United Kingdom is the payee.

So far the United Kingdom has mostly been the payer. Turn the coin over. Suppose a United Kingdom company receives a payment that its foreign payer deducts, but which the United Kingdom would treat as an exempt dividend.

The first line of defence is not in Part six A at all. It sits in the dividend exemption in Part nine A of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, which I will call the two thousand and nine Act. A distribution received by a large company is exempt only if, among other conditions, no deduction is allowed for it abroad. The test is whether a resident of any territory outside the United Kingdom gets a deduction under that territory's law. Small companies face the same test.

That is a linking rule. If the payer abroad gets a deduction, the United Kingdom recipient loses the exemption, and the receipt is taxed. The mismatch closes from the payee's side, without the hybrid rules lifting a finger.

H M R C's guidance explains how this sits with Part six A. Where a payment is deductible for the payer but treated as a distribution in the payee's country, the two sets of rules overlap. There is no statutory order, but the distribution exemption may be considered first. And where another country has an equivalent linking rule and taxes the receipt, the United Kingdom will not usually deny the payer's deduction. H M R C refers such cases to a specialist team.

The Undertow facts show the reverse. Marrovia, in our invented case, has no linking rule. It exempts the coupon whatever happens in the United Kingdom. That is precisely why the United Kingdom, as payer's country, must make the primary response.

Where the United Kingdom payee is caught by the hybrid rules themselves, the secondary response in chapter three applies. If the payer's country has not counteracted, the United Kingdom payee is charged on the relevant amount as income, in addition to whatever it already includes.

The lesson for an answer is to check both ends of the payment. Ask how the payer's country treats it and how the payee's country treats it. Then ask which country's rules respond first. A good answer names both countries and both rules, even where only one of them in the end bites. In a question, look for a dividend paired with a deduction abroad. That pairing is the trigger.

Hybrid entities, payees and establishments.

The next group of chapters deals with mismatches caused not by the instrument but by the entity in the middle.

Chapter five covers the hybrid payer. A company pays, and its own country gives a deduction. But the investor's country treats the payer as transparent, so it disregards the payment altogether. The payee, often the investor itself, includes nothing. The response is to let the hybrid payer deduct the payment only against dual inclusion income. Any surplus waits. If the payee is in the United Kingdom and the payer's country does nothing, the payee is taxed instead.

Picture a United Kingdom company whose foreign parent treats it as transparent. It pays interest to that parent. The United Kingdom gives a deduction, but the parent's country sees a payment from itself to itself, and ignores it. Nothing is included anywhere. So the United Kingdom company may deduct the interest only against income that both countries tax.

Chapter six deals with transparent establishments, meaning permanent establishments. A United Kingdom permanent establishment of a foreign company may claim deductions for deemed payments to its own head office. If the head office's country ignores those internal payments, there is a mismatch. The establishment's deduction is limited to dual inclusion income, with the excess carried forward.

Chapter seven covers the hybrid payee. Here the payee is the hybrid. A reverse hybrid is the textbook case. Its own country treats it as transparent, while its investors' country treats it as a company, so nobody taxes what it receives. The payer's deduction is the primary target. A United Kingdom investor may be taxed as the secondary response. The Finance Act twenty twenty two widened this chapter, with retrospective effect, to cover other transparent entities as well as partnerships.

H M R C's guidance adds a useful point here. Where a payment to a reverse hybrid is caught by a C F C charge, that charge can count as inclusion, so no mismatch may remain. Hold on to that point. It comes back in Project Undertow.

Chapter eight covers the multinational payee. A company receives a payment through a permanent establishment that no country taxes, because the head office country exempts branch profits and the branch country does not recognise the branch. The payer's deduction is reduced.

Notice the pattern across all four chapters. Identify the hybrid element. Measure the mismatch. Then apply the response the chapter gives, in the right country.

Double deductions.

The second family of mismatches is the double deduction. One expense, two deductions.

Chapter nine deals with hybrid entities. A company, say a United Kingdom subsidiary, is a taxable person here but transparent to its foreign parent. Its expenses are deducted in the United Kingdom, and they also flow up and are deducted against the parent's income abroad.

The primary response falls on the investor. Where the investor is in the United Kingdom, its deduction is allowed only against dual inclusion income. The secondary response falls on the hybrid entity. If the investor's country does not counteract, and the two are in the same control group or the arrangement is structured, the United Kingdom restricts the hybrid entity's own deduction.

Here is the arithmetic. Suppose, for this example only, a United Kingdom company is owned by a parent in a country with no hybrid rules. That country treats the United Kingdom company as transparent. The United Kingdom company has two million pounds of expenses, deductible in both countries. It also has one point four million pounds of income taxed in both, which is dual inclusion income.

The United Kingdom applies the secondary response. The company deducts one point four million pounds now. The other six hundred thousand pounds is carried forward, to be set against future dual inclusion income. This year's tax is one hundred and fifty thousand pounds higher, but the relief is deferred, not destroyed. The law also allows stranded deductions to be released in some cases, where no more dual inclusion income can arise.

Chapter ten applies the same idea to dual resident companies and to companies with permanent establishments abroad. If an amount is deductible both in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, the United Kingdom restricts it to dual inclusion income.

Dual inclusion income can be lumpy. One company in a group may have more than it needs while another has too little. The Finance Act twenty twenty one added chapter twelve A, which lets a group allocate surplus dual inclusion income from one company to another. It applies for claimant accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty one.

Because the restricted amount waits for future dual inclusion income, the deferred tax question from chapter six follows. Is it probable that such income will arise?

The tax function's job here is tracking. Dual inclusion income is not a figure in the accounts. Someone must compute it every year, by company and by entity, and keep the carried-forward amounts alive.

Imported mismatches.

Chapter eleven reaches further. It asks whether a United Kingdom payment funds a mismatch that happens somewhere else.

This is the chapter that can make a United Kingdom borrower need facts about companies it never deals with.

Picture a chain. A United Kingdom company pays interest to a group company abroad. That company, in turn, makes a hybrid payment to a third territory, where a mismatch arises. The United Kingdom payment is ordinary, but it feeds the mismatch. Chapter eleven denies the United Kingdom deduction to the extent of the mismatch it funds, where the parties are in the same control group or the arrangement is structured.

An example helps, with every country invented. A United Kingdom company borrows from a group finance company in country A, which has hybrid rules matching the O E C D's. The finance company funds itself with a hybrid instrument from a group company in country B, which has no such rules. Country A can counteract that hybrid itself, so the United Kingdom need do nothing. But if country A had no way to counteract it, the United Kingdom deduction would be at risk, because the United Kingdom money feeds the mismatch.

As first enacted, this chapter was very wide. It could reach a mismatch that another country's own hybrid rules were already dealing with. The Finance Act twenty twenty one narrowed it, generally from the tenth of June, twenty twenty one. Now it bites only on a mismatch that is not capable of being counteracted under the law of a territory whose hybrid rules match the O E C D's.

That twenty twenty one package was the United Kingdom correcting its own over-reach. It also carved out certain debt relief situations, and dealt with transparent funds. Since then, Part six A has not been amended by the Finance Act twenty twenty five or the Finance Act twenty twenty six.

Imported mismatches matter most to groups whose parent or financing hub is abroad, where a United Kingdom company sits at the end of a long funding chain. Tarnmoor is parented in the United Kingdom, so its exposure is smaller. Even so, the tax function asks the question whenever a United Kingdom company borrows from a group company overseas.

Chapter thirteen of Part six A adds a targeted anti-avoidance rule, for arrangements designed to escape the other chapters. And a counteraction can be revisited, under chapter twelve, if income later turns out to be included after all.

Project Undertow.

Back to Group Year Four, and Tom Hesketh's memo for the board. Everything in it is part of our invented story.

Before he wrote a word, Tom asked the adviser three questions. How exactly would Marrovia tax the coupon? Who would be the debtor? And where would the eighty million pounds come from? The answers drove everything that followed.

The adviser's paper made a simple claim. Tarnmoor Finance would deduct five point six million pounds a year, saving one point four million pounds of corporation tax. Marrovia would exempt the coupon as a dividend. To fund the notes, Tarnmoor plc would subscribe eighty million pounds of new shares in Tarnmoor Capital.

The paper admitted one cost. Tarnmoor Capital is a controlled foreign company, so a C F C charge would follow. But the adviser assumed the finance company exemption, which taxes only a quarter of qualifying loan profits. On that basis the charge would be three hundred and fifty thousand pounds, and the net saving one point zero five million pounds a year.

Tom's memo started somewhere the deck had skipped. Would the United Kingdom even see debt?

Perpetual notes held by a company associated with the issuer are what the distribution rules in the Corporation Tax Act twenty ten call equity notes. Interest on them is treated as a distribution. A distribution is not deductible at all. H M R C's own manual gives perpetual securities as its example.

The adviser had an answer. The notes would let Tarnmoor Finance defer or cancel the coupon, they would have no other significant equity features, and Tarnmoor Finance would elect to treat them as hybrid capital instruments. An instrument within that regime is not an equity note, so its coupon stays interest.

That regime replaced earlier rules for regulatory capital. H M R C describes its aim as allowing coupon deductions in all sectors, but only for instruments that are, in essence, debt. It was never meant as a door for schemes, and its purpose test says so.

But the rules give the election no effect where arrangements have a main purpose of obtaining a tax advantage. Undertow had no other purpose. So Tom's first conclusion was blunt. There was a serious risk that the coupon would be a distribution, with no deduction from the start.

Suppose the election stood. Then the hybrid rules took over.

Tom's memo.

Tom worked through the rules in the order a marker would want.

First, the hybrid rules. The payment is under a financial instrument. Tarnmoor Finance is within corporation tax. The mismatch arises from the notes' terms, because Marrovia reads their perpetual, subordinated features as equity. And the two companies are related, both wholly owned by Tarnmoor plc. Chapter three applies. The whole five point six million pounds is a mismatch, and the primary response falls on Tarnmoor Finance as payer. On the hybrid rules alone, the deduction worth one point four million pounds is denied.

Second, withholding. If the coupon is interest, it is yearly interest paid by a company. The notes would not be listed, so they are not quoted Eurobonds. Marrovia has no treaty with the United Kingdom. And the private placement exemption needs a lender in a territory with a suitable treaty, and a security entered into for genuine commercial reasons. So the withholding rules in Part fifteen of the Income Tax Act two thousand and seven would require Tarnmoor Finance to deduct income tax at twenty per cent, one point one two million pounds a year. Coming next, the rate becomes twenty two per cent from twenty twenty seven to twenty eight, which would make it one point two three two million pounds.

Third, the C F C charge. The finance company exemption needs a qualifying loan relationship, and a loan to a United Kingdom debtor is not one. The coupon would come from capital invested from the United Kingdom, so it would pass the gateway. The charge on Tarnmoor plc would be twenty five per cent of five point six million pounds, one point four million pounds. The income tax withheld counts as creditable tax, leaving two hundred and eighty thousand pounds to pay.

Now the interaction. H M R C's guidance says income that has suffered a C F C charge may be treated as ordinary income. It is treated as the income of a company holding at least a quarter of the controlled foreign company, to the extent the statute allows. On that reading, the C F C charge could stand in for the missing Marrovian tax, and the deduction might survive. Tom's memo did not need to settle the point, because neither answer helps.

Fourth, the other gates. Transfer pricing would ask whether an independent finance company would issue perpetual notes at seven per cent at all. The corporate interest restriction counts interest paid to group companies abroad. In a year when the group's interest was already restricted, as in Group Years One and Two, the extra five point six million pounds would simply be disallowed. And section four four one, the unallowable purpose rule of the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, would ask why Tarnmoor Finance was party to the notes. The only answer was tax.

So the memo set out the outcomes. If the coupon is a distribution, there is no deduction at all, and the scheme has nothing to offer. If the deduction survives because the C F C charge counts as inclusion, the one point four million pound saving is matched by one point four million pounds of withholding and C F C charge. If any rule denies the deduction while the C F C charge still bites, the group pays one point four million pounds a year more than if it had done nothing.

The best case was break-even. The worst case was a loss every year, plus the cost of breaking the group's published promise not to use tax avoidance schemes. The board rejected Undertow in a single meeting.

The minute recorded three reasons. The scheme could not beat doing nothing. It would have created an annual dispute with H M R C over several regimes at once. And it conflicted with the tax strategy. Tarnmoor Capital went on lending to Tarnmoor Vallaria, as before, and Tarnmoor Finance's funding stayed plain.

Notice how Tom built the memo. He did not stop when he found the first problem. A board needs to know whether a scheme fails on one ground or on six, because a scheme that fails on one ground invites the adviser to come back with a fix. A scheme that fails on six does not. That is also how an examiner rewards an answer about a cross-border financing. Each regime is a separate set of marks.

A low rate is not a hybrid.

Undertow worked as a test case because it had a genuine hybrid element. Many questions do not, and that is where candidates go wrong.

The examiners reported, after the November twenty twenty five sitting, that some candidates thought a low-tax territory on its own made something a hybrid, and wrote generic anti-avoidance answers instead. A payment to a company taxed at nine per cent is not a hybrid mismatch. If it is fully included in that company's income, there is no mismatch, however low the rate.

The low rate is a matter for other regimes. Transfer pricing tests the price. The C F C rules test whether profits have been diverted from the United Kingdom. The global minimum tax in chapter thirty tops up low effective rates. The hybrid rules have a narrower job. They catch a difference in characterisation, and only that.

So the first question in any hybrid answer is always, where is the hybrid? Is there an instrument two countries read differently? An entity one sees as a person and the other sees through? A permanent establishment one country recognises and the other ignores? A company resident in two places? If you cannot point to one, the rules do not apply, and the examiners have twice criticised candidates who raised them anyway.

The interactions follow a sequence, and H M R C has said how it sees it. Its guidance says it would expect the hybrid rules to apply before the corporate interest restriction. It also says transfer pricing and the hybrid rules must be applied together. Companies cannot compare them and pick the better answer, or choose the order. The arm's length test is run with the hybrid rules fully applied to both the actual and the arm's length position, and then the hybrid rules are checked again.

The unallowable purpose rule stands alongside, and an amount it disallows cannot come back in under any other rule.

Hybrids have appeared once as a whole question in recent sittings. November twenty twenty five, question six, was a ten mark discursive question. It covered hybrid entities and instruments, deduction non-inclusion and double deduction mismatches, primary and secondary responses, and the return. The answers were mixed.

The other appearance was a warning. In November twenty twenty four, a question about a group buying a United Kingdom company carried no hybrid trigger, yet some candidates brought hybrids in anyway.

Expect hybrids to arrive alongside other regimes. The favourite companions on this paper are transfer pricing, the interest restriction and the C F C rules, exactly the regimes Undertow touched. When a scenario describes an intra-group financing across a border, run the same checklist Tom ran. Is it debt under United Kingdom law? Is there a hybrid element? What does transfer pricing say about the amount? Does the interest restriction bite? Is there withholding? Does a C F C charge follow? Is there an unallowable purpose?

So the technique is this. Find the hybrid element and name it. Name the mismatch, deduction non-inclusion or double deduction. Name the chapter. Say which country responds first and what the response is. Compute the amount if numbers are given, including dual inclusion income and carry forward. Finish with the administration. Keep it tight, because a ten mark question earns about twenty one minutes.

Administration and the tax function.

Because the rules are self-executing, the work falls on the company.

The counteraction goes into the corporation tax computation. A denied deduction is added back, and any taxable amount under a secondary response is brought in as income. There is no H M R C notice to wait for.

The return asks about it. The supplementary pages called C T six hundred B cover controlled foreign companies, the foreign branch exemption, and hybrid and other mismatches. They ask whether the company has made a counteraction under Part six A, the totals counteracted, and any claims to allocate or consent to an allocation of surplus dual inclusion income. They are completed only where a company has something to report.

The tax function's tasks follow. Keep a register of instruments and entities whose treatment may differ abroad. Track dual inclusion income and carried-forward restricted deductions, company by company. Ask overseas advisers how each payment is treated in the payee's country, because the United Kingdom answer often turns on foreign law. H M R C also offers non-statutory clarification on how the rules apply.

Acquisitions deserve special care. A target may hold instruments or entities that are harmless in its old group but hybrid in the new one, once the relationships change. Due diligence should map them before completion.

And one loose end is worth knowing. The definition of tax in Part six A still mentions diverted profits tax, at least in the text we checked. Yet that tax has been replaced by the unassessed transfer pricing profits charge, for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. Chapter thirty tells that story.

The best hybrid planning is not to need the rules. A tax function in a group like Tarnmoor works on that basis.

Keep instruments plain. An intra-group loan that is debt everywhere, with a fixed term and an ordinary coupon, rarely creates a mismatch. Perpetual, subordinated or convertible features invite a different reading abroad. Before a group company issues anything unusual to a related party overseas, the tax function asks how the payee's country will treat it, and gets that answer in writing.

Watch entity elections. Some countries let a parent choose to treat a foreign subsidiary as transparent. That choice, made abroad for local reasons, can turn a plain United Kingdom company into a hybrid entity overnight. The double deduction and hybrid payer chapters then follow. So the group's register should record every entity whose classification differs between countries.

Remember who is related. A twenty five per cent investment is enough. Joint ventures and consortium companies, such as Helmside in our invented story, can be related to their investors for these purposes. And a company that joins or leaves the group changes its relationships on the day it moves.

Document the analysis. Where the answer depends on foreign law or on a judgement about whether a mismatch arises from an instrument's terms, the file should show who advised, what they said and when. Where a position is uncertain and large, the uncertain tax treatment rules in chapter four may require the group to notify H M R C.

And keep the ethics in view. Tarnmoor publishes a tax strategy saying it does not use tax avoidance schemes. Undertow would have broken that promise even if every computation had worked. Tom's memo said so, in one line, at the top.

What to take away.

Hybrid mismatches arise when two countries characterise the same payment, entity or establishment differently. The O E C D's final report of the fifth of October, twenty fifteen, targeted outcomes, not motives. The United Kingdom's rules are in Part six A of the International Act, for payments made on or after the first of January, twenty seventeen. They replaced notice-based arbitrage rules and apply automatically.

There are two outcomes. A deduction non-inclusion mismatch is a deduction here with no ordinary income there. A double deduction is one amount deducted twice. Primary and secondary responses make sure the mismatch is neutralised once.

Most chapters need related parties, meaning a control group or a twenty five per cent investment, or a structured arrangement. Between related parties there is no purpose test. Withholding tax is ignored, and a C F C charge counts as tax.

Chapter three covers financial instruments. The payer's deduction is reduced first, and the payee is taxed second. An under-taxed coupon is scaled. One million pounds taxed at five per cent against a full rate of twenty per cent gives a mismatch of seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds.

Chapters five, seven and eight cover hybrid payers, hybrid payees and multinational payees. Chapter six covers permanent establishments. Chapters nine and ten cover double deductions, with deductions allowed against dual inclusion income and the rest carried forward. Two million pounds of expenses against one point four million pounds of dual inclusion income leaves six hundred thousand pounds to carry forward. Chapter twelve A allows surplus dual inclusion income to move around a group.

Chapter eleven covers imported mismatches, narrowed in twenty twenty one to mismatches not capable of counteraction in a territory with matching rules. Part six A was not changed by the Finance Acts of twenty twenty five or twenty twenty six.

In our invented case, Project Undertow failed every test. Perpetual notes held by an associated company risk being equity notes, and the hybrid capital instrument election fails where tax is a main purpose. If the coupon is interest, the hybrid rules deny a deduction worth one point four million pounds. Withholding at twenty per cent takes one point one two million pounds. A full C F C charge applies, because a loan to a United Kingdom debtor is not a qualifying loan relationship. Transfer pricing, the interest restriction and the unallowable purpose rule all wait behind. The best case was break-even, the worst a loss of one point four million pounds a year.

And remember the examiners' lesson. A low tax rate is not a hybrid. No hybrid element, no hybrid answer.

The global minimum tax deals with the low rates themselves, and it is where corporation tax goes next. Chapter thirty turns to the global minimum and the end of diverted profits tax.


Chapter thirty: The global minimum and the end of diverted profits tax.

A floor under the world.

In October twenty twenty one, more than one hundred and thirty five countries agreed something that tax policy had never managed before. They agreed a minimum. The largest multinational groups would pay at least fifteen per cent on their profits in every country where they operate, or someone, somewhere, would collect the difference. The deal was struck through the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which I will call the O E C D, and its wider Inclusive Framework of countries. The United Kingdom wrote its share of the deal into the Finance Number Two Act twenty twenty three, which I will call the Pillar Two legislation.

Seven years earlier, the United Kingdom had reached for a blunter weapon. In his Autumn Statement on the third of December, twenty fourteen, the Chancellor, George Osborne, announced a diverted profits tax. The press called it the Google tax. It sat outside corporation tax, charged a higher rate than corporation tax, and made the company pay before it could argue. For accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, it is gone. Its work now belongs to a charge inside corporation tax, on what the law calls unassessed transfer pricing profits.

Both changes share a single idea. Profit should be taxed somewhere, at a fair rate, and a group that shifts it away should gain nothing. So this chapter asks two linked questions. When a large group's profits end up somewhere taxed below the floor, who collects the difference? And now that diverted profits tax has gone, what stops a group from pricing its own dealings so that profit quietly leaves the United Kingdom?

This is chapter thirty, the last chapter of Part Four, on profits that cross borders. Everything in it is awareness level on the Advanced Technical paper, grade three in the syllabus grid. That covers multinational top-up tax, domestic top-up tax and diverted profits tax. None of them was examined between May twenty twenty three and May twenty twenty six. The Living Law only signposted these rules, so we start from first principles, but we keep to the depth that an awareness topic deserves. Its close neighbours are chapters twenty six and twenty seven, on controlled foreign companies and transfer pricing. Throughout, we apply the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, under the Finance Act twenty twenty six.

Why a minimum tax.

Start with the problem. Profit is easy to move and hard to pin down. A group can put its patents, its brands or its lending in a subsidiary in a low tax country, and pay that subsidiary royalties or interest from everywhere else. Transfer pricing asks whether the price is right. Controlled foreign company rules, chapter twenty six, ask whether the parent's country should tax the subsidiary's profit. But neither rule touches the low rate itself. And for decades countries competed on that rate, each cutting a little to attract the mobile profit of large groups.

The minimum tax does not forbid a low rate. A country may still tax at nine per cent, or at nothing. What changes is that the low rate stops working for the largest groups, because the difference up to fifteen per cent is collected anyway. Picture a floor fitted under every country's tax rate. If a country leaves a gap below the floor, another country fills it. The precise rule is this. For each country where a group operates, the group works out an effective tax rate on a common measure of profit. Where that rate is below fifteen per cent, a top-up tax brings it up to fifteen.

In December twenty twenty one the O E C D published model rules for this, called the global anti-base erosion rules. I will call them the GloBE rules. As commentators describe the arrangement, countries were not obliged to adopt them, but those that did were expected to follow the model, so that the pieces would fit together across borders. A floor only works if every country measures the room the same way. The whole project is usually called Pillar Two. A separate first pillar is not on this paper.

Is it a good idea? That is a live debate, and the paper will not ask you to settle it. Supporters say it ends a race to the bottom that drained public revenue and rewarded paper structures over real investment. Critics say it erodes a country's right to set its own taxes, blunts tax incentives that small economies use to attract real activity, and buries large groups in compliance. Both points have force, and economists still argue about the evidence. The law, for now, has chosen the floor, and the United Kingdom has built it into two taxes.

The United Kingdom's two taxes, and who is in.

The first is multinational top-up tax, in Part three of the Pillar Two legislation. It applies to accounting periods commencing on or after the thirty first of December, twenty twenty three. Its main engine is the income inclusion rule. A United Kingdom parent of a qualifying group pays top-up tax on the low taxed profits of its members abroad. The Finance Act twenty twenty five added a second engine, the undertaxed profits rule, for accounting periods commencing on or after the thirty first of December, twenty twenty four. It is a backstop. Where low taxed profit escapes every income inclusion rule, perhaps because the parent's country has none, other countries collect a share.

The second is domestic top-up tax, in Part four of the same Act, from the same date in twenty twenty three. It applies the same arithmetic to the group's United Kingdom entities, so that any top-up on United Kingdom profit is collected by the United Kingdom, not by a parent's country abroad. H M R C's manual describes it as the United Kingdom's qualified domestic minimum top-up tax. So the order of collection is this. The country where the profit arises has first claim, through its own domestic top-up tax, which is credited in the group calculation. Then the parent's country collects through the income inclusion rule. The undertaxed profits rule mops up anything left.

Who is in? The threshold is in section one hundred and twenty nine of the Pillar Two legislation. A group qualifies if the revenue in its ultimate parent's consolidated accounts exceeds seven hundred and fifty million euros in at least two of the four previous accounting periods, with short periods scaled down, and at least one member is located in the United Kingdom. Notice the word exceeds. The statute says it, and so does H M R C's manual. But H M R C's online guidance on whether you need to report says seven hundred and fifty million euros or more. That only matters for a group at exactly the line, and there the statute governs.

Now meet our invented group, Tarnmoor. Every company, person and country in it is invented for teaching. Tarnmoor P L C is a widely held engineering group listed in London. It is the ultimate parent entity, the company at the top of the consolidated accounts. Its consolidated revenue in Group Year One was one thousand, one hundred and eighty million pounds. At the story's invented exchange rate of one euro fifteen to the pound, that is about one point three six billion euros, and every year from Group Year One to Group Year Seven is far above the line. In our invented case Tarnmoor was already in scope before Group Year One, so Tarnmoor P L C long ago registered as the group's filing member.

Measuring the rate.

The GloBE rules do not use any country's own tax computation. They start from the accounting profit of each group entity, as used for the consolidated accounts, and make a set of adjustments of their own. The result is called GloBE income. Against it they set covered taxes, broadly taxes on income, including the group's own deferred tax adjustments and some taxes paid by other members on that entity's profit.

The effective tax rate is then worked out country by country, not company by company. All the group's entities in one territory are blended together. Total covered taxes in the territory, divided by total GloBE income in the territory, gives the jurisdictional rate. If it is below fifteen per cent, H M R C's manual explains, the top-up percentage is fifteen per cent less that rate.

The top-up percentage is not applied to the whole profit. First, the rules deduct a substance-based income exclusion. It is a deduction in proportion to the payroll costs and tangible assets the group has in the territory, a rough return on real people and real plant. What remains is the excess profit, and the top-up percentage applies to that. A territory with many staff and factories may owe little or nothing even at a low rate. A territory holding only patents or loans gets almost no exclusion. In the Tarnmoor figures that follow, we leave the exclusion out, which overstates the top-up a little, and we treat accounting profit as GloBE income.

Here is the misconception to drop. People say that under Pillar Two every company must now pay at least fifteen per cent. It is not true. First, the rules reach only groups over the threshold. Second, the test is a blended rate for each territory, so one company at ten per cent and its sister at twenty may together clear the floor. Third, the measure is GloBE income and covered taxes, not taxable profit and tax paid. A United Kingdom company whose current tax is low because of full expensing does not create a top-up, because the GloBE rules count the deferred tax as well. As chapter six explained, the accounts themselves keep Pillar Two out of deferred tax under the temporary exception in I A S twelve, and show any top-up tax separately as current tax.

So the rule is a floor for each territory of a large group, measured on its own base. It is not a minimum rate for each company.

Tarnmoor's Marrovian test.

In our invented case, the group's finance company, Tarnmoor Capital, is resident in Marrovia, an invented country with a corporation tax rate of nine per cent and, in the story, no domestic minimum tax of its own.

In Group Year Five its profit is five point one million pounds, interest of five point four million less three hundred thousand of expenses. Marrovia taxes that at nine per cent, which is four hundred and fifty nine thousand pounds.

The United Kingdom also taxes some of that profit. As chapter twenty six shows, Tarnmoor Capital is a controlled foreign company, which I will call a C F C. After the finance company exemption, a quarter of its profit is chargeable, one point two seven five million pounds. Tarnmoor P L C pays a C F C charge of two hundred and four thousand pounds on it, after credit for the Marrovian tax.

Now the Pillar Two step. Section one hundred and seventy nine of the legislation pushes a parent's C F C tax down to the C F C for this purpose, so it counts as a covered tax of Marrovia. For mobile income such as interest, the amount pushed down is capped. The cap is fifteen per cent less the local rate, applied to that income. Here that is six per cent of five point one million pounds, or three hundred and six thousand pounds. The C F C charge of two hundred and four thousand pounds sits inside the cap, so all of it moves.

Marrovia's covered taxes are therefore four hundred and fifty nine thousand plus two hundred and four thousand, which is six hundred and sixty three thousand pounds. Divided by five point one million, the effective rate is thirteen per cent. The top-up percentage is two per cent. Two per cent of five point one million pounds is one hundred and two thousand pounds. Tarnmoor P L C pays it as multinational top-up tax under the income inclusion rule. The full working is in the reading edition.

Look at the total. Marrovian tax, the C F C charge and the top-up come to seven hundred and sixty five thousand pounds. That is exactly fifteen per cent of five point one million. Without the push-down, the top-up alone would have been three hundred and six thousand pounds, exactly what the C F C charge and the top-up now make together. The floor holds whichever route the money takes. The same arithmetic in Group Years One to Four, on a profit of three point three million pounds, gives a top-up of sixty six thousand pounds a year.

Elsewhere the floor does not bite on the story's figures. Vallaria taxes Tarnmoor Vallaria at twenty per cent. The United Kingdom companies pay twenty five per cent, so on the story's figures there is no domestic top-up tax. Tarnmoor Ireland, Irish resident from Group Year Four, pays Ireland's twelve and a half per cent trading rate, below the floor. Who collects any Irish top-up depends on Irish law, which this paper does not examine, so the story leaves it aside.

Safe harbours.

A full GloBE computation for every territory, every year, is a heavy task. The law offers safe harbours, routes that treat a territory's top-up as nil without the full calculation.

The most used is the transitional country-by-country reporting safe harbour, in Schedule sixteen to the Pillar Two legislation. It borrows figures from the group's country-by-country report. A group may elect for it for accounting periods commencing on or before the thirty first of December, twenty twenty six, and ending on or before the thirtieth of June, twenty twenty eight. A territory passes if it meets any one of three tests. The de minimis test needs revenue under ten million euros and profit under one million euros. The simplified effective tax rate test compares tax with profit before tax and needs a rate of at least fifteen per cent for periods beginning before twenty twenty five, sixteen per cent for periods beginning in twenty twenty five, and seventeen per cent for periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. The routine profits test is met if profit is no more than the substance-based income exclusion. If a group does not use the safe harbour for a territory in one year, it cannot return to it for that territory later. Once out, always out.

In real calendar terms, a group with a calendar year gets the harbour for twenty twenty six, at the seventeen per cent test, and that is its last year. A group whose year runs from July twenty twenty six to June twenty twenty seven also gets that year.

In our invented case we run the numbers on this year's rules. Vallaria, at twenty per cent, passes the seventeen per cent test where the harbour is available, and that saves the group a computation it would win anyway. Marrovia fails all three tests. Tarnmoor Capital's revenue, about six point two million euros, is under ten million, but its profit, nearly six million euros, is far above one million. Its rate is below seventeen per cent. And a finance company with a small office has almost no substance-based exclusion. So Marrovia always needs the full calculation.

Two other harbours are worth recognising. The transitional safe harbour for the undertaxed profits rule protected a parent's territory with a nominal corporate rate of at least twenty per cent, for periods of up to twelve months commencing by the end of twenty twenty five and ending before the thirty first of December, twenty twenty six. The qualified domestic minimum top-up tax safe harbour lets a group that pays an accredited domestic top-up tax in a territory treat the top-up there as nil under everyone else's rules, so one calculation does. The Finance Act twenty twenty six adds simplified calculations for members that are not material.

Registration, returns and a moving rulebook.

The administration is where an awareness question may well find its marks.

A qualifying group must register within six months after the end of its first accounting period as a qualifying group, even if no top-up tax is due. A filing member then files a GloBE information return within fifteen months after the end of each accounting period, or eighteen months for the first. No deadline falls before the thirtieth of June, twenty twenty six. If the information return is filed with a qualifying authority abroad, the United Kingdom member may notify that instead. The United Kingdom self-assessment return for the top-up taxes follows the same timetable. H M R C announced a transitional approach for the first wave. It would charge no late filing penalties on submissions made before the first of August, twenty twenty six.

In our invented case, Tarnmoor P L C is the filing member. For Group Year Five, which ends on the thirty first of December, its information return, its United Kingdom return and its payment of the one hundred and two thousand pounds are due by the thirty first of March, Group Year Seven, fifteen months on. In the group accounts the top-up is current tax, shown separately, with no deferred tax, as chapter six explained.

The rulebook keeps moving. The Finance Act twenty twenty six, in Schedule eight, makes a long list of changes. They include elective qualified domestic top-up taxes, rules for permanent establishments and for flow-through parents, a qualifying undertaxed profits tax, group relief payments counted as covered taxes, and the simplified calculations. The general start date is accounting periods beginning on or after the thirty first of December, twenty twenty five, with an election to apply them back to the start.

Coming next, and not law. In January twenty twenty six the O E C D released what is called the side-by-side package, designed, as its name suggests, to let some countries' own minimum tax systems operate alongside the GloBE rules. On the thirteenth of July, twenty twenty six, the government published draft legislation for the Finance Bill twenty twenty six to twenty seven to bring it in. The draft would apply to periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, and includes elective safe harbours, one aimed at groups with United States parents. It is proposed, not law, and it is not examinable on the Finance Act twenty twenty six.

Diverted profits tax, and pay now, argue later.

Now the other half of the chapter. Diverted profits tax was in Part three of the Finance Act twenty fifteen. It applied to accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty fifteen. It had two limbs. The first caught a United Kingdom company whose arrangements with a related party involved entities or transactions lacking economic substance. The second caught a foreign company that arranged its affairs to avoid having a taxable presence in the United Kingdom, the avoided permanent establishment. The rate was twenty five per cent, set above corporation tax on purpose. For accounting periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty three, it rose to thirty one per cent, six points above the new main rate.

The design was as important as the rate. H M R C issued notices, and the company had to pay the tax before it could argue. Review and appeal came later. The aim was plain. A group facing an immediate cash bill at a premium rate had every reason to agree its transfer pricing on the ordinary corporation tax basis instead.

The design met its first test in the courts in twenty seventeen. H M R C issued Glencore Energy U K Limited with a charging notice of twenty one million, one hundred and twenty nine thousand, three hundred and forty nine pounds, plus interest, for its nine month accounting period to the thirty first of December, twenty fifteen. Glencore did not wait for the statutory review and appeal. It asked the High Court for judicial review of the notice.

The case is Glencore Energy U K Limited versus H M R C, decided by the High Court in twenty seventeen. Mr Justice Green refused permission. The statute provided its own route, a review and then an appeal to the First-tier Tribunal, and that was an adequate alternative remedy. Judicial review is a remedy of last resort. Glencore appealed, and later that year the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on the same ground. Judicial review would be right only in an exceptional case.

Glencore's lesson is the one the design intended. Pay now, argue later. The tax would be argued, if at all, after the money had moved.

The weakness lay elsewhere. A free standing tax, outside corporation tax, sat awkwardly with double tax treaties and the mutual agreement procedure between tax authorities. That is the problem the replacement solves.

From diverted profits tax to unassessed transfer pricing profits.

Section forty six of the Finance Act twenty twenty six, with Schedule five, repealed diverted profits tax for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. In its place is a new Part four A of the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act, running from section two hundred and seventeen A to section two hundred and seventeen T.

Watch the commencement, in real calendar terms. A company with a calendar year is under the new rules for twenty twenty six. A company whose year ran from the first of April, twenty twenty five, to the thirty first of March, twenty twenty six, stays under diverted profits tax for that whole year, and moves to the new rules from the first of April, twenty twenty six. Old periods keep the old tax, so an enquiry into an earlier year can still involve diverted profits tax, and an adviser must check the period before naming the charge.

Which brings us to the second misconception of the chapter. Diverted profits tax still exists. For current periods it does not. For any accounting period beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, the answer is unassessed transfer pricing profits, and on a paper examined on the Finance Act twenty twenty six, that is the name to use.

What does the new charge tax? Unassessed transfer pricing profits are profits that a transfer pricing requirement brings into charge, but that the company has not reflected in its own return. Chapter twenty seven explains the transfer pricing rules themselves. The new charge has no measure of its own. It borrows the arm's length price, and taxes the gap between that price and the return. The charge is corporation tax, so the government's documents say treaties and the mutual agreement procedure apply to it. The rate is the underlying corporation tax rate plus six per cent. At the main rate of twenty five per cent, that is thirty one per cent. Diverted profits tax's separate notification duty has not been kept.

And the avoided permanent establishment limb? It has no direct successor in the new Part. On this book's reading, that work now falls to the rewritten definition of a permanent establishment in the Finance Act twenty twenty six, with its principal role test for dependent agents, which chapter twenty three explains. The government has not put it in exactly those words.

Three gates.

Unassessed transfer pricing profits are not charged at the premium rate just because a price was wrong. Three gates must all open.

The first is an effective tax mismatch outcome. The underlying corporation tax amount is United Kingdom tax, at the underlying rate, on the profit the company should have reported. The corresponding amount is the tax the other party pays on the matching profit. The gate opens only if the corresponding amount is less than eighty per cent of the underlying amount. H M R C's manual gives an example. A United Kingdom company pays twenty million pounds for services worth fifteen million. The unassessed profit is five million pounds, and United Kingdom tax on it would be one point two five million. The overseas company pays one million pounds of tax on the same five million. That is exactly eighty per cent, so there is no mismatch.

The second gate is the tax design condition. It is met if it is reasonable to assume that the arrangements were designed to reduce, eliminate or delay United Kingdom tax. H M R C's manual says this is not the main purpose test found elsewhere, and that the charge will not apply merely because a group moves a whole activity to a lower tax country. The target is separating United Kingdom activity from the income it produces.

The third gate is that the profits must not arise wholly from excepted loan relationship arrangements, meaning loans and the derivatives that hedge them. H M R C's guidance adds that a loan inside a wider arrangement does not automatically qualify.

For this example, suppose a United Kingdom distributor in another group overpays a royalty by four million pounds to a related company taxed at five per cent. United Kingdom tax on four million would be one million pounds. The other company pays two hundred thousand, only twenty per cent of that. The first gate opens. If the design condition is also met, the charge at thirty one per cent is one point two four million pounds. Had the company corrected the price in its own return, it would have paid one million. The premium is two hundred and forty thousand pounds.

Now Tarnmoor. The invented Vallarian rate of twenty per cent is exactly eighty per cent of the United Kingdom's twenty five. So on the story's simplified figures, a United Kingdom to Vallaria provision never opens the first gate. Calder's sale of its process valve business to Tarnmoor Vallaria in Group Year Three is the test. When the price was later raised by two million pounds, as chapter twenty seven tells, United Kingdom tax on the increase was five hundred thousand pounds, and Vallarian tax on the matching profit four hundred thousand. Eighty per cent, not less. And the sale moved a real business in any case. Marrovia is different. Nine per cent is only thirty six per cent of twenty five, so a Marrovian provision would open the first gate. The one United Kingdom to Marrovia deal ever proposed, Project Undertow, was a loan, and the board rejected it anyway.

Pay first, and what the examiner wants.

The procedure keeps the old pay first design, now inside corporation tax.

A designated H M R C officer may give a preliminary notice no later than four years after the end of the accounting period. The company has thirty days to make representations, and only on limited grounds. The officer then has sixty days from the preliminary notice to make an assessment, or thirty days after a closure notice if that is later. Then comes a fifteen month period for amendments. During it the company may amend its return to bring the profits into ordinary corporation tax, though not in the last twenty one days, and H M R C may correct or increase the assessment.

The company must pay. Postponement is allowed only for tax equal to tax already paid on the corresponding profits. It may appeal only after paying and after the period for amendments, within thirty days. The tribunal may reduce the charge to the ordinary rate if a gate was not in fact open. And no relief, deduction or set-off of any description is allowed against the profits or the tax.

The lesson for a tax function is simple. The charge is a lever, not a destination. Correct transfer pricing in the company's own return removes the exposure, and even after a notice, an amendment brings the profits back to the ordinary rate.

So Tarnmoor's tax function, led in the story by Tom Hesketh, keeps two lists. For unassessed transfer pricing profits, it lists every cross-border provision with a counterparty taxed at less than eighty per cent of the United Kingdom rate, and makes sure the transfer pricing documentation supports the price in the return. For Pillar Two, it gathers data from every entity well before the fifteen month deadline, decides each year, territory by territory, whether a safe harbour election is available and wanted, and reconciles the C F C charge with the top-up so nothing is counted twice.

In the exam, these topics are awareness level, grade three. None was examined between May twenty twenty three and May twenty twenty six. At awareness level the marks go to recognition, a sentence or two showing the rule exists and when it applies.

Diverted profits tax has a history on this paper, as a trap. The examiners reported, after the May twenty twenty three sitting, that time was wasted on diverted profits tax in a question about a loan, because it does not apply to loan relationships. The same discipline holds now. For any period beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, say unassessed transfer pricing profits, not diverted profits tax. And do not raise it unless the question gives you a low-taxed related party, a pricing problem and a hint of design.

For Pillar Two, the likely marks are the threshold and its two of four test, which tax applies to which entity, registration within six months, the fifteen month return, and the accounting exception. Do not attempt a full GloBE computation unless the requirement asks for one.

What to take away.

Pillar Two puts a fifteen per cent floor under the profits of large multinational groups, measured territory by territory. More than one hundred and thirty five countries agreed it in October twenty twenty one, and the United Kingdom enacted it in the Finance Number Two Act twenty twenty three.

Multinational top-up tax, from the thirty first of December, twenty twenty three, makes a United Kingdom parent pay top-up on low taxed members abroad through the income inclusion rule, with the undertaxed profits rule as backstop from a year later. Domestic top-up tax collects any top-up on United Kingdom profits first.

A group is in if consolidated revenue exceeds seven hundred and fifty million euros in at least two of the previous four periods. The statute says exceeds. Some H M R C guidance says or more.
