The effective rate is covered taxes over GloBE income for each territory. The top-up percentage is fifteen per cent less that rate, applied to profit after the substance-based income exclusion.

In our invented case, Marrovia's nine per cent plus the pushed down C F C charge of two hundred and four thousand pounds gives thirteen per cent on five point one million pounds in Group Year Five. Tarnmoor P L C pays one hundred and two thousand pounds of top-up tax. Everything together comes to exactly fifteen per cent.

The transitional country-by-country safe harbour runs out with periods commencing in twenty twenty six, when its simplified rate test is seventeen per cent. Once out, always out.

Register within six months of the end of the first qualifying period. File the information return and the United Kingdom return within fifteen months, eighteen for the first. The side-by-side package is proposed, not law.

Diverted profits tax ran from the first of April, twenty fifteen, at twenty five per cent and later thirty one per cent, and a pay now, argue later design that survived the Glencore challenge. For accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, it is repealed. Unassessed transfer pricing profits are charged as corporation tax at thirty one per cent, the main rate plus six, through three gates. The other party's tax is under eighty per cent of the United Kingdom tax, the design condition is met, and the profits do not arise wholly from excepted loan arrangements. Pay first. No reliefs. Correct pricing in the return removes the charge.

So, who collects the difference? The country where the profit arises if it chooses to, then the parent's country, then everyone else. And what stops profit leaving through mispricing? Transfer pricing, backed now by a premium rate of corporation tax that the group can avoid simply by getting the price right.

Next, Part Five puts it all together. Chapter thirty one follows a single deal, Tarnmoor's purchase of Ridgeway from Jess Hartley, through every rule in this book.


Part Five: Putting It Together.

Chapter thirty one: The Ridgeway deal.

Completion day.

On the first of April, some years after the events of the last thirty chapters, Tarnmoor P L C bought a bicycle company. The price was four and a half million pounds, paid in cash. The seller was Jess Hartley, and the company was Ridgeway Holdings, the parent of Ridgeway Cycles. Our invented group, Tarnmoor, its people and its numbers are invented for teaching, as they have been throughout this book. So is Jess, whose story The Living Law told. Ireland, which will matter later, is real.

By Tarnmoor's standards it was a small deal. Tarnmoor's revenue runs to more than a billion pounds a year. Ridgeway's taxable profit is about six hundred thousand. Yet when Tom Hesketh, the group head of tax, opened the file that morning, the list of tax points ran to two pages. That is the question for this chapter. Why does a small acquisition by a large group touch almost every rule in this book, and how do you find them all, in order, without missing the ones that carry marks?

This is chapter thirty one, the first chapter of Part Five. It is the capstone. It teaches no new rule. Every rule it uses was taught earlier, and each time I will name the chapter that owns it. What it adds is the method, the order and the interactions. The examiner calls this the interaction of taxes, and it is how most twenty mark questions are built. It also closes the last open thread of The Living Law, the question Jess never settled about her Dublin showroom.

The statutes are the familiar ones. The Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, the two thousand and nine Act. The Corporation Tax Act twenty ten, the twenty ten Act. The Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, the International Act. And the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act nineteen ninety two, the Gains Act. As always, the numbers apply the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, whatever year the story has reached.

The road to Ridgeway.

The Living Law followed Jess Hartley from a cycle business she ran herself, through incorporation and a holding company structure, to a group with two companies. Ridgeway Holdings owns Ridgeway Cycles. Jess owns all of Ridgeway Holdings, and her shares cost her one hundred and sixty two thousand pounds. Along the way the group bought and later sold another business, Wharfe Wheels. Ridgeway Cycles opened a second unit in Skipton, and then a showroom in Dublin.

The Dublin showroom is a branch, a permanent establishment of Ridgeway Cycles in Ireland, not a separate company. In its first year it lost eighty thousand pounds and in its second, thirty thousand. Both losses reduced Ridgeway's United Kingdom profits at once. In its third year it made one hundred and twenty thousand pounds, and in its fourth, two hundred thousand. Ireland taxed that at its trading rate of twelve and a half per cent, twenty five thousand pounds. The United Kingdom taxed it again, as part of Ridgeway's profits, and gave credit for the Irish tax. Jess never made the election that would take the branch out of United Kingdom tax. The Living Law, chapter twenty six, left that question open.

Chapter thirty one of The Living Law imagined an offer of four million pounds for the group, if a buyer came back tomorrow. It was a hypothetical, and no sale happened then. This is the real one, at its own price, four and a half million pounds.

Today, Ridgeway Cycles makes about four hundred thousand pounds a year from its United Kingdom trade and about two hundred thousand from Dublin. On six hundred thousand pounds, corporation tax at twenty five per cent is one hundred and fifty thousand. Less the Irish credit of twenty five thousand, it pays one hundred and twenty five thousand. Ridgeway's year ends on the thirty first of March, so the deal falls on the first day of an accounting period. That is a gift for the analysis, and you will see why.

Jess's own side takes one paragraph, because this paper does not examine it. She is an individual selling shares. Her gain, before costs, is four and a half million pounds less one hundred and sixty two thousand, about four point three four million pounds. It is charged to capital gains tax, with business asset disposal relief if she still meets its conditions, as The Living Law, chapters eighteen and thirty one, explained. No corporation tax, no shareholding exemption, nothing for the buyer to compute. Note it in one line and move on, which is exactly what an answer to this paper should do.

Walking every floor.

Think of an Advanced Technical question as a building inspection. A good surveyor does not wander the house looking at whatever catches the eye. She walks every floor, in the same order, with the same checklist, and writes down what she finds on each one, including the floors where she finds nothing. The checklist is what stops her missing the damp in the cellar while admiring the roof.

Here is Tom's checklist for a share acquisition, and it is the one this chapter follows. First, the transaction itself, meaning stamp duty and the buyer's costs. Second, the target's tax attributes, such as losses, capital losses and past intra-group transfers. Third, the thresholds that move, starting with associated companies and instalments, and then every size test the group already passes. Fourth, the group regimes the target now joins. Group relief, the deductions allowance, the annual investment allowance, research and development. Fifth, governance and compliance. The senior accounting officer, the tax strategy, uncertain tax treatments, transfer pricing, the interest restriction and the global minimum tax. Sixth, the target's own special features, here the Dublin branch. Seventh, the accounts, which means deferred tax in the consolidation. Eighth, the people. Who stays, what they are paid, and when it is deductible. And last, a recommendation, because if the question asks for one, the marks for it are there to be taken.

Two exam rules shape the walk. The first concerns the words tax consequences. The chief examiner has said, after the November twenty twenty five and May twenty twenty six sittings, that those words mean every tax in the syllabus, including stamp duty and stamp duty land tax. A named tax means only that tax. The second is that excluded means excluded. If the question says ignore transfer pricing, a paragraph on it earns nothing.

Now the misconception that this chapter exists to kill. A small acquisition is a small tax job. It is not. The size of the target barely matters. What matters is the size of the group it joins. Ridgeway goes from a two company family business to a member of a listed group of eleven companies that count as associated, a worldwide group for the interest restriction, a multinational group for the global minimum tax, a group whose transfer pricing exemption for small companies no longer applies, and a group with a senior accounting officer. Almost every compliance setting changes on completion day, and some change a year later. The tax on Ridgeway's profits hardly moves. Everything around it does.

The price of the paper.

Start on the ground floor, with the transaction. Tarnmoor P L C buys shares, so the tax on the purchase is stamp duty on the stock transfer form. The rate is half of one per cent, rounded up to the nearest five pounds. Half a per cent of four and a half million pounds is twenty two thousand, five hundred pounds, which needs no rounding. The buyer pays. The form must be presented for stamping within thirty days of execution, or interest and penalties run. Chapter twenty one owns these rules.

There is no stamp duty land tax, even though Ridgeway Cycles occupies property in Skipton. The land stays where it was, inside the company. Only the shares changed hands. And there is no stamp duty group relief, because Jess is an individual. Relief needs a seventy five per cent relationship between transferor and transferee, and an individual is never in a group.

The twenty two thousand, five hundred pounds is a cost of acquiring the shares. It is not deductible for corporation tax. It goes into Tarnmoor's base cost. That base cost will rarely matter, because after twelve months Tarnmoor's holding should qualify for the substantial shareholding exemption on any later sale, as chapter eighteen explained. But it goes in the computation, and it is half a mark.

Tarnmoor's other costs follow the line chapter thirteen drew for Calder, after the Supreme Court's decision in Centrica in twenty twenty four. Costs of appraising whether to buy anything at all can be management expenses. Once the board decides to buy this particular target, the costs of buying it are capital and give no relief. Tom asks for the date of that board decision, because the invoices fall either side of it.

Before any of this, the contract itself carries tax. Chapter twenty explained that a buyer of shares inherits the company's past, so tax that belongs to Jess's years must stay Jess's. Tarnmoor's due diligence looks hardest at three things. The profit Ridgeway has attributed to Dublin, because the Irish and United Kingdom figures must agree. The payroll, because employment taxes are where owner-managed companies most often slip. And the returns, to confirm that nothing is open with H M R C. The tax deed then makes Jess liable for any tax arising from the years before completion, with payments treated as a reduction in the price.

One line for value added tax, which this paper does not examine. Ridgeway Cycles might join Tarnmoor's value added tax group, and that is a decision for another adviser on another day.

Counting the family again.

The third floor is where most candidates lose marks, so walk it slowly. Ridgeway Cycles now has associated companies. Companies are associated if one controls the other, or both are under common control. Overseas companies count. Dormant companies do not. Chapter three owns the rules.

Ridgeway Holdings is the first question. It controls Ridgeway Cycles, so it should count. But the twenty ten Act ignores a company that carries on no trade or business, and section eighteen F extends that to certain passive holding companies. To qualify, the holding company must carry on no trade, have at least one fifty one per cent subsidiary, and be passive throughout its accounting period. That means it holds no assets except shares in those subsidiaries, and has no income except dividends that it passes straight up to its own shareholders. In our invented case Ridgeway Holdings meets those conditions. So the Tarnmoor tax team writes a rule into the integration plan. Ridgeway Holdings must not keep a bank balance, must not lend money, and must pay on any dividend it receives in the same period. Break any of those, and it starts to count.

That leaves Tarnmoor's own family. After the demerger, the sale of Tarnmoor Actuators and the strike off of the dormant pumps company, Tarnmoor has ten companies that count, and Ridgeway Cycles makes eleven.

Now the two timings. For marginal relief, a company is associated if it is associated at any time in the accounting period. So for Ridgeway's first year in the group, its marginal relief limits are divided by eleven at once. That changes nothing in practice. Its profits were already far above the upper limit, so it already paid at the main rate.

Instalments are different. H M R C's manual says associated companies are counted as at the day before the accounting period begins. For Ridgeway's first group year, that day is the thirty first of March, the day before completion. On that day Ridgeway Cycles was owned through Jess's holding company, which is passive, and Jess owned nothing else that counts. Its divisor is one. The large company threshold is the full one and a half million pounds. Profits of six hundred thousand pounds are nowhere near it. So in its first year in the group, Ridgeway is not large and pays no instalments. Its tax is due nine months and one day after the year end, as before.

Its second year is the trap. On the day before that year begins, Ridgeway has ten associated companies. Its divisor is eleven. The large threshold becomes one and a half million pounds divided by eleven, one hundred and thirty six thousand, three hundred and sixty four pounds. The very large threshold is twenty million divided by eleven, about one point eight two million pounds. Ridgeway's profits are above the first and well below the second. So it is large. But the instalment regulations give a large company a year of grace. It does not pay by instalments if it was not large in the previous twelve months and its profits do not exceed ten million pounds, also divided by eleven, nine hundred and nine thousand and ninety one pounds. Ridgeway passes both tests. Still no instalments.

The third year is when the cash moves. The grace year still counts as a year in which the company was large. H M R C's manual and practitioners' worked examples read the regulation that way. So in its third group year Ridgeway pays as a large company. On profits like today's United Kingdom profits, its tax would be about one hundred thousand pounds, paid in four instalments of twenty five thousand, in months seven, ten, thirteen and sixteen. Treasury needs those dates two years in advance.

The same counting ripples back through the group. Every Tarnmoor company with a December year end has eleven associates for marginal relief in the Ridgeway year. For instalments, the count changes only from the period that begins the following first of January. A six hundred thousand pound business has moved every instalment threshold in a group of eleven companies. That is the misconception, refuted in one paragraph.

What the shares bring with them.

The second floor is the target's tax history, and here the inspection is short. Ridgeway Cycles has no trading losses to bring forward. The Dublin losses were relieved years ago, against its own profits. So the change of ownership rules in Part fourteen of the twenty ten Act, which chapter fourteen used on Brackenwell, have nothing to bite on. Ridgeway has no capital losses either, so the pre-entry loss rules of chapter seventeen are silent. Write one line saying so. A nil answer with a reason is still an answer.

What about past transfers between Ridgeway Holdings and Ridgeway Cycles? If either had moved an asset to the other at no gain, no loss within the last six years, the degrouping charge would be the worry. It does not arise. The two companies leave Jess's ownership together and stay together, and Ridgeway's little group simply becomes part of Tarnmoor's. Chapter seventeen explained why a company leaving with its own subsidiary does not trigger the charge.

Then the group regimes switch on. Ridgeway Cycles joins Tarnmoor's group for group relief on completion. Before that day nothing could pass, and from that day it can. Its year runs to March, while most of Tarnmoor's companies end in December. So any relief between them follows chapter fifteen's overlapping period rule, time-apportioned on each side.

Both new companies countersign the standing nomination that lets Tarnmoor P L C allocate the group's single five million pound deductions allowance, as chapter fourteen described. Ridgeway has no losses, so this costs it nothing. But a company left out of the nomination gets no allowance at all, and the paperwork is cheaper now than later.

The annual investment allowance is now shared. Chapter eight explained that a group has a single one million pound allowance for all members' periods ending in the same financial year to the thirty first of March. Ridgeway's first group year ends on a thirty first of March. It shares the allowance with the December periods of Tarnmoor's companies that ended nine months earlier. Ridgeway gets whatever the group allocates to it, and if nobody allocates, it gets nothing.

Research and development changes too. Ridgeway is now linked to a large enterprise, so it is not a small or medium sized enterprise for any purpose. Any claim it makes is under the merged scheme's expenditure credit, at twenty per cent, taxable and set against its liability. The extra relief for loss-making intensive companies is out of reach. Chapter ten owns these rules.

The compliance settings change.

The fifth floor is governance, and it is the one candidates under-sell. In November twenty twenty four, question five set exactly this scenario. A multinational bought a small United Kingdom company, and candidates had to explain its new obligations. The marking guide put six and a half marks on transfer pricing alone.

Transfer pricing first. In Jess's hands Ridgeway was a small enterprise, so transfer pricing did not apply to it, as chapter twenty seven explained. That exemption measures size across linked enterprises. Linked to Tarnmoor, Ridgeway is large, and transfer pricing applies from completion. Its dealings with other United Kingdom group companies fall inside the exemption for United Kingdom to United Kingdom transactions, for chargeable periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six. Hold that thought, because the branch decision will test it.

The senior accounting officer rules turn on United Kingdom incorporation. Both Ridgeway companies are English. But a company joins the senior accounting officer's certificate only for a financial year in which it was a group member at the end of the previous one. Ridgeway's previous year ended on the thirty first of March, the day before completion. So its first year with the senior accounting officer, Nadia Kerr, is its second year in the group. The certificate for that year is due nine months after its end. Chapter four owns this.

Tarnmoor's published tax strategy now covers Ridgeway. Its returns must notify any uncertain tax treatment above the five million pound threshold, which is unlikely at this size, but the question must be asked. And the group's procedures to prevent the facilitation of tax evasion, the defence to the corporate criminal offence, must now reach a showroom in Dublin, whose staff are associated persons of Ridgeway Cycles. A foreign tax evasion facilitation offence exists for exactly that case.

Tarnmoor's country-by-country report and its transfer pricing master file now include Ridgeway, and the Dublin showroom's results appear among the group's Irish figures. Records that a family company kept for its own use must now meet a listed group's standard.

Administration tightens. Ridgeway is now a member of a group that is not small, so H M R C's enquiry window runs to twelve months after the filing date, not twelve months after delivery. And it cannot join Tarnmoor's group payment arrangement while its year end differs from the others'. Calder had the same problem until it moved to December.

The corporate interest restriction now sees Ridgeway as part of Tarnmoor's worldwide group. Tarnmoor's reporting company files for the whole group, and under the Finance Act twenty twenty six rules it must be appointed for each period by more than half of the eligible United Kingdom companies. Ridgeway Holdings and Ridgeway Cycles are now two of those. Tarnmoor still carries disallowed interest forward from earlier years. So every pound of tax E B I T D A has value. That is tax earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and chapter twenty eight explained it. Ridgeway's profits add a little interest capacity. Keep that in mind too.

Last on this floor, the global minimum tax. Tarnmoor's revenue is far above seven hundred and fifty million euros, so Ridgeway's companies become constituent entities of the group at once. In the United Kingdom, domestic top-up tax covers them. The Dublin showroom is a permanent establishment, and the global anti-base erosion rules, the GloBE rules, treat it as a separate entity located in Ireland. That too will matter in a moment.

The Dublin question.

Now the sixth floor, which Jess left unfinished. Should Ridgeway Cycles elect to exempt its foreign branch profits? Chapter twenty five owns the rules, and three options are on the table. Elect for the exemption. Turn the branch into an Irish subsidiary. Or move the branch into Tarnmoor's existing Irish company, Tarnmoor Ireland.

Begin with the election, under section eighteen A of the two thousand and nine Act. Once it takes effect, the profits and losses of every foreign permanent establishment of the company are left out of its taxable profits. The branch's profit is measured as the United Kingdom and Ireland treaty would attribute it. Irish tax on exempt profits is not creditable, because there is no United Kingdom tax to credit it against.

Three features decide the answer. First, the election covers every branch of the company, now and in future, in every country. Second, it takes effect from the start of the company's next accounting period, which the statute calls the relevant day. Third, once that day arrives, it can never be revoked.

Then the trap The Living Law flagged, the opening negative amount. A company cannot take United Kingdom relief for branch losses and then elect just as the branch turns profitable. The law looks back six years before the election takes effect. Net branch losses in that window that later profits have not matched become an opening negative amount. Until that amount is matched by later branch profits, those profits stay taxable.

For Ridgeway the look-back is harmless. The branch lost one hundred and ten thousand pounds in its first two years, and made three hundred and twenty thousand pounds in the next two alone. By the end of its third year the losses were already matched, with ten thousand pounds to spare. Every year since has been profitable. Whatever the six year window catches, the branch's net result inside it is a profit. There is no opening negative amount.

So the arithmetic is simple. Today Ridgeway pays United Kingdom tax of one hundred and twenty five thousand pounds a year. With the election, its United Kingdom profit is four hundred thousand pounds and its tax is one hundred thousand. Ireland still collects its twenty five thousand. Total tax falls from one hundred and fifty thousand pounds to one hundred and twenty five thousand. The saving is twenty five thousand pounds a year, the United Kingdom top-up on the Irish profit.

Now the interactions, because a capstone answer must test that figure against the rest of the building. The full working is in the reading edition.

First, the interest restriction. Tax E B I T D A is built from taxable profits. Once the branch is exempt, its two hundred thousand pounds leaves Ridgeway's taxable profits and so leaves the group's tax E B I T D A. At thirty per cent, that is sixty thousand pounds of interest capacity. If the group is restricted, or is still reactivating old disallowed interest, that capacity is worth up to fifteen thousand pounds of tax. If the group has capacity to spare, it is worth nothing.

Second, the global minimum tax. Without the election, the United Kingdom tax on the branch's profit is treated as tax of the branch, so the Irish branch bears tax at the full United Kingdom rate. With it, the branch bears only twelve and a half per cent, below the fifteen per cent floor. On a simplified view that ignores the carve-out for real substance, that is up to five thousand pounds a year of top-up tax. Who collects it depends on Irish law, which this book does not teach. Either way, it is a cost to the group.

Third, transfer pricing. The exemption for United Kingdom to United Kingdom transactions does not apply to activities that the branch exemption takes out of charge. So if Tarnmoor ever charges Ridgeway for services used in Dublin, that charge must be at arm's length.

Fourth, the guard rail. An exempt branch could be a place to park mobile income, so the law withholds the exemption for branch profits that would pass the controlled foreign company gateway. A showroom selling bicycles is nowhere near that rule. Its profits sit below the low profits limit that the rule borrows from the controlled foreign company code.

Fifth, attribution. Without the election, the split of profit between Skipton and Dublin only moved the credit around. With it, every pound attributed to Dublin is taxed at twelve and a half per cent, not twenty five. H M R C will care about that split, so it must be documented on arm's length principles.

So the honest answer is that the election saves something between five thousand and twenty five thousand pounds a year, depending on the group's interest position and the minimum tax computation. It never costs money, on these facts, while the branch is profitable.

Two other doors.

The second option is to turn the branch into a company. Section one four oh of the Gains Act lets a United Kingdom company transfer a trade it carries on abroad through a permanent establishment to a non-resident company, with all its assets or all except cash, wholly or partly for shares. If it then holds at least a quarter of the new company's ordinary share capital, the net gain on the transfer is postponed, in proportion to the share part of the consideration. Ridgeway Cycles would hold all the shares of a new Irish subsidiary, so the conditions can be met. Chapter twenty five owns the rule.

Postponement is all it gives. The deferred gain returns if Ridgeway sells the shares, or if the subsidiary sells the transferred assets within six years. The branch's goodwill and customer relationships fall under the intangibles rules, not the gains rules, so chapter eleven's regime applies to them. Its plant leaves Ridgeway's pools with balancing adjustments.

Then the new company has to live somewhere. It is resident in Ireland only if its board really manages it from Ireland, as chapter twenty two explained. If Tarnmoor's executives took its decisions in Leeds, it would be United Kingdom resident, and the relief would fail at the first condition.

And it would be a controlled foreign company. Walk chapter twenty six's order of attack. It is a non-resident company controlled from the United Kingdom, so it is a controlled foreign company. Take the entity exemptions next. The tax exemption fails. Irish tax at twelve and a half per cent is below seventy five per cent of the United Kingdom rate, which is eighteen point seven five per cent. Do not rely on the excluded territories exemption either. Ireland's place on that list was not confirmed for this book. But the low profits exemption works. Profits of two hundred thousand pounds are within the five hundred thousand pound limit, and almost none of them are non-trading. So there is no charge today. If the showroom grew, the next stop would be the trading profits gateway, and that would need a careful look at where its people and decisions really sit.

So the subsidiary reaches the same twelve and a half per cent as the elected branch, but by a longer road. It means a transfer, a new company, residence management, transfer pricing on every bicycle Skipton sells to Dublin, and controlled foreign company monitoring every year. Its one advantage is that it leaves Ridgeway Cycles free of an irrevocable election.

The third option fails at once. If Ridgeway Cycles transferred the Dublin trade to Tarnmoor Ireland for new shares, it would hold a tiny fraction of that much larger company, far below a quarter, so section one four oh is unavailable. Nor can the transfer be at no gain, no loss within the gains group, because Tarnmoor Ireland has been resident in Ireland since Group Year Four, and the Dublin assets would be outside the United Kingdom charge in its hands. Gains, and intangibles credits at an arm's length value, would all crystallise now, to move a bicycle showroom into a valve distributor.

Ireland, unlike the invented Vallaria of chapter twenty five, is a member state of the European Union. So the old cross-border relief in section one four oh C is at least in view. Chapter twenty five explained why its wording after Brexit needs care, and Tom does not rely on it.

The recommendation.

Tom's paper to the boards of Tarnmoor and Ridgeway Cycles, in our invented case, recommends the election. Three reasons. It removes the United Kingdom top-up on the Dublin profit, a saving of up to twenty five thousand pounds a year. Its costs are small and fit the facts. Ridgeway has no other foreign branches and no plans for any, and if Tarnmoor ever wants a loss-making venture abroad, it can put it in a different company. And unlike incorporation, it needs no transfer, no new company and no annual controlled foreign company review.

Timing comes next. Ridgeway Cycles makes the election in its first year in the group. The relevant day is the first of April after that, the start of its next accounting period. So in its first group year the Dublin profit is still taxed in the United Kingdom, with credit, and the exemption runs from its second year. Tom did notice, while the heads of terms were being drafted, that an election made by Jess's company before completion would have started on completion day, a year earlier. He chose not to ask for it. It would have been an irrevocable choice made before Tarnmoor's due diligence had finished, for a prize of twenty five thousand pounds. In our invented case the board minute records that reasoning, and the election is made only after the board has approved it. The election is the company's own act, so the minute and a copy of the election go on the permanent file, where a finance director ten years from now can find out why the Dublin profits are missing from the return.

The paper also records what is coming. Draft legislation for the Finance Bill twenty twenty six to twenty seven, published in July twenty twenty six, would make the branch exemption compulsory for accounting periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty seven. It would replace the opening negative amount rules with restrictions on carrying branch losses forward. That is proposed, not law. Under the Finance Act twenty twenty six, which your exam tests, the exemption is still an election. Ridgeway has no branch losses to carry forward, so even if the draft became law, its answer would not change.

One last point on the branch. If Tarnmoor later moves Ridgeway's year end to December, as it did with Calder, the election timing and the instalment tests both need to be run again, because both key off the dates of accounting periods.

The group accounts.

The seventh floor is not tax law at all, and it is where the examiner's tax accounting marks hide. Tarnmoor's consolidated accounts must record Ridgeway's assets at fair value on the acquisition date. The valuers find a brand and customer relationships that Ridgeway's own accounts never showed, worth eight hundred thousand pounds between them.

A share purchase changes nothing in Ridgeway's tax position. Ridgeway Cycles built that brand itself, so it has no tax cost, and buying the shares gives no step up. In the group accounts, then, the assets carry eight hundred thousand pounds more than their tax base. That is a taxable temporary difference, and at twenty five per cent it needs a deferred tax liability of two hundred thousand pounds. The liability is part of the acquisition accounting. It increases goodwill by the same two hundred thousand pounds. No deferred tax is recognised on goodwill itself, because goodwill is the residual, and grossing it up would only increase it again. Chapter six owns these rules.

As the group accounts amortise the customer relationships, the liability unwinds through the deferred tax charge, and the group's effective tax rate is unaffected. If the brand is treated as having an indefinite life and is not amortised, its share of the liability stays. None of this touches Ridgeway's own accounts or its tax return. Two more accounting points belong on the list. The accounting standard for business combinations allows up to a year after the acquisition to finalise the fair values, so the deferred tax figure can move during that year, and goodwill moves with it. And any top-up tax that the Dublin branch might bear under the global minimum rules creates no deferred tax at all, because the accounting standards carry a specific exception for it, as chapter six explained.

The planning point is documentation. The purchase price allocation, meaning the split between net assets, identified intangibles and goodwill, drives the deferred tax, the impairment tests and later the gain on any sale. Tom files the valuers' report with the acquisition papers, alongside the board minute on the election. In an answer, the deferred tax needs three points, not one. The temporary difference and why it arises. The rate and the figure. And where the other side of the entry goes. Candidates who stop at the liability leave the last of those on the table.

Keeping Jess.

The eighth floor is people. Tarnmoor wants Jess to stay, so she remains managing director of Ridgeway Cycles for two years, on a salary of ninety thousand pounds. On top, she gets a retention bonus of sixty thousand pounds, payable twenty four months after completion if she is still there. Both are paid by Ridgeway Cycles, whose trade she serves. Chapter twenty explained why that matters. If Tarnmoor P L C paid instead, it would be paying for services to another company and might get no deduction.

The salary is an ordinary trading deduction. The bonus is a timing puzzle, and the rule is the one chapter seven taught. If remuneration charged in the accounts is not paid within nine months after the end of the period of account, it is deductible only when paid.

Suppose Ridgeway accrues the bonus evenly, thirty thousand pounds in each of its first two group years. The bonus is paid on the first of April two years after completion, the first day of its third group year. The first year's thirty thousand is paid twelve months after that year ends, too late. So it is deducted in the third year, when paid. The second year's thirty thousand is paid one day after that year ends, well within nine months. So it is deducted in the second year. Same sixty thousand pounds, two different years.

One adviser's check. The bonus must really be pay for staying and working, at a commercial level, conditional on service. If the facts showed it was really part of the price for Jess's shares, Ridgeway Cycles would be paying a capital sum on its owner's behalf and would get no deduction at all. The service condition and the market level of the pay are the evidence. The same thinking applies to any payment to Jess for loss of office if she leaves early. H M R C's view, as chapter twenty explained, is that a payment connected with a change of ownership is unlikely to be wholly and exclusively for the trade.

And one line for the other Hartley in these pages. Dan Hartley, made redundant when Calder closed his division in Group Year Three, is working elsewhere now. This book leaves his later career where it found it, open.

How the examiner would mark it.

Imagine this deal set as a twenty mark question. You have about forty two minutes, at roughly two point one minutes a mark. The marking guide will give half a mark to a mark for each correct point. That means twenty to forty separate, findable points.

The guide for November twenty twenty four's question five is the model. It gave four marks to filing and instalments, three to country-by-country reporting, six and a half to transfer pricing, three and a half to the interest restriction, and three to stamp duty. The examiners reported that most candidates found transfer pricing, but some wrote at length on it and ignored easier points, and some raised hybrid mismatches that nothing in the question triggered.

So the order of work matters. Bank the quick marks first. Stamp duty of twenty two thousand, five hundred pounds, payable by the buyer within thirty days. The associated company count and the two timings. No instalments in the first year, the grace year in the second, instalments from the third. The senior accounting officer from the second year. Transfer pricing switched on because the exemption for small companies is lost. Each is one line with a reason. Add the points that score for saying nothing changes. No losses to restrict. No degrouping charge. No stamp duty land tax. A marker can only tick what is on the page, and a correct nil, with its reason, is a point like any other.

Then the branch, which is where the recommendation marks live. Set out the three options in turn. Give a short table of tax with and without the election, all in pounds. State the opening negative amount test and its result. State the conditions for section one four oh and why the Tarnmoor Ireland route fails. Then recommend, naming the option and the main reason. After May twenty twenty three's question two, the examiners reported that some candidates failed to give the recommendation and lost marks.

Two final disciplines. Do not restate Jess's history. The marker knows it. And if the question asks about corporation tax only, Jess's capital gains tax and the stamp duty are outside it, however much you know about them.

What to take away.

A small acquisition is not a small tax job. The size of the group the target joins sets the compliance load, not the size of the target.

Walk every floor in the same order. The transaction, the target's history, the thresholds, the group regimes, governance and compliance, the special feature, the accounts, the people, and then the recommendation.

In our invented case, Tarnmoor P L C bought Ridgeway Holdings from Jess Hartley on the first of April, some years after Group Year Seven, for four and a half million pounds. Stamp duty was twenty two thousand, five hundred pounds, paid by the buyer within thirty days, and added to the cost of the shares. There was no stamp duty land tax, because only shares changed hands.

Ridgeway Holdings is a passive holding company under section eighteen F of the twenty ten Act, so it does not count as an associated company. Keep it passive. Ridgeway Cycles has ten associated companies. For marginal relief they count at once. For instalments they count from the day before each accounting period begins. So Ridgeway's divisor is one in its first group year, and it is not large. In its second it is eleven, giving a large threshold of one hundred and thirty six thousand, three hundred and sixty four pounds, but the year of grace applies, because its profits are under nine hundred and nine thousand and ninety one pounds and it was not large before. It pays instalments from its third group year, about twenty five thousand pounds a quarter.

No losses come with the shares, so there is nothing to restrict. Group relief, the deductions allowance and a share of the annual investment allowance start on completion. Transfer pricing applies, because the small company exemption is lost. The senior accounting officer's certificate covers Ridgeway from its second group year. The interest restriction and the global minimum tax now include it.

The Dublin branch should elect for the exemption. There is no opening negative amount, because one hundred and ten thousand pounds of early losses were matched by three hundred and twenty thousand pounds of profit within two years. The election saves up to twenty five thousand pounds a year, from one hundred and twenty five thousand pounds of United Kingdom tax to one hundred thousand. Some of that may come back through lost interest capacity, up to fifteen thousand pounds, and minimum top-up tax, up to five thousand on a simplified view. The election is irrevocable and covers every future branch of the company. It takes effect from the start of the next accounting period. Incorporation under section one four oh only postpones gains, and creates a controlled foreign company that today sits inside the low profits exemption. A transfer to Tarnmoor Ireland fails the twenty five per cent condition.

In the group accounts, the eight hundred thousand pound fair value uplift on Ridgeway's brand and customer relationships carries a deferred tax liability of two hundred thousand pounds, which increases goodwill.

Jess stays for two years on ninety thousand pounds a year. Her sixty thousand pound retention bonus, paid by Ridgeway Cycles, is deducted thirty thousand in the second group year and thirty thousand in the third, because of the nine month rule.

So why does a small deal touch every rule in the book? Because a company joining a group inherits the group's thresholds, its regimes and its obligations, all at once or one period later. The answer to Jess's last open question is yes, elect. Under the law your exam tests, it is still a choice, and on these facts it is a good one.

One chapter remains. Chapter thirty two turns from the law to the craft. It is about how to put all of this in front of a marker, in three and a half hours, in a form the marker can reward.


Chapter thirty two: The Advanced Technical craft.

One sentence in the instructions.

In the Candidate Instructions for the October twenty twenty six sitting, the Chartered Institute of Taxation printed a sentence that every candidate should learn by heart. In its words, calculations left in the spreadsheet and not copied to the answer box will not be marked.

That sentence arrived with new exam software. From October twenty twenty six, the Institute's papers are sat on R M Assessment Master, which replaced the program candidates had used for years. The new system puts a spreadsheet on the screen, right under the place where you type your answer. It is a gift and a trap. You can add up a capital allowances pool in seconds. And if you leave it there, the marker never sees it.

The sentence is a fair summary of the whole paper. The Advanced Technical paper does not reward what you know. It rewards what you put in front of the marker, in a form the marker can credit, within three and a half hours.

This chapter is about that craft. It is not question practice. You have the Institute's past papers and your own question bank for that. It is the set of habits that turns thirty one chapters of law into marks. The chapter gathers what every Exam lens box in this book has said, adds the facts about the paper and the day, and checks them against the Institute's own documents. The law you will be examined on, for a sitting in twenty twenty seven, is almost certainly the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, under the Finance Act twenty twenty six, which is the law this book teaches.

Chapter two, on where corporate tax law lives, began this work with research in the exam room. Here we finish it. There is no syllabus grade for this chapter, because its subject is the paper as a whole. Every grade quoted here comes from the twenty twenty six syllabus grid, and every comment about past papers comes from the question papers, suggested answers and examiners' reports the Institute publishes for each sitting. Where a fact is my own arithmetic rather than the Institute's statement, I will say so. The question for the chapter is simple. What does this paper reward, and how do you give it that in two hundred and ten minutes?

The shape of the paper.

The paper is the Chartered Tax Adviser Advanced Technical paper, Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups. Until November twenty twenty two it was called Taxation of Major Corporates. The new name, from twenty twenty three, signals where the weight sits now. Groups, consortia, interest, and everything that crosses a border.

It lasts three hours and thirty minutes. There are normally six questions, each worth ten, fifteen or twenty marks, and one hundred marks in all. The pass mark is fifty per cent. Every paper from May twenty twenty three to May twenty twenty six had six questions, and the usual mix was three twenties, two fifteens and one ten. Four of those seven papers ran twenty, fifteen, fifteen, twenty, twenty, ten, in that order.

The Institute describes the scenarios plainly. They will typically be based around multinational groups and larger companies that may be listed, with no individual controlling shareholders. So owner managers, close company loans and profit extraction are not this paper's business. Our invented group, Tarnmoor, a listed engineering group with no controlling shareholder, was built to match that description.

The syllabus has three elements. Corporation tax, including corporation tax on chargeable gains. Capital allowances. And stamp duty and stamp duty land tax at awareness level. At least seventy per cent of the corporation tax element comes from core material.

Core means grade one on the syllabus grid. Non-core is grade two, and awareness is grade three. Grade one topics are examined at depth, with computations. Grade two needs working knowledge and the main computation. Grade three needs recognition. On the twenty twenty six grid, which is the grid this book is built on, controlled foreign companies, transfer pricing, the corporate interest restriction and hybrid mismatches are all core.

The Institute also tells you what kind of adviser it is testing. Candidates, it says, are not expected to have deep knowledge of all tax areas but should be able to identify what the potential tax issues are. That is the job of a corporate tax trainee in a large firm. Spot the issue, explain it precisely, and know enough to coordinate the specialists.

The style follows from that. Requirements say calculate, with explanations, or explain, or discuss, and sometimes recommend. No question on this paper between twenty twenty three and twenty twenty six asked for a letter, a report or an email. That format belongs to the Application and Professional Skills paper. Here you write technical prose and computations, and roughly half the marks are computational.

The day itself.

Your likely sitting is the fourth of May, twenty twenty seven, at half past two in the afternoon, with results in July. The fallback is the twenty sixth of October, twenty twenty seven, also at half past two, with results in January twenty twenty eight. The Institute's timetable shows this paper in that afternoon slot alongside Cross Border and Environmental Taxes. One line on the Institute's exam entry page gives the twenty eighth of October for the autumn sitting, so check your own entry confirmation before you book the day off.

You sit the paper in a test centre, at a Windows computer with one twenty four inch monitor, in a room of perhaps twenty to twenty five terminals. Your Candidate Information email arrives about three weeks before the exam. Print it. Write your legislation username and password on it, and nothing else, because no other notes are allowed on that sheet.

Arrive at least thirty minutes early. The Institute recommends an hour. If you are more than thirty minutes late you will not be admitted. You may not leave in the first forty five minutes or the last ten.

What you may bring is short. Pens, pencils and an eraser. Your own physical calculator, basic or scientific, whose memory may be checked. Ear plugs. Your printed candidate email. Still water or a non-fizzy drink, and quiet snacks without nuts. No watches of any kind. That last rule matters, because the clock you will rely on is the one on the screen.

You will find two sheets of note paper on the desk, and you can ask for more. Nothing on that paper is marked, and it stays in the room. Use it for a plan, a timeline, or a quick list of issues. Never use it for working you want credit for.

When the paper opens, spend a minute on the resources before the first question. Log in to the legislation, open the tax tables on screen, and check that both respond. If anything fails, tell the invigilator at once, while there is still time to fix it.

None of this is glamorous. But a candidate who arrives flustered, with a legislation password that will not work, has lost marks before reading a word. A work subscription to the legislation products will not log in on the day. Buy the student product early, and practise on it until finding a Part of an Act takes seconds.

Inside R M Assessment Master.

The screen has two halves. On the left sits the question scenario, with any exhibits shown as small thumbnails you can open. The requirements appear at the bottom of the scenario and again at the top right. Under the requirements on the right is the answer box. Below the answer box is a spreadsheet, a version of SpreadJS that behaves much like Excel.

The spreadsheet is a calculator with columns. It is not part of your answer. You must copy your working into the answer box, with control C and control V. And when you copy it, think about what the marker will see. The examiners cannot see the formulae behind your cells. A cell that shows four hundred and twelve thousand pounds tells them nothing about where that number came from. So every working must be shown in words and figures. Proceeds, less cost, less indexation, equals the gain. Not just the gain.

There is also an on-screen calculator, and a flag function that lets you mark a question or a part to return to. And there is a timer. Ten minutes before the end, it turns red and flashes. That is the only time warning you will get.

The Institute says candidates must have practised using the software before they reach the test centre, and it puts a practice test on its website before each sitting. Use it more than once. Find out how a table pastes into the answer box, how long that takes, and how it looks once pasted. Discover that now, not at a quarter to six on the day of the exam.

Here is the misconception this chapter most wants to kill. It runs like this. The marker will see my working because the computer holds it. The marker sees only the answer box. A perfect computation sitting in the spreadsheet scores nothing. A rough computation, copied across with a one-line reason beside each figure, can score most of the marks even if the final number is wrong.

The examiners have said exactly that, in another context. After the November twenty twenty three sitting, on the senior accounting officer question, they told candidates to show their workings, because marks can be earned even when the conclusion is wrong. They said it again after May twenty twenty five, on a transfer pricing computation. The software change makes their advice sharper. Working that is not visible is working that does not exist.

So build a habit. Do the arithmetic wherever is quickest. Then, before you move to the next requirement, copy it into the answer box, label each line, and check that it pasted cleanly.

The tax tables.

Behind an open book icon in the software are three resources. The tax tables, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's Model Tax Convention, and links to the legislation. The rules are strict. In the Institute's words, candidates cannot access anything other than Online Legislation and the Tax Tables. The Model sits inside the software alongside them. Nothing else comes in.

The tax tables are on your desk in hard copy and also on screen as a P D F. For this paper they give the corporation tax rates, the European definition of a small or medium sized enterprise with notes for research and development and transfer pricing, the research and development expenditure credit rate, the enhanced support rates for research and development intensive companies, the capital allowance rates, the interest rates of His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, H M R C, including those on instalments, the lease percentage table for short leases, the retail prices index for indexation, and the stamp duty and stamp duty land tax rates.

Two things follow. You need not memorise a rate the tables give you. And you must know exactly what the tables do not give you. They do not give the order of the steps in the expenditure credit. They do not tell you whether notional tax is at twenty five or nineteen per cent. They do not tell you when a research and development claim must be notified. They do not give the conditions for any relief. Those are your marks.

Now the trap for twenty twenty seven. As at October twenty twenty six, the Institute's tables page offers only the twenty twenty six tables. Those reflect the Finance Act twenty twenty five, with a main pool writing down allowance of eighteen per cent. A paper set on the Finance Act twenty twenty six uses fourteen per cent, for chargeable periods beginning on or after the first of April, twenty twenty six, and it has the new forty per cent first-year allowance. The twenty twenty seven tables, when they appear, should show the new figures. Until then, practise with fourteen per cent, and know how a hybrid rate works for a period that straddles the change. Chapter eight did the arithmetic.

Practise with the tables you will actually have. Learn where each figure sits on the page, so that finding the lease percentage for a lease with twenty seven and a half years left is a ten-second job, not a two-minute hunt.

Legislation and the treaty.

The legislation comes from Croner-i or from Tolley's Digital Library. Both are student products bought in advance. You cannot make notes in either. You may highlight, and you may use the products' tags and folders. A tag may hold a section number or a topic name. The Institute's own example pairs the corporate rescue exception with section three six one D of the two thousand and nine Act. A tag must not reproduce a pro forma or a formula, and invigilators may check.

So the legislation is a map, not a crib. Its value is speed. In the exam you will not have time to read a Part of an Act from the start. You will have time to open the right section, confirm a condition or a time limit, and cite it.

Build your tags around the regimes this book has taught. In the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten, which I will call the International Act, tag Part two for double tax relief, Part four for transfer pricing, Part six A for hybrids, Part nine A for controlled foreign companies, and Part ten with Schedule seven A for the corporate interest restriction. In the Corporation Tax Act two thousand and nine, tag the branch exemption in section eighteen A, the loan relationship rules in Part five with the unallowable purpose rule in section four four one, intangible assets in Part eight, research and development in Part thirteen, and the timing rules for remuneration. In the Corporation Tax Act twenty ten, tag group relief in Part five, the loss restriction in Part seven Z A, change of ownership in Part fourteen, and Part twenty two. In the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act nineteen ninety two, which I will call the Gains Act, tag section one seven one, section one seven nine, the leases schedule and the substantial shareholding exemption in Schedule seven A C.

Practise on the product you will use on the day, because each publisher lays out the Acts and its search differently.

Then the treaty. The O E C D Model is available only as an on-screen P D F, with no hard copy, and the version published for the exam contains the twenty seventeen articles. It is a fallback. When a question supplies an extract from a real or invented treaty, the extract is the treaty for that question. After the November twenty twenty three sitting, the examiners reported that some candidates ignored the supplied treaty article and used the Model text instead. The question turned on a tie-breaker, and the supplied article used place of effective management. Read the extract, quote its article number, and apply its words to the facts.

One more point about sources. The paper rewards statute. H M R C's manuals are its view, not law, and you will not have them in the room. If you rely on a known H M R C practice, say so, briefly, as H M R C's view.

The clock.

Two hundred and ten minutes for one hundred marks gives about two point one minutes a mark. The Institute publishes no official timing, so that figure is simple arithmetic, but it is the right starting point. A twenty-mark question is worth about forty two minutes. A fifteen-mark question about thirty one and a half. A ten-mark question about twenty one.

There is no separate reading time. Reading and planning come out of each question's budget. A sensible habit is to spend the first few minutes of each question reading the requirement, then the scenario, and jotting a list of issues on the note paper before you type.

Turn the budget into checkpoints before the day. Take the usual order, twenty, fifteen, fifteen, twenty, twenty, ten, and suppose the paper starts at exactly half past two. Question one should end at twelve minutes past three. Halfway, after question three, you should be at a quarter past four with fifty marks attempted. Question five should end at thirty nine minutes past five. The timer flashes at ten to six, and the paper ends at six. The full table is in the reading edition. If the start slips, shift every checkpoint with it.

The most valuable timing rule is the one the examiners keep repeating. Bank the easy marks on every question. On a typical marking guide, the first half of a question's marks come quickly. They are for spotting the issues, stating the rules and doing the standard computation. The last few marks come slowly. They are for a subtle interaction, or a point most candidates miss. Over-running on one question to chase its last two marks costs you the first five marks of the next.

So when the budget for a question runs out, stop. Leave a line in the answer box listing what you would have done next. Flag the question. Move on. If time remains at the end, come back.

The ten-minute warning is for finishing, not for starting. When the timer flashes, make sure every requirement has something in its answer box, copy across any working still in the spreadsheet, and give any recommendation you have not yet given.

One last timing point. The paper rewards breadth across the requirement more than depth on one point. A candidate who makes ten correct points in two lines each will usually outscore one who makes four points in a paragraph each. That is not an argument for shallow answers. It is an argument for making each point once, precisely, and moving on.

Reading the requirement.

Every question ends with requirements, and the requirements are the marking guide in disguise. Read them before the scenario. Then read the scenario knowing what you are looking for.

Notice the verbs. Calculate, with explanations, means a computation in which each line carries a short reason. Explain means prose, with the rule, its authority and its application to these facts. Discuss means weigh the options and reach a view. Recommend means name an option and give the main reason. After the May twenty twenty three sitting, the examiners reported that some candidates failed to give the recommendation and lost marks. A recommendation is one sentence. Never leave it out.

Notice the mark split. A twenty-mark question split eight, six and six, as in May twenty twenty six, tells you how long to spend on each part. Do not write three pages for a part worth three marks.

Notice the scope words. The examiners have drawn a clear line. Where a question asks for the tax consequences, consider every tax in the syllabus, including stamp duty and stamp duty land tax. Where it names a tax, nothing else scores. Stamp taxes are the classic missed marks. After the November twenty twenty five property question, the examiners noted that few candidates considered stamp duty land tax, so those marks were lost.

Notice what is excluded. In May twenty twenty six, a question on an overseas construction contract said transfer pricing was excluded. Some candidates discussed it anyway. Many discussed the residence or migration of the United Kingdom company, which the question was not about. In May twenty twenty three, candidates wasted time on diverted profits tax in a question about a loan, although that tax never applied to loan relationships, and for periods beginning on or after the first of January, twenty twenty six, it no longer exists at all. In November twenty twenty four, some raised hybrids where nothing in the facts was hybrid. Each of those paragraphs earned nothing, and each one cost time.

Notice when the question asks you to identify further information. The syllabus says a candidate should be able to identify the information still needed, and the May twenty twenty six deferred tax question tested it. A short list of precise questions, each tied to a rule, earns marks.

And notice the rubric on the front of the paper. All workings should be shown and made to the nearest month and pound unless the question specifies otherwise. The rubric also tells you to assume that the previous year's legislation continues to apply. Candidates answering by reference to more recently enacted legislation or tax cases will not be penalised. Candidates who answer by Scots law may use land and buildings transaction tax instead of stamp duty land tax.

How the marks are made.

The Institute publishes suggested answers with a full marking guide. Read a few and the pattern is obvious. Marks come in halves and wholes. A condition correctly stated is half a mark or one mark. A correct figure is half a mark or one mark. A correct conclusion is another half. A set of conditions for roll-over relief might be worth one and a half.

That tells you how to write. On that arithmetic, a twenty-mark question needs somewhere between twenty and forty distinct, correct points. Each should be short, in its own sentence or line, and easy to find. A marker scanning your answer should be able to tick as they read.

Several habits follow.

List every item in a computation, including the ones that need no adjustment, with a few words of reason. A nil adjustment with a correct reason earns its mark.

State the authority briefly. Section one seven nine of the Gains Act, or the substantial shareholding exemption in Schedule seven A C. The section number shows the marker you know which rule you are applying.

Do not restate the question. The examiners have said so repeatedly. Copying the facts back earns nothing.

Do not pad. After May twenty twenty six, the examiners described the interest restriction administration answers as adequate but padded with irrelevant detail. General paragraphs about a regime, written before you reach the facts, are padding.

Do not stop at a conclusion when a computation is asked for, and do not stop at a computation when an explanation is asked for.

Here is the second misconception. It says that Advanced Technical depth means writing everything you know. It does not. Depth on this paper means applying the right rule to these facts, with the conditions, the exceptions and the interaction that the facts raise. The examiners have praised, again and again, answers tied to the scenario. After the November twenty twenty four sitting they reported that higher marks went to answers that did exactly that.

What if the question seems wrong? The chief examiner's advice, after the May and November twenty twenty five sittings, was to re-read the question first. If you still think there is an error, state it, state your assumption, and answer on that basis. A sensible assumption, clearly stated, is never penalised for being an assumption. Results are moderated, and the pass mark may be adjusted for a paper's difficulty, so one strange question will not sink you on its own.

What about presentation? The papers from May twenty twenty three to November twenty twenty five said additional marks may be awarded for presentation. The May twenty twenty six paper dropped that line. Do not count on marks for neatness. But layout still decides whether the marker can find your points, and a marker who cannot find a point cannot give the mark.

Layouts.

The examiners expect conventional layouts, and they say so when candidates do not use them. After the May twenty twenty four capital allowances question, they noted that some candidates did not use a conventional layout. Here is the set this book has taught, in one place.

The corporation tax computation runs from profit before tax, through each adjustment with its reason, to the tax-adjusted trading profit. Then capital allowances, other income and gains, total profits, reliefs in their statutory order, taxable total profits, corporation tax with any marginal relief, the expenditure credit set off, and the amount payable with its instalment dates. Chapter seven built it.

Capital allowances go in columns. First-year allowances and full expensing, main pool, special rate pool, single asset pools, and a column of allowances claimed. Chapter eight built it.

A chargeable gain runs proceeds, costs of disposal, cost, enhancement, indexation to December twenty seventeen, any relief, and the chargeable gain. Roll-over relief shows the proceeds not reinvested. Chapters sixteen and seventeen built it.

The corporate interest restriction follows its statutory steps. Aggregate net tax-interest expense, aggregate tax E B I T D A, which means tax earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, thirty per cent of it, the debt cap, the interest capacity, the disallowance, and its allocation. Chapter twenty eight built it.

A controlled foreign company is attacked in order, company by company. Is it a controlled foreign company at all? Does an exemption apply? If so, stop. Which gateway lets profits through? Then the twenty five per cent test, apportionment, creditable tax and the charge. Chapter twenty six built it.

Double tax relief goes in columns by source, with deductions allocated and the credit limited to the lower of the foreign tax and the United Kingdom tax on that income. Chapter twenty four built it.

Deferred tax separates fixed asset differences from short-term differences, shows the opening and closing balances and the movement, and ends with the total tax charge. Chapter six built it.

Group relief across non-coterminous periods is a time line. Each overlapping period has its surrenderable amount, the claimant's available profits, and relief at the lower figure. Chapter fifteen built it.

Then one rule that cuts across all of them. Keep one unit in each table. Pounds, or thousands of pounds, never both. The examiners raised it after the May twenty twenty six group question. Take a computation you already know, Tarnmoor Engineering's for Group Year Two in our invented case. Total profits are twenty six million pounds. Group relief takes away seventeen point oh nine five million. Taxable total profits are eight point nine oh five million, and the corporation tax is two million, two hundred and twenty six thousand, two hundred and fifty pounds. In thousands that last figure has a decimal. That is fine. Switching units halfway down the table is not. The reading edition shows both versions side by side.

Every one of these layouts can be typed as a simple table in the answer box, or built in the spreadsheet and pasted. Practise both, and choose the one you can do fastest without losing the labels.

What the examiners keep saying.

Read seven sets of examiners' reports, from May twenty twenty three to May twenty twenty six, and nine messages come back again and again.

One. Answer the requirement asked. Time spent on excluded or unrelated topics earns nothing.

Two. Do not restate the question, and do not pad with general detail.

Three. Bank the easy marks on each question. Over-running for the last marks rarely pays.

Four. Show your workings. Marks are available even when the final figure is wrong.

Five. Use a conventional capital allowances layout.

Six. Give a recommendation when one is asked for.

Seven. Use the supplied treaty extract, not the O E C D Model, when an extract is given.

Eight. Tax consequences means every tax in the syllabus. A named tax means only that tax.

Nine. Keep pounds and thousands of pounds consistent.

Behind those messages sit the topic traps, and the Exam lens boxes in this book have collected them. A handful deserve repeating, because they have cost candidates marks at more than one sitting.

Roll-over relief is chargeable on the proceeds not reinvested, not on the gain. Short lease status is judged on the unexpired term at the date of the transaction, and an assignment is not a grant. Indexation cannot create or increase a loss, and a capital loss is never set against income. A no gain, no loss transfer passes on the transferor's cost, not market value.

On controlled foreign companies, the twenty five per cent apportionment threshold is not the control test, and once one exemption applies you stop. After May twenty twenty six, the examiners also criticised answers for not mentioning obvious points, such as how the controlled foreign company legislation works. Two lines on how the charge works and who pays it are almost free marks.

On the interest restriction, a transfer pricing adjustment to interest reduces the net tax-interest expense but not tax E B I T D A, and a disallowance never changes tax E B I T D A.

On depreciatory transactions and value shifting, the November twenty twenty four examiners put it crisply. Depreciatory transactions do not consider motive and only apply to losses. Value shifting is motive based.

On marginal relief, the examiners after May twenty twenty six warned that whilst the marginal rate of tax between the thresholds is twenty six point five per cent, this is not the rate that should be applied in full.

On double tax relief, after November twenty twenty five, they reported that nearly all candidates failed to realise that the royalties can be treated as one source and the foreign tax credits aggregated.

And on the compliance questions, which are among the most common on this paper, the traps are counting. Count associated companies on the right day. Apply the large group enquiry rules to a member of a large group. Use the accounts for the year ending in the parent's financial year for the tax strategy thresholds. Test the senior accounting officer rules on companies incorporated in the United Kingdom, whatever their residence.

Learning from the papers.

The Institute publishes, for each sitting, the question paper, suggested answers with a marking guide, and the examiners' report. From May twenty twenty four it has also published example candidate scripts, banded by mark, from forty to fifty, through fifty to sixty and sixty to seventy, to over seventy. They are the most useful study material you will find. Read a script that scraped a pass next to one that scored over seventy on the same question. The difference is rarely knowledge. It is usually coverage, precision and layout.

The papers also tell you what the examiners like to set. Across the seven papers from May twenty twenty three to May twenty twenty six, every sitting had a corporation tax computation of fifteen or twenty marks, often ending in instalments and a current and deferred tax charge. Capital allowances appeared standalone or inside nearly every computation. Property gains, leases and group roll-over came five times. The shareholding exemption and reorganisations came five times. Groups and consortia six times. International questions on residence, permanent establishments, the branch exemption or migration have come at every sitting since November twenty twenty four. Controlled foreign companies four times, including two full twenty-mark questions. Transfer pricing five times. The interest restriction four times. Compliance and governance eight times.

They also have favourite combinations, and this book was built to mirror them. A computation with capital allowances, losses, instalments and deferred tax. Transfer pricing with the interest restriction. A permanent establishment with the branch exemption, incorporation of the branch and a controlled foreign company. A property disposal with roll-over, the fixtures election, capital allowances and stamp duty land tax. The sale of a subsidiary with the degrouping charge, the shareholding exemption, the change of ownership rules and an enquiry. Chapter thirty one, on the Ridgeway deal, showed the method for a question that touches many regimes at once.

Some core topics have not been examined between twenty twenty three and twenty twenty six. Demergers, transactions in securities, liquidations, the corporate criminal offence and the general anti-abuse rule among them. Do not read silence as safety. A core topic can be set at any sitting.

Around the paper sits the Joint Programme. You must pass the Professional Responsibilities and Ethics exam before you sit an Advanced Technical paper. The Tax Knowledge and Skills paper must come before, or at the same sitting, and the Institute recommends sitting it first. A pass on the Advanced Technical paper is valid for seven sessions. If you fail the specialist paper, the programme lets you switch to another specialist paper on the same route, subject to your employer.

The pass rates are encouraging. They ran from fifty nine to seventy four per cent across the seven sittings, and the May twenty twenty six figure was the highest, at seventy four. After May twenty twenty four the chief examiner reported that Joint Programme candidates had the highest pass rates. That is reassurance, not a promise. Individual questions, such as the controlled foreign company apportionment in May twenty twenty five, have been answered poorly.

Two things to watch before your sitting. As at October twenty twenty six, the Institute had published no twenty twenty seven grid and no twenty twenty seven tax tables. When they appear, check every grade this book relies on, and check the rates. And from May twenty twenty eight the qualification changes. This paper continues, with four to six questions. The interest restriction, hybrids and intangible assets fall to non-core, and gains on leases leave the syllabus. A new learning outcome asks candidates to critically evaluate and communicate the output of information generated by other parties or by Artificial Intelligence. None of that applies to a twenty twenty seven sitting. It does show where the profession is heading.

What to take away.

The paper is three and a half hours, normally six questions of ten, fifteen or twenty marks, usually three twenties, two fifteens and one ten. One hundred marks, a pass mark of fifty, and at least seventy per cent of the corporation tax element from core topics. Scenarios are listed groups with no controlling individual. The style is technical prose and computations, never a letter.

Your likely sitting is the fourth of May, twenty twenty seven, at half past two, with the twenty sixth of October as the fallback. Arrive early. No watches. Bring a physical calculator. The note paper is not marked.

On R M Assessment Master, calculations left in the spreadsheet and not copied to the answer box will not be marked, and the examiners cannot see formulae. Copy every working across, with labels. The timer flashes ten minutes before the end, and that is the only warning.

The resources are the tax tables, the O E C D Model as an on-screen P D F, and Croner-i or Tolley legislation with tags but no notes. A supplied treaty extract beats the Model. The twenty twenty six tables show eighteen per cent. The law for your sitting is fourteen.

Budget two point one minutes a mark. Forty two minutes for twenty marks, thirty one and a half for fifteen, twenty one for ten. Halfway is a quarter past four. Bank the easy marks, then move on.

Read the requirement first. Calculate, explain, discuss, recommend. Tax consequences means every tax, a named tax means that tax alone. Excluded means excluded.

Marks come in halves and wholes, so write many short, precise points, each with its authority. Show workings, because a wrong answer with visible working still scores. State any assumption and carry on.

Use the conventional layouts, and one unit per table.

So what does this paper reward? Not what you know, but what you show. The right rule, applied to these facts, laid out where the marker can see it, inside the time.

Next, the conclusion steps back from the exam and from Tarnmoor, and asks what the whole of the larger company's tax system adds up to.


Conclusion.

The book began with one loan and two answers. A company called L L C Five borrowed about four billion dollars from its own group. Transfer pricing asked whether strangers would have lent on those terms, and said yes. The unallowable purpose rule asked why the company borrowed, and took every pound of the deductions away. The Court of Appeal decided it in twenty twenty four, and the Supreme Court refused permission to go further.

Thirty two chapters later, that case looks less like a puzzle and more like a summary. A larger company lives under several rules at once, each asking its own question. The adviser's job is to know which questions are being asked, and to ask them all.

This conclusion does four things. It answers the four questions the book set out with. It revisits the debates the book has carried. It looks at what is coming, separating what is law from what is only proposed. And it asks what a large group's tax function will look like in the years after your exam. The law it describes is the law for the financial year twenty twenty six, and the facts about what is coming are as they stood on the ninth of October, twenty twenty six, when this book was finished.

One taxpayer or many.
